en: The Annotated Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra: A Definitive Edition of the Explication of the Meaning, Volume One.
Compiled by the Yunqi Master Gudé and his disciple Cifan Zhìyuàn. Definitive Edition.

Regarding the meaning of the title: Opening the scroll, the eight characters beginning with "The Buddha Spoke" (*buddha-bhāṣita*) constitute the title of the Dharma; the twelve characters beginning with "For those of later learning" (*paścāt-śikṣamāṇa*) constitute the title of the person.

Below the title of the Dharma, I shall provide a detailed explanation. Now, prior to entering the text, it is appropriate to briefly state the general outline according to the title. Regarding... [the title]... approximately... [the following].

There are four pairs: first, the pair of the general and the specific; "general" refers to the single character *jing* (sūtra), while "specific" refers to the five characters beginning with "Buddha-spoken" (*fo-shuo*).

Second, the pair of the agent and the object; the "agent" is that which expresses, namely the character *jing*, while the "object" is that which is expressed, namely the aforementioned five characters.
Third, the pair of teaching and principle; the Buddha’s spoken sūtra is the teaching, while Amitābha is the principle. Fourth...
The pair of person and dharma: the Buddha is the person, and Amitābha is the dharma.
Regarding the word "Buddha" (Śakyamuni): he descended from Tuṣita Heaven to be born in the royal palace as Prince Siddhārtha;
after leaving home and practicing austerities for six years, he attained equal and perfect enlightenment. If one explains its meaning, the word "Buddha" is [as follows].
In Sanskrit, this is translated as "the Awakened One" (*buddha*). It refers to one who has fully realized the nature and characteristics of phenomena, possessing three meanings:

first, self-awakening, which is the realization that one's own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing; second, awakening others, which is the realization that all dharmas are none other than suchness;

and third, perfect awakening, where these two types of awakening are complete in principle and thus termed "perfect. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, it likewise manifests three meanings: the first is the initial...

1. Awakening (*bodhi*) is the wisdom that realizes. 2. Original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is the principle realized. 3. Ultimate awakening (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*) is the merging of wisdom and principle, where the beginning and the original are non-dual.
The "Buddha" mentioned in this sutra refers to Śākyamuni Bhagavān, in whom all three forms of awakening are perfected.
Furthermore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains that there are ten meanings of "Buddha," while Tiantai speaks of the "six stages of realization" (*liu ji*) and Huayan of the "ten bodies" (*shi shen*).
The details are fully provided in the subsequent text. As for "exposition" (*deśanā*):

it is named after its function of proclaiming and unfolding [the Dharma], and its meaning is that of thorough elucidation and gladdening. Its essence consists of the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).

"Thorough elucidation" refers to the full manifestation of the Tathāgata’s fundamental resolve for world-transcendence; "gladdening" refers to the joy felt by sentient beings upon attaining benefit. Now, because the Tathāgata has long practiced and long...

Having realized the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance and harbored it within his breast, whenever he encountered a suitable opportunity, he would expound it using the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
Thus, he fulfilled his original aspiration and enabled others to obtain benefit according to their respective capacities; hence, it is called "preaching."
Amitābha is a Sanskrit term; in this [language], it is translated as "Immeasurable. This is because his merit, wisdom, physical marks, and radiance are all entirely immeasurable.
When this Immeasurable Buddha was formerly in the stage of causes, he was the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
He made forty-eight vows; he now dwells in the Western Quarter, gathering those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and leading them back to the Pure Land.
Therefore, Śākyamuni Tathāgata proclaimed this for the sake of the multitudes.

Regarding the term "sūtra" (經), there are many interpretations, yet they do not exceed the four meanings subsumed by the principle of "permanence" (常). "Permanent" means that which does not change throughout the three periods of time;

because all Buddhas speak thus, it is called permanent. "Dharma" (法) refers to the common track of the ten realms; because the four types of noble beings and the six classes of ordinary beings attain liberation through it, it is called Dharma.
"Piercing" (貫) means to thread together the meanings that ought to be known. If there were no words and letters, [these meanings could not be conveyed].

It is called "penetrating" (*guan*) because it pierces through principles and meanings so that they may be clearly observed. It is called "gathering" (*she*) because it gathers and sustains all sentient beings;
for without words, one could not enlighten beings and enable them to emerge from the sea of birth and death.
As an excellent model for the thousand petals [of the lotus] and a constant norm for the hundred spirits, it elucidates the truth and benefits all things; thus it is designated as a *sūtra*.
Furthermore, this sutra was translated during the Tang dynasty as the *Sutra on the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha’s Acceptance*.
The present title is used because people delight in hearing the name "Buddha," and because when one speaks of the "Buddha," all meritorious virtues are thereby encompassed.

"Commentary" (*shu*) means "to loosen" (*shu*) and "to penetrate" (*tong*). This refers to the fact that the principles and meanings within the sutras are exceedingly profound and subtle, making them difficult to fathom;
thus, one uses the commentary to loosen and penetrate them, so that no doubts or obstructions remain. It also carries the sense of "organizing the principles. An ancient saying goes:
"A person has hair, which they comb and groom every morning; the body has a mind—why not do the same? Now, this work organizes the profundities within the sutras.
The *Li* (Principle) enables people to open and penetrate the ground of the mind.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) means to abridge; it follows the original commentary (*shu*) while adding brief explanations, so that the subtle meanings of the sutra and its commentary may be made as clear as ice melting away.
"Scroll" (*juan*) carries the meaning of "rolling up and containing. Within a single fascicle, there are contained inexhaustible principles and immeasurable Dharma-gates.
Regarding the title "Learner" (*xue-zhe*): it means "to emulate. Those who awaken later must necessarily emulate what those who have already awakened have done; therefore, the ancients...

There are those who, after attaining great enlightenment, remain in the stage of a student for the rest of their lives; the Great Master’s self-designation as a "junior scholar" (houxue) is also based on this principle.
"Guhang" (Ancient Hangzhou): in antiquity it was called Hangzhou; during the Southern Song dynasty, when the capital was established there, it was renamed Lin’an.

Its current name, Hangzhou, represents a restoration to its ancient title. "Yunqi" is the name of a temple located at the foot of Wuyun Mountain. Previously, it was situated upon the summit of the mountain.
Five-colored auspicious clouds swirled above it, and for this reason the mountain was named [Mount] Wuyun (Five Clouds).

Subsequently, five clouds gathered and settled within a valley to the west of the mountain, remaining there for a long time without dispersing. People of the time marveled at this and called the place Yunqi Ou (Cloud Dwelling Valley).

During the Song dynasty, Chan Master Zhifeng built a temple there, naming it Yunqi Temple. Over the years, it fell into ruin and neglect. The Great Master, appreciating its seclusion and tranquility, [chose it as his dwelling].
He sat cross-legged among them, and people of the time built a hall for him; thus the monastery was restored. "Śramaṇa" is translated here as "diligent rest":

one diligently cultivates precepts, concentration, and wisdom, while resting and extinguishing greed, hatred, and delusion. There are four distinct types: the Superior Path (jina-mārga), the Explanatory Path (deśanā-mārga), the Sustaining Path (jīvita-mārga), and the Defiled Path (malina-mārga).
"Superior" refers to Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the like; "Explanatory" refers to those who preach the True Dharma; "Sustaining" refers to those who practice...
Regarding "those of virtuous character": "defiled" refers to those who engage in various heterodox practices. "Zhu Hong" was his dharma name; he was styled Lianchi.
A native of Renhe, he received the tonsure under the monk Xingtian and traveled extensively to consult various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). Under Xiaoyan, he attained a profound realization.

He subsequently thatched a hut in a deep valley to advocate for the Pure Land. Having reached fifty years of monastic seniority and eighty years of worldly age, his karmic conditions for transformation were exhausted;
he passed away while reciting the Buddha’s name. Regarding the term "narrator" (*shuozhe*): it means one who transmits and narrates. The *Music Record* (*Yueji*) states:

"One who understands the inner essence of ritual and music can create them; one who recognizes the outward forms of ritual and music can transmit them. The creator is called a sage (*sheng*); the narrator is called a worthy (*xian*). This scripture...
Although several ancient commentaries have circulated in the world, their wording, while incisive, is too concise; their principles are faintly revealed rather than fully manifest.

This present sub-commentary synthesizes the traditions of Tiantai and Xianshou, unifying the two schools of Nature and Characteristics (*xingxiang*). It fuses phenomena and principle (*shili*) and brings both doctrine and exposition to full clarity.
It articulates what the former sages wished to express but could not, and unveils what previous worthies had left unspoken; it may truly be called a unique creation for all time.
The term "narrative" (*shu*) used here is a humble expression. Regarding the "classification" (*ke-fen*):

within the classification, the general preface explaining the overall meaning contains two senses. First, it provides a general preface to clarify the intent of the entire sutra in order to praise its nature.
Second, it serves as a detailed exposition of the self-nature Amitābha and the pure land of the mind-only, intended for practice and cultivation.
This is the fundamental basis. Thereafter, one relies on this understanding to initiate practice, upholding the Name and seeking rebirth through aspiration.

Even those of dull faculties can achieve rebirth by solely relying on the phenomenal aspect and single-mindedly upholding the Name. Thus, it universally benefits all three types of faculties, encompassing both the superior and the inferior.
To establish the final expedient means of the Dharma-ending age constitutes the general purport of this sutra. Second, regarding the general introduction and the general meaning of the commentary:

first, by expressing one’s intent in response to the times; second, through these two sections, it clarifies that this single sutra integrates both phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*), and is fully endowed with both nature and characteristics (*svabhāva* and *lakṣaṇa*).

Yet, the people of the time cling to either nature or characteristics, each remaining stuck in one extreme. Consequently, the vast Dharma-gate has been left in confusion and remains unrecognized. Therefore—
I have exhausted my thoughts over many years, repeatedly wearing through the leather-bound bamboo slips [of the scriptures] to compose this sub-commentary (*śū-cāo*).

"Opening the chapters" refers to the separate opening of topical sections; this refers to the general initiation of the ten gates. "Explaining the text" refers to the analytical interpretation of the scriptural passages;
this refers to the specific explanation of the meaning of the text. Although the general purport is clear, the original text remains unelaborated; therefore, the chapters are separately opened.
Section: Explaining the scriptural text so that the profound meaning of this sutra is fully and exhaustively detailed, ensuring that every person understands it.
Regarding the summary and explanation of the meaning of the mantra: while the mantra itself is inherently unexplainable, its meaning can be explained.

The meaning of the mantra is to uproot the seeds of karma and be reborn in the Pure Land. Although this mantra was originally not attached to the sutra, it is now concluded here and explained accordingly.
The commentary clarifies that this Dharma-gate of the Pure Land manifests the perfect interfusion of the Exoteric and Esoteric, and the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle.
Furthermore, it reveals that this practice of Nianfo by holding the name is a great divine mantra, a great illuminating mantra, and a supreme, unequaled mantra.

Regarding the three divisions of the Prologue, the Main Body, and the Circulation: Dharma Master Dao’an of the Jin dynasty categorized the teachings of one lifetime transmitted to the East into these three parts.
The "Prologue" (xu) refers to the beginning or thread;

just as a silkworm’s cocoon can yield all its silk once the thread is found, so too can the intent of an entire sutra be understood once its prologue is grasped. Furthermore, the "Prologue" is like the eastern and western walls [of a house].

Just as by examining the arrangement of a wall one knows the depth and shallowness of the hall’s inner sanctum, so by examining the introductory preface one clarifies the wondrous meaning of the entire scripture.

Regarding the "Orthodox Canon" (Zhengzong): this refers to the primary tenet upheld by a single scripture. For example, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, it is that there is only the One Vehicle Dharma, neither two nor three;
in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it is the elucidation of the eternally abiding true mind and the exclusive cultivation of the Samādhi of Perfect Illumination. This...

The purity of the environment and its inhabitants (*dharmatā* and *sattva*) as described in the Sūtra is precisely this [faith and aspiration for rebirth]. The preceding introduction (*nidāna*) correctly introduces this;
the subsequent dissemination (*parīndanā*) correctly disseminates this. "Flowing" means non-abiding; "penetrating" means being unobstructed.
To cause this wondrous Dharma to reach from this realm to other realms, and from the present to the future, without any hindrance—this is called "flowing."
The "General Preface" (Tongxu) follows the "Introductory Section" (Xunfen): by penetrating the core of the sutra, one first grasps the beginning of the means for transcending the mundane;
thus, following the text into contemplation, one comes to know where the Great Way ultimately leads. Therefore, the "Opening Chapter" (Kaizhang) follows the "Main Body" (Zhengzongfen):
by uprooting the seeds of karmic obstructions, one naturally flows into the ocean of purity. Thus, the "Concluding Explanation" (Jieshi) follows the "Circulation Section" (Liutongfen).

Regarding the purification of karma: karma precedes suffering and follows afflictions (*kleśa*). The differences among the ten realms of existence all arise from the differences in the karma one has created.
As it is said in ancient teachings: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created will not be forgotten.

It is further said that among the Buddha’s ten powers (*daśabala*), the power of karma is most profound. And it is also said: "All lands in the ten directions are born in dependence upon the power of karma. Therefore...
Karma must not fail to be purified. "Faith" refers to being free from doubt; it means having deep conviction and no uncertainty regarding the sublime principle of the Pure Land.
"Practice" refers to tending toward its realization; it means clearly understanding the Name of Amitābha in every thought-moment.

"Vow" refers to the longing for attainment; it means directing one's heart and mind toward the World of Ultimate Bliss. These are the three provisions for the Pure Land, and they are also in accord with [the Dharma].
This accords with the great principles; by this, one is naturally able to cultivate deep patience, and thus it serves as the "Prologue" (xuán) for the provision of faith (*śraddhā*).

Those who read the sutras skillfully enter contemplation according to the text, and thus it opens the chapters for the provision of practice (*pratipatti*). Recognizing where all things ultimately converge, there is no one who does not aspire toward it, and thus it concludes with the commentary for the provision of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
First, regarding the clarification of "nature": nature is the eternally abiding true mind; its entire substance is the world of Ultimate Bliss and Amitābha Buddha.
This initial clarification is intended to prevent people from perceiving Amitābha Buddha as existing outside of their own nature.
Thus, the ancients said: "If you recognize another as the Buddha, you yourself become a demon. It is also said: "Seeking within oneself is better than seeking elsewhere. However, by means of...
Beginningless darkness and movement obstruct this quiescent clarity; therefore, by borrowing that name and title, I reveal my own mind.
Yet, while Amitābha Buddha truly exists in the Western Quarter, even this Buddha of the West does not exist outside of one's own mind.
"Phenomena are identical to principle; principle is identical to phenomena. The Great Master clarified this at the outset because he feared that the deluded and ignorant might misunderstand.
Second, regarding the praise of the sutra: the sutra is the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra) spoken by the Buddha.

It is praised because this sutra is the foremost skillful means (*upāya*) among the entire Tripitaka, and because it is what all Buddhas of the ten directions collectively extol. By these four characters— [the title of the sutra]... [text truncated]... [four characters] — [it is praised].
The Name universally accommodates the three faculties and directly penetrates the five teachings;

because by relying on the sutras and upholding [the Name], one can manifest one's own nature within a single lifetime, allowing one to ascend directly from the stage of an ordinary being to the tenth bhūmi.

Regarding the "three conditions for resonance": As for "time," it refers to the present age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*). As for "resonance," because we are currently in the period of the Final Dharma, the faculties of beings are mostly shallow and thin;

those within the Buddhist teachings are either ignorant or mad. Consequently, regarding this subtle and wondrous dharma-gate, some roll up their sleeves to dismiss it as a minor teaching (*hīnayāna*), while others laugh loudly to denounce it as a provisional vehicle (*upāya-yāna*).
Furthermore, some spend their days merely moving their prayer beads, or exhaust their years...
One merely counts the yellow beans. The Great Master’s compassionate heart was so profound; how could one not be moved to sorrow on his behalf? Fourth, regarding the "Explanation of the Intent":

"Intent" refers to the intention behind the Great Master’s composition of the commentary (*śāstra*). "Explanation" (*shu*) means to set forth. This differs slightly from the previous explanation of the character *shu*. The Great Master’s fundamental purpose lay entirely in benefiting both [self and others]. He wished to inspire true faith in sentient beings; therefore, he... [extremely]... (Note:

The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a commentary on a Buddhist text, likely concerning the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* or a similar work given the mention of "counting yellow beans" and the "Great Master" [Nanyue Huairang]).)

This is the discussion of the vast merit of mindfulness of the Buddha. Indeed, wishing to use a single phrase of Amitābha to universally lead all sentient beings out of the ocean of suffering—how could one not be loquacious?
Regarding the "five requests for empowerment": "empowerment" refers to the supportive protection (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Three Jewels; "requesting" means to pray or entreat.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all those who compose writings dedicate them to the Three Jewels, silently hoping for their supportive protection.

This is because the mental power of a single individual is limited, whereas the Buddha possesses great compassion for all beings without distinction (*apratihata-mahāmaitrī*). Thus, he can cause those who pray with sincere devotion to spontaneously attain superior wisdom. Therefore...
Please add [the following] as the general preface:

The two phrases "spiritual luminosity" (*lingming*) signify pure truth; the two phrases "not turbid" signify the severance of delusion. "Spiritual luminosity" refers to illumination that is penetrating and thorough;
it means this essence of illumination extends horizontally throughout the ten directions. "Profound stillness" (*zhanjì*) refers to quiescence that is eternal and constant; it means this stillness...
Its substance vertically exhausts the three periods of time; this is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as "the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading.

As for cultivation and realization, they are not non-existent; yet because it cannot be defiled, it is not turbid. Since all phenomena of floating dust are none other than the substance of wondrous enlightenment, it is not clear.
When deluded, it seems to turn away, yet this essence fundamentally does not belong to delusion, and thus there is no turning away. Upon awakening—

It appears as if there were a direction toward it, yet since this essence fundamentally does not belong to awakening, there is no direction toward it. This is precisely what the *Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* means when it says:
"All sentient beings are originally Buddhas; birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday."

"How great!"—this is a word of praise. Because it is not an illusion and does not perish, it is called the "True Substance. Even seeing is already beyond seeing; since seeing cannot reach it, what is there to contemplate?
As for the Buddhas of the three periods of time, when they arrive here their mouths hang upon the wall; what is there to discuss?
The term "it is only" (*kevalam*) is a phrase used for concluding the summary.
[Commentary: This sutra takes "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) as its central tenet. "Intrinsic nature" refers to the Buddha as the inherent virtue of sentient beings;
it is neither self nor other, neither cause nor effect. It is the very essence of the perfect and eternal Great Enlightenment. And that which this sutra discusses...
The practice of the Dharma is precisely for the purpose of manifesting this essence of awakening. This is because, by relying upon the nature of the mind, one invokes its name;
once the name is manifested, one can take that name as a support to contemplate the nature of the mind, whereby the nature of the mind easily manifests.
Furthermore, within the sutras, all phenomena—the environment and its inhabitants—are revealed to be my own mind. Infinite Light is the illumination of self-nature, and Infinite Life is...
The self-nature is quiescence; Avalokiteśvara is self-nature compassion; Mahāsthāmaprāpta is self-nature wisdom; the Śrāvaka is self-nature truth;
the Bodhisattva is self-nature conventionality; and the various adornments are self-nature’s myriad virtues and myriad practices.
If even a single hair’s breadth of a dharma were to arise from outside the mind, it could not be called the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Question: The full manifestation of one's own nature belongs to the *Avataṃsaka*. From what point below this does such [a teaching] arise?
Answer: The *Avataṃsaka* is the king of all sutras; all other sutras are its retinue. This present sutra takes the ocean of the *Avataṃsaka*'s nature as its central theme.
Since you take the *Avataṃsaka* as your primary authority, what prevents you from relying upon its nature (*dharmatā*)?

Furthermore, since the revelation and manifestation [of the truth] occurred through the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, no matter which sūtra it may be, they are all collectively wondrous and can all be said to accord with that nature.

Regarding the fact that all sutras do not depart from self-nature (*svabhāva*): the twelve divisions of the teachings of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) each and every one return to the wondrous nature;
every word fully encompasses *tathatā*. For if they were to depart from self-nature, they would all become the realm of Māra.

The spiritually awakened is not like wood or stone, which lack consciousness, nor like empty space, which is dull and insentient. To be manifest means to stand forth with one’s essence fully revealed, without obstruction or hindrance.

Those who cannot be called "spiritually awakened" possess brightness—such as the sun illuminating the day with its radiant clarity and the moon illuminating the night with its cool light—but though they have such brilliance, they do not manifest spiritual awakening. Since they do not manifest it themselves, others likewise [cannot perceive it].
It cannot be named; it illuminates without conditions and knows without deliberation—this is called "divine comprehension.
The great earth cannot discern its beginning, and even the Ultimate Sage has not exhausted its summit; thus it is called "unfathomable.

That it does not illuminate objects beneath overturned basins is because the light of the sun and moon belongs to the realm of conditioned phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas this [divine comprehension] does not belong to that realm. That its brilliance encompasses heaven and earth and penetrates metal and stone is because...
Because the light of the mind pervades the entire dharma-realm, and because all dharmas are none other than Buddha-dharma, there is nothing that it does not penetrate.

If "penetration" were contrasted with "obstruction," then penetration would merely become obstruction; it is not by opposing obstruction that one speaks of the penetration of penetration—this is true penetration.
"Untainted" means that from the beginning it has never been associated with defiled dharmas, nor has it confronted any sensory objects.

"Unwavering" means that throughout all eternity it remains as-it-is (*tathatā*), without any change or variation. It cannot be called "tranquil" because, although the great earth is eternally quiescent by nature, [it is not yet the ultimate stillness].
Yet the mountains of earth and stone are filled with impurities and lack clarity, unlike pure lapis lazuli, which is translucent both inside and out—this is called "luminous purity.
To be free from even a single thread of silk and for not even a speck of dust to remain is called "being without dregs.

That which cannot escape the kalpa of destruction is because when the three calamities arrive, the fires of the kalpa blaze forth, reducing Mount Sumeru and the seven golden mountains entirely to ashes.

Therefore, when one traces it back, it has no beginning; when one extends it forward, it has no end. This is because the self-substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is neither born at a prior limit nor extinguished at a subsequent limit;
it is ultimately eternal, constant, uninterrupted, and non-differentiated. Regarding "neither eternal nor non-eternal":
there is non-eternality outside of eternity, yet this very eternity is also not [merely] eternal. When both extremes of eternity and non-eternality are discarded, that is true eternity.

It is said that there is existence. That which does not receive even a single speck of dust is turbidity; this is "existence. Only when one is fully endowed with all phenomena can it be called existence.

Now, the self-nature is detached from all the differentiated characteristics of phenomena—namely, it is not the characteristic of existence, not the characteristic of non-existence, not the characteristic of both, not the characteristic of neither, not the characteristic of unity, not the characteristic of difference, not the characteristic of being neither one nor different, and not the characteristic of unity.
The characteristic of difference and simultaneity does not establish even a single atom as non-existent; how, then, could there be any turbidity?
To say "there is nothing" while not abandoning a single dharma is incorrect. True "nothingness" is established only when not a single atom is posited.
Now, the self-nature is replete with all meritorious virtues; that is to say, it possesses the meaning of great wisdom and luminosity, and thus shines everywhere.

Because it is the meaning of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the meaning of true and authentic cognition, the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and even the meaning of being fully satisfied without any deficiency, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It does not abandon a single dharma, nor is it non-existent. What, then, would there be to purify?
To abandon this and go elsewhere can alone be called "turning one's back. Now, without departing even a single step, precious flowers spring forth;
without leaving the courtyard, they encircle the walking trees. Though one wished to let them go, where could they possibly go? Therefore, there is no turning away.
To welcome something that has come from somewhere can only be called "orientation" (*mukha*). Now, however, there is neither going nor staying;
it comes in this way, unmoving and unarisen. It comes in this way. If one wishes to welcome it, from where could one welcome it? Therefore, there is no orientation.

Regarding the statement that "the mind encompasses both good and evil, as well as ordinary beings and sages": Mencius spoke of the goodness of human nature (*xing shan*), while Tiantai spoke of the evil of human nature (*xing e*).
One [Mencius] spoke from the perspective of phenomenal manifestation (*shi zao*), while the other [Tiantai] spoke from the perspective of the inherent perfection of principle (*li ju*).

Now, within the reality-as-it-is of emptiness (*ru shi kong zhong*), since good cannot be established, how could evil exist? The Patriarch said: "Vast and open, there is no sage; it is not even non-sage. The Sūtra says: "As for the term 'ordinary being' (*fanfu*)."
This is neither ordinary nor extraordinary. Existence and non-existence are as described above. Its nature has no prior limit, for it is not born;

its nature has no subsequent limit, for it does not perish. It is fundamentally complete from the beginning; there is no dharma that can be added, for it is not increased. Originally, not a single thing exists.

There is no dharma that can be diminished, for it is not subject to diminution. The thousandfold distinctions between defilement and purity are not one; yet their single flavor and equality are not different.
This is because all verbal expressions are merely provisional names without reality, being unattainable as they merely follow deluded thoughts.
Regarding "attaining its name based on its essence": commonly, the term "great" (mahat) is a designation used in contrast to "small. Here, however, it is not so;
it directly points to the essence of the nature (*dharmatā*) and names it "great. As for its possessing the two meanings of "permanence" (*nitya*) and "pervasiveness" (*vyāpin*):

the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "That which is called 'great' is named 'permanent. This clarifies that the essence is without change or alteration. Furthermore, it says, "That which is called 'great' has a nature as vast and expansive as empty space."
This clarifies that its essential nature is all-pervasive and beyond comparison with any phenomenon; it is the greatest in the world, such that nothing can surpass empty space.
A sutra says: "Due to delusion there is empty space; thus space has a beginning. This Dharma is without beginning. It further says:

"When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty spaces of the ten directions all vanish away; thus space has an end. This Dharma is without end. This is [the meaning of] verticality.

There is no phenomenon that can be compared to it. Furthermore, it is said: "The empty space of the ten directions arises within your own mind; it is like a single fleck of cloud appearing in the vast clarity of the sky.
While space has its limits, this Dharma has none. This means that it is universally pervasive in the horizontal dimension, such that no phenomenon can serve as a comparison.
The metaphors of gold and the moon are likewise beyond compare.
Within the three realms, all is deceptive; only this is truly real. That which is "empty" (虚) is unreal, like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent.
That which is "deceptive" (偽) is not true, like brass that resembles gold, yet is ultimately not gold. It is as they say: even Mount Tai may crumble and split apart.
The great ocean may run dry; all splendor and glory inevitably fade and decline; all kinsmen and retinues must eventually part.

Only within the True Suchness (Tathatā) of all phenomena is there ultimate reality—namely, that which "existed before heaven and earth, formless and fundamentally solitary, able to be the lord of the myriad phenomena, yet not withering with the four seasons."

"That which is not illusion does not perish. This is from the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*). The Sūtra says: "Because the illusory body perishes, the illusory mind also perishes.

Because the illusory mind perishes, the illusory objects also perish. Because the illusory objects perish, the extinction of illusion also perishes. Because the extinction of illusion perishes, that which is not illusion does not perish.
This means that this nature is devoid of change and remains eternally constant; it is not like various illusions, which ultimately vanish.
It is extinguished, yet it cannot be destroyed. This is from the *Awakening of Faith*. The treatise states: "From the very beginning, it is free from all names and characteristics;
it is ultimately equal and indestructible. This means that this nature is not destroyed when in a state of defilement, and the *dharmakāya* is not ruined, unlike [conditioned phenomena].
Conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction.
That "the myriad dharmas do not transcend the substance of the one mind" means that all myriad dharmas are the substance of my own mind;

it does not mean that there is a substance of mind existing apart from the myriad dharmas. The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states: "The True Suchness of Mind is precisely the Great Totality of the One Dharma Realm."
Regarding the essence of the dharma-gate of marks, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. It further states:
"The nature of all floating dust and illusory transformations is truly the wondrously enlightened and luminous essence. As it is said: "When things fall, they are not other than themselves;
whether horizontal or vertical, they are not mere dust. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all fully reveal the body of the Dharma King."

Regarding the statement that "the essence which encompasses both characteristic and function is called the 'essence' (*tǐ*)," the *Awakening of Faith* says: "First is the Greatness of Essence (*tǐ-dà*):

it refers to the fact that the *tathatā* of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing. Second is the Greatness of Characteristic (*xiàng-dà*): it refers to the fact that the *tathāgatagarbha* is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits.
Third is the Greatness of Function (*yòng-dà*): it is able to give rise to all mundane and supramundane causes and effects of goodness."
Therefore, now, whether in terms of characteristics or function, they all return to this essence as the true essence.

Regarding the phrase "inconceivable" and below, this first provides a combined explanation: "the path of mind and speech is cut off" means that from the very beginning, it is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental objects;
all dharmas cannot be spoken of and cannot be conceptualized, and this is called True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, regarding the section "That which is inconceivable" below, this is the subsequent analytical explanation. The Dharma is free from the perception of marks;

that is to say, that which has marks is conceivable, whereas that which is markless is difficult to conceive. As soon as you raise your mind, the afflictions arise first; this is the fault of thinking. Thinking is also merely a vain labor.

This is because such reflection is ineffective. When the mind intends to take an object but deliberation vanishes, it is because as soon as the mind is raised with the intent to take an object, thought and deliberation vanish first;
for when one contemplates true suchness (tathatā) as being without marks (animitta), the mind itself is immediately severed.

Regarding "the perfection of principle": the nature of reality is perfectly interfused and cannot be analyzed; it is like the mutual penetration of the one and the many, the reciprocal fusion of the large and the small, the intermingling of the true and the false, and the non-duality of defilement and purity.
Regarding "partiality of expression": for example, to speak of the "one" is to neglect the "many";

to speak of the "large" is to lose the "small"; to discuss the "true" is to contradict the "conventional"; and to speak of the "defiled" is to contradict the "pure. This is what is meant by the saying: "To open one's mouth is to create duality."
The "peg" (kīla) [is like] raising an eyebrow—it misses by two or three [notches]. This means that speech has gone astray; because words cannot fully express it, this is the failure of speech.
"The mouth wishes to speak but the words perish" means that as one opens the mouth wishing to speak, the words are already lost.

This refers to when the ultimate principle transcends language, leaving no room for the mouth to function. As for the "virtuous heavenly maiden," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Sovereign Heavenly King..."
There was a celestial maiden named Śubhavaktrā; from her mouth issued a single sound that corresponded perfectly with hundreds of thousands of kinds of music.
Regarding names that express the ultimate principle: if it were named "True Suchness" (*tathatā*), one could conceive of it as being non-deceptive and unchanging;

if named "Perfect Enlightenment" (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*), one could conceive of it as being fully endowed with voidness and spirit; if named "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*), one could conceive of it as being free from faults and transcending all negations.
None of these, however, are names for the ultimate principle. Now, naming it "Inconceivable" (*acintya*) is the name for the ultimate principle.
"Ultimate" is a name to which nothing can be added.
Regarding "Dharmatā" and "Buddha-nature," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Buddha" is called awakening (*bodhi*), while "Dharma" is called non-awakening.
Thus, wisdom is taken as the Buddha and principle is taken as the Dharma. Based on this, Xianshou [Zhiyan] stated that insentient things lack cognition and awareness, pointing to their...
Nature constitutes the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Sentient beings possess cognition; their nature is therefore designated as buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

Although these two natures are distinguished as belonging respectively to the sentient and the insentient, the dharma-nature can also extend to sentient beings, because sentient beings are themselves one among all dharmas.
Thus it is said: "The dharma-nature includes the category of the insentient, whereas the buddha-nature is restricted solely to sentient beings."
It does not extend to insentient things, because wood, stone, and the like lack sentience and awareness. Therefore it is said: "Buddha-nature is spoken of only within the category of sentient beings.
Furthermore, regarding that which is designated as Buddha-nature, its self-nature actually extends to both types [sentient and insentient]. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "If a person wishes..."
One realizes the principle of consciousness as true emptiness; the True Suchness within the mind extends everywhere externally. Sentient beings and insentient things share one and the same essence;

every place is identical with the True Dharma-realm. That it is stated thus here is simply because this sutra emphasizes single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth through aspiration;
it thereby uses the realm of that Buddha to manifest one's own mind, specifically pointing to the Buddha-nature of sentient beings.
Regarding the nature [of reality] as being "self-existent" (*zì*), there are two meanings: first, the "self" of spontaneity (*zìrán*); second, the "self" of the individual self (*zìjǐ*).

That which is *dharmatā*—suchness itself—is not something produced through effort; it is the wondrous nature that is innate and not attained through cultivation. When deluded, there is no loss; when awakened, there is no gain.
All things are perfectly formed and inherently abide in suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, this is the "self" of spontaneity. This is my...

The self does not belong to others. There are those among the non-Buddhists who reckon it to be spontaneous, or reckon it to be caused by conditions, or reckon it to be empty space, or reckon it to be granted by a deity;
these are manifold and beyond counting. All of these are deluded, taking the self to be a thing and being turned about by it.

They do not know that this nature originally does not descend from heaven, nor is it born from the earth, nor is it granted by a person; rather, it belongs to the person themselves and does not belong to another.
In relation to others, this is one's own self. In relation to all phenomena, it is called the fundamental mind; in relation to initial awakening, it is called fundamental enlightenment.
Knowledge without knowing is called true knowledge; awareness without consciousness is called true awareness. It is devoid of all delusion.
That which is without change or variation is called *tathatā* (Suchness).
If one follows the interpretation provided below within this very sutra, the explanation of the introductory text is now complete. Below, the various sutras are further correlated;
first, we shall correlate "light" and "life-span" according to this specific sutra. Regarding "transcending duality and fusing": light and life-span appear to be relative phenomena, yet...

In reality, to mention light is to integrate it with life-span, and to mention life-span is to integrate it with light; fundamentally they are not two separate things, so how could there be any opposition between them?
When it says "all merits" refers to the immeasurable merits of the untainted nature (*anāsrava-dharma*), it means they are complete, perfect, and inconceivable.
As for using this phrase to correspond to the two phrases "neither turbid nor clear," it is because there is only clarity and turbidity [in the conventional sense].
If there were orientation and aversion—that is, if there were duality and a lack of pervasive integration—it would not be a merit of the nature, nor would it be immeasurable.
Now, being without clarity or turbidity, orientation or aversion, all these merits are immeasurable.

That the entire body is the person themselves means that in the Sanskrit language it is called Amitābha, which here [in Chinese] is translated as Immeasurable Life and Immeasurable Light; yet its self-nature is quiescent. Thus...
This immeasurable life is the illumination of self-nature; this is immeasurable light. The non-duality of quiescence and illumination is the fusion of light and life.
Thus, is Amitābha Buddha not precisely the self-nature of the person themselves?
Furthermore, the first phrase clarifies the absence of inferiority, which corresponds to the three greatnesses (*trimahātmya*). Regarding the greatness of function (*vṛttimahātmya*):

it means that the minds of sentient beings possess boundless wondrous functions. As the *Śāstra* states: "The third is the greatness of function, because it can give rise to all worldly and world-transcending causes and effects of goodness.
Now, this numinous clarity illuminates everything; this is precisely what can give rise to all worldly and world-transcending goodness.

This refers to cause and effect. Regarding the "greatness of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇamahatva*): it means that the minds of sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and characteristics of the Tathāgata.
The *Śāstra* states: "The second is the greatness of characteristics, meaning that the Tathāgata-garbha is fully endowed with immeasurable innate merits.

Now, this profound stillness which contains all things is precisely what is meant by being fully endowed with immeasurable innate merits. Regarding the "greatness of essence" (*svabhāvamahatva*): it means that sentient beings...
The mind is the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the One Dharma-realm. The Treatise states:
"First is the greatness of essence (*tài-dà*), meaning that the *tathatā* of all phenomena is equal, without increase or decrease. Now, this numinous mind is free from dependence;

it transcends both extremes, which is precisely the undifferentiated equality of neither increasing nor decreasing. It is simultaneously three and one, where both are extinguished and both are preserved.

The essence is not the characteristics or the function; even down to the function, it is not the essence or the characteristics—this is threefold. Furthermore, apart from the essence there are no characteristics or function;

apart from the characteristics there is no essence or function, and so forth—this is oneness. When oneness is identical to the three, oneness vanishes; when the three are identical to oneness, the three vanish; thus both vanish.
Yet, when oneness is identical to the three, the three remain; when the three are identical to oneness, oneness remains; thus both remain.
Furthermore, when it exists, it is already extinguished; when it is extinguished, it is already existent. It is neither extinguished nor existent, and is thus inconceivable.
Moreover, the first phrase speaks of "illumination," which corresponds to the three virtues (tridharmakāya) below: the light of wisdom that universally illumines the dharma-realm is called *prajñā*;
being free from all defilements and attaining great sovereignty is called *vimukti*; and the essence of the mind, free from thought, is the single dharma-realm.

The "marks" (lakṣaṇa) are called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). These three types [of bodies] all possess the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; therefore, they are all referred to as "virtues.

However, there are the three virtues accomplished through cultivation on the level of the fruit, and the three virtues inherently possessed within the nature on the level of the cause. Here, it refers specifically to the three virtues inherent within the nature on the level of the cause.
Furthermore, the four dharmadhātus below are correlated with the four dharmadhātus. "Dharma" (dharma) means a norm or rule. "Dhātu" has two meanings: nature (*prakṛti*) and portion (*bhāga*).

Regarding the *vastu-dharmadhātu*, the character *dhātu* carries the meaning of "portion," because each of the various distinct phenomena—such as the form and mind of sentient beings—has its own specific limit or measure.
Regarding the *tathatā-dharmadhātu*, the character *dhātu* carries the meaning of "nature," because [it is the nature] of the form and mind of sentient beings... [and so forth].
Regarding the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle (*dharmadhātu*): although there are distinctions among phenomena, they share a single ontological nature;

thus, principle is manifested through phenomena, and phenomena are established by means of principle. This is because phenomenon and principle mutually integrate, their essential natures interpenetrating one another. Regarding the Dharma-realm of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena:

all phenomena, with their distinct boundaries and characteristics, are harmoniously integrated according to their true nature. Thus, unity and multiplicity are mutually identical, and the large and the small are interpenetrating. [The text continues with] "layers..."
Because it is profound and inexhaustible, it is inconceivable. Regarding its correspondence with the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*):

the first three dharma-realms belong to the common teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) and are thus still conceivable; the final one belongs exclusively to the distinct teaching of the Huayan One Vehicle and is therefore inconceivable.
As for its inclusion within the Perfect [Teaching]: some say that the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena belongs solely to the Huayan, yet this sutra...

How could this be possible? Therefore it is said: "Among the teachings of the One Great Vehicle, only the *Avataṃsaka* is perfectly complete (*paripūrṇa*). Being complete, it is able to encompass all;

thus there are no other sūtras that do not ultimately converge within the *Avataṃsaka*. Now, this present sūtra contains a small portion of the non-obstruction between phenomena and phenomena (*śaśva-vastu-asangha*)."
Therefore, it is possible to subsume [all teachings] within the Perfect [Teaching].
Now, regarding the general meaning of the introductory section, the reason for first clarifying "nature" (xing) is that all dharma-gates fully return to self-nature;

among the thousands of sutras, there is no other cause [for liberation]. Thus, this practice of reciting the Buddha’s name for rebirth must first clarify that the Amitābha of self-nature is the fundamental basis.
Thereafter, with single-minded devotion, invoke the Name and pray for rebirth in the Pure Land;

you will surely swiftly realize non-arising (*anutpāda*) in that jewel-adorned realm and directly enter the ranks of the sages, extensively delivering sentient beings. This means first awakening to the *dharmadhātu* of Vairocana, and subsequently cultivating the practices of Samantabhadra.
Even if one does not understand the essential nature of reality and lacks the intention to cultivate practice, should one nonetheless attain rebirth, it will only result in the lowest grade. First...
Is it not here that the intent of clarifying one's own nature lies?
[Preface] The two lines beginning with "Clarifying turbidity" first describe the method of practice. The two lines beginning with "Three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*" next praise its transcendent excellence.
As for "clarifying turbidity to achieve purity": by casting the name of the Buddha into a distracted mind, the distracted mind cannot help but become pure, just like water.

When a pure pearl is cast into turbid water, the turbid water cannot but become clear. Those who previously turned their backs and headed elsewhere have long wandered abroad, never thinking of their native land;
now they turn their spirits toward the precious realm to behold the Compassionate Honored One.
A single thought is wisdom; a brief word is the object. To transcend incalculable eons is for wisdom to be supreme; to be equal to all the sages is for the object to be wondrous.
"Yuan" (Complete) refers to the *saṃkhyeya-kalpas* (incalculable eons).

Question: When the practices of the three *saṃkhyeya-kalpas* are fulfilled, one immediately sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and attains perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Now, those who practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), even if they attain rebirth [in the Pure Land], have not yet attained Buddhahood.
Why, then, is it said that they bypass the three *saṃkhyeya-kalpas*? Answer: The present "three *saṃkhyeya-kalpas*" are defined in terms of faith and understanding (*adhimukti*).
For one who has perfected the merit of samādhi, although their practice may not yet be complete, the Dharma-body is already manifest.

Because the ultimate fruit of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* has been realized through understanding, it can also be said that they have "transcended" [the stages]. This is spoken in terms of understanding (*adhimukti*), without regard for the completion of meritorious practice.

Furthermore, "transcending the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*" is a statement of ultimate truth; it does not necessarily refer solely to understanding. It is only when the practices of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are fulfilled that one finally attains perfection.

The Buddha: This refers to the Buddha at the culmination of the fruit in the Tripiṭaka (Hīnayāna) teachings. The present sutra belongs to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching; merely attaining rebirth in the upper realms allows one to ascend to the First Ground.

Thus, the Buddha at the culmination of the fruit in this teaching is equal to those at the seventh stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching. Is this not to transcend the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas in a single thought-moment?
There are two aspects of this wondrous function. When the Tathāgata preaches the sutra, it is the wondrous function of benefiting others:

by means of these four characters, he universally draws sentient beings out of the sea of suffering—is this not supremely wondrous? When sentient beings uphold the name, it is the wondrous function of self-benefit:
by means of these four characters, they directly cause those at the stage of initial resolve to ascend to the ground of wisdom—is this not also supremely wondrous?
Commentary: Regarding "ultimate equality," the Treatise states: "All dharmas, from the very beginning, are free from all names and characteristics;
they are ultimately equal, being solely the one mind. Now, the essence of tranquil illumination has no distinction between clarity and turbidity, nor between facing toward or turning away."
This is precisely what is meant by "identical to a single flavor" and "the sole true thusness"; therefore, it is called "ultimately equal," for it is nothing other than the one mind.

Regarding the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), the preceding section clarifying the "oneness of nature" was explained from the perspective of the gate of true thusness (*tathatā-mukha*); now, this praise of the sutra is...

This is explained in terms of the gate of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). The *Śāstra* states: "Based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates: first, the gate of the suchness of mind (*citta-tathatā-mukha*);

second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind (*citta-utpāda-nirodha-mukha*). As for the suchness of mind, it is the essence of the great universal characteristic dharma-gate of the single dharma-realm (*eka-dharmadhātu-mahāsāmānya-lakṣaṇa-dharmamukha-vastu*).
As for the arising and ceasing of mind, because it relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind that arises and ceases; that which is called "non-arising" [is the suchness of mind].
It is not extinguished; it is in conjunction with arising and ceasing, being neither identical nor different. This is called the *ālaya-vijñāna*, and so forth.
This is precisely the gate of arising and ceasing.
Regarding "not knowing according to reality" and "not being aware that there is such a thing as thought," the Treatise states: "The *ālaya-vijñāna* has two meanings:
first, the meaning of awakening; second, the meaning of non-awakening. What is called the meaning of awakening refers to the essence of mind being free from thought."
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body. As for the meaning of "non-awakening," it refers to not knowing, as they truly are, that the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) is one.
Because of this non-awakening, the mind arises and possesses conceptualization. (Current Explanation: One does not know that the Dharma of True Suchness is one.

This refers to not comprehending the single flavor (ekarasa) of reality as it is. Upon attaining the vision of the nature of mind, the mind is immediately and eternally abiding; this is called "knowing according to reality" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
This very lack of such knowledge is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). When the mind gives rise to a thought, this is the "mark of karma" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). As the Treatise says:
Based on non-awakening, the movement of the mind is termed "karma. Although this involves mental movement, it is extremely subtle;
as a single phase of dependent origination where subject and object are undifferentiated, it corresponds precisely to the self-substance division (*svabhāva-bhāga*) of the ālayavijñāna.

"Enveloped by ignorance, one loses the root and flows toward the branches. Here, "ignorance" refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), which is the failure to know things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*).
"Enveloped" means that it obscures the true nature (*tathatā*). "Root" refers to the true nature; "branches" refer to the three subtleties and six coarsenesses (*tri-sūkṣma-ṣaṭ-sthūla*).
Having lost the root and flowed toward the branches, one becomes thoroughly confused regarding the true essence. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like clear water, pure and clean..."
It is thus by nature. There are those among the people of the world who take the dust of that soil and cast it into clear water;

the water loses its purity, its appearance becomes turbid, and this is called "muddiness. Then, to make it clean again, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like settling turbid water in a clean vessel;
if it remains still and deep without movement, the sand and soil will naturally sink, and the clear water will appear before you. This is called the first subduing of the guest [impurity]."
"Dust-like afflictions" refers to removing the silt so that pure water remains; this is called the "perpetual severance of fundamental ignorance.

Regarding the phrase "that which is induced by ignorance," this ignorance is itself the fundamental ignorance. "Awakening" is original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), while "dust" refers to the three subtleties and six coarsenesses.
From the arising of the "karmic mark" due to ignorance, up to the point of creating karma and receiving retribution, one gradually moves further away from the Truth.
Such awakening follows after the dust of objective realms, like a destitute son who abandons his father and flees; thus it is called "turning one's back.
To "return along the path one went" means that there is no need to seek a separate way home; by simply following the path back to the house, one immediately returns to see the father.
First, the grasping at names is destroyed, thereby emptying the attachment to a personal self (*pudgala*). Next, the characteristic of the continuous cognition is destroyed.
It sweeps away the attachment to dharmas. Next, it destroys the three subtle levels of the ālayavijñāna so that one returns to the essence of awakening;
this is what is meant by "heading toward. Regarding the phrase "cultivation and realization are not non-existent": Chan Master Nanyue Huairang visited the Sixth Patriarch.

The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? Huairang replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch said, "What kind of thing comes in such a manner? Huairang said, "To describe it as a single thing would not be correct."
The Patriarch said, "Is there still any need for cultivation and realization? [Nanyue] replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, defilement is not permitted.

Now, speaking from the perspective of a sentient being’s single lifetime of cultivation and realization, there appear to be traces of clarification and return; thus, cultivation and realization are indeed not non-existent.
Yet, in terms of its intrinsic nature, there is truly no gain or loss, nor increase or decrease; thus, defilement is simply not obtained.

There are four kinds of non-retrogression: being born in the Land of Common Dwelling because one has not yet severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes non-retrogression by vow; and the destruction of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kāma*) [constitutes non-retrogression by practice].
Birth in the Land of Expedient Means constitutes non-retrogression in practice, whereby one shatters the sands of delusion and partially breaks through ignorance.

Birth in the Land of True Reward constitutes non-retrogression in wisdom, whereby one exhaustively destroys the three delusions. Birth in the Land of Quiescent Light constitutes non-retrogression in rank. Thus, the names of these stages of non-retrogression are identical.
Yet, they are distinguished by their respective depths and shallowness.

Regarding the characters "power" (*li*) and "exertion" (*yòng*), they internally contain three meanings: first, the power of the inherent qualities of one's own nature; second, the power of the practitioner’s mindfulness;
and third, the power of Amitābha’s vows. The power of one's own nature is like a boat; the power of mindfulness is like oars and rudders; and the power of the vows is like...
Favorable winds; the three powers are complete and perfect, for one will certainly ascend to the other shore.
The Three Piṭakas refer to the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. Furthermore, there are the Buddha-piṭaka, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and the Śrāvaka-piṭaka. The twelve divisions [of scripture] refer to:

Sūtra, Geeya (Verses), Vyākaraṇa (Prophecies), Gāthā (Isolated Verses), Udāna (Spontaneous Utterances), Nidāna (Causes and Conditions), Avadāna (Parables), Itivṛttaka (Past Events), Jātaka (Birth Stories), [Veyyākaraṇa (Explanations), Abbhutadhamma (Marvelous Phenomena), and Upadeśa (Instructions)].

Regarding the Vaipulya, Adbhuta, and Upadeśa [piṭakas], as for their arising from the essential nature and characteristics: the Buddha realizes the equality of true thusness (tathatā) and its inherent qualities as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;

subsequently, he manifests the functional activity of the Reward and Transformation bodies to expound this sūtra. This is the activity of the Tathāgata, which certainly arises from the essential nature and characteristics.

Now, when sentient beings rely on the sutras to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, they may suddenly transcend and realize [enlightenment]. This is possible precisely because of the intrinsically existing True Suchness (tathatā) and the inherent nature-virtues (dharmatā-guṇa);
it is through these that such power and function arise. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] emerges from the essence and its characteristics.

To speak in accordance with the nature [of reality] refers to the *Avataṃsaka*; to speak with straightforwardness refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. As for those in whom skillful means has not yet been manifested:

it is because the *Avataṃsaka* speaks exclusively of the ocean of nature as perfectly interfused, where dependent origination is unimpeded, phenomena mutually identify and enter one another, like the layered meshes of Indra’s net.
Regarding the six characteristics, the ten mysteries, the four kinds of dharma realms, and so forth—noble ones of the two vehicles are still like the deaf and mute;

how then could ordinary beings of the final dharma age be able to cultivate and realize them? Therefore, these skillful means had not yet been fully revealed. In the Lotus Sūtra, the direct and upright teaching abandons skillful means and speaks only of the Unsurpassed Way.
It opens the gate of skillful means to reveal the true aspect; it opens the provisional to manifest the real, unifying the three and returning to the one—all of which [are not...].

The expedient means for advancing in practice are explicitly revealed; thus, there are also those where the expedients are not yet manifest. Those that are vast and expansive are difficult to maintain, such as the extensive cultivation of the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
Those that are profound and subtle are beyond comprehension, such as the direct awakening to the one mind (*ekacitta*).

Regarding "attaining the Perfect and Sudden through skillful means": invoking his name is the skillful method. To be born in the highest grade of the highest level is to ascend directly to the first stage (*bhūmi*);
how could this not be the Perfect and Sudden? It serves as a secret key to universal penetration and a divine elixir for transforming one's bones, as praised in the subsequent text.
Furthermore, "the former is the inferior" concludes these two sections. "Innate virtue" (*xingde*) and "cultivated virtue" (*xiude*) originate from the Tiantai teachings.

"Self-nature purity" (*zixing qingjing*) and "purity through the removal of defilements" (*li gou qingjing*) originate from the *Awakening of Faith*. "Purity of nature" (*xingjing*) and "exhaustion of hindrances" (*zhangjin*) originate from the *Complete Enlightenment Sutra* (*Yuánjué jīng*).

The phrase "mutually fused" (*hùróng*) encompasses all three of the aforementioned types. As for their "mutual fusion and non-duality," it means that cultivation arises entirely from nature, and cultivation is identical to nature.

There is no cultivation apart from nature, and no nature apart from cultivation. Furthermore, the traditional saying that "nature is pure and hindrances are exhausted, merging into non-duality" means that when one gives rise to cultivation based entirely upon nature, one shatters the ignorance within that very nature and severs the birth-and-death within that very nature.

Thus, throughout the entire day there is the fundamental essence, and throughout the entire day there is the practice. Nature being pure is itself the exhaustion of hindrances. When one realizes that the entirety of cultivation is identical to nature, although...
It shatters ignorance, yet there is nothing to be shattered. Although it cuts off birth and death, there is nothing to be cut off. Day after day is its function;
day after day is its essence. When obstructions are exhausted, this is the purity of nature.

Preface. Thus, when our World-Honored One "first" (*chà*) taught the Three Vehicles: the word "thus" (*gù*) serves to connect with the preceding [discussion of] the wondrous functioning of the Tathāgatagarbha.
"Our" (*wǒ*) is a term of intimacy. "First taught the Three Vehicles" refers to the Dharma spoken during the forty years following the *Avataṃsaka* and prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
"Ultimately returning to the single reality" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

This sutra sweeps away the attachment to the provisional teaching of the "burnt-out city," resolves the stagnation of the "grass hut," opens the gate of expedient means, and reveals the wondrous principle of ultimate truth. Therefore...

Regarding "bestowing precious gifts equally": it is like the sons leaving the house and being granted great chariots equally; these chariots are high and wide, adorned with various jewels, and so forth.
Regarding "further bestowing extraordinary grace":
"extraordinary grace" refers to a favor that exceeds the ordinary; because there is such supreme and wondrous [benefit] above, [the father] further bestows this special kindness.
Therefore, this sutra was further brought forth within the temporal teachings of a single lifetime. [Commentary:
"That which is not ultimate" refers to provisional means adapted to circumstances; it is not the fundamental intent of the world-transcending [Buddha]. As the sutra says:
"These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with sentient beings; entering the Mahayana is the root. For this reason, I speak this sutra. This is [the meaning].
Furthermore, regarding the fact that there are fundamentally no three vehicles, as the sutra says: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma;
there is neither a second nor a third. Regarding the provisional teaching of three vehicles, as the sutra says:
"Except for what is taught through the Buddha’s skillful means, [it is] merely by using provisional names to guide sentient beings."
Regarding "initially attaining perfect enlightenment and expounding the Great Avataṃsaka": this refers to the Tathāgata’s attainment of equal and right enlightenment at the site of Bodhi,
where, together with the Dharma-body Mahāsattvas of the forty-two stages, as well as the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings whose roots of goodness from past lives had matured—
like the moon enveloped by clouds— he preached for them the *Pūrṇa-sūtra*, the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas, which are the causal flowers that serve as adornments.
Regarding the ocean of the fruit of the One Vehicle, which is difficult for those of the Great Teaching to enter:

while Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and the various great Bodhisattvas each attained understanding and benefit, the śrāvakas of superior virtue and the bodhisattvas who had accumulated practices were as if deaf and blind, their vision blocked and their hearing severed.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata cast off his precious and magnificent Vairocana robes and donned the tattered, soiled garments of a six-foot-tall form.
He returned to the Deer Park and taught the provisional teachings of the Three Vehicles—the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās.

It was only later that he brought these provisional means back to the ultimate reality. Following the Āgamas, there were further periods of censure during the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras) and refinement through the Prajñāpāramitā.
After more than forty years, it was only at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra that he was finally able to bring them all back to the One Vehicle. "Provisional" refers to...
Third: "Reality is itself one" refers to the Great Vehicle, namely the Great White Ox Cart, which is the wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna.

This does not distinguish between those of great or small faculties; these three phrases correspond to what was previously taught upon the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment—the exposition of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

That is to say, the *Avataṃsaka* exclusively connects with those of superior faculties, while those of inferior faculties are entirely excluded. Now, however, [the teaching] extends upward from non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas down to...
For the sake of universally benefiting the ordinary people who wander aimlessly through the three faculties, this teaching does not wait for the fourfold ripening of the faculties.

In contrast to the Great Teachings, which are difficult to apply and involve five stages of instruction—meaning that in the *Lotus Sūtra* one must wait for the faculties to reach maturity before being able to return to the ultimate truth—this teaching does not require censure or the trouble of refinement; one immediately attains the Western [Pure Land].
To return to the original point:

regarding those who are promoted out of their regular order, this refers to the practice in this land where one gradually severs delusions before emerging from birth and death—much like an official who must necessarily ascend through the ranks according to formal qualifications.
However, in the present Dharma-door of Mindfulness of the Buddha, it is not necessary to sever [delusions] gradually.

Delusion. Yet, upon attaining rebirth [in the Pure Land], one immediately transcends birth and death. This is analogous to being granted a high office directly, without following the gradual sequence.
An "official by荫 (yin)" refers to one who, through cultivation in this land, completes their merit and fulfills their practice before finally achieving the fruit of sainthood;
such a person is like an official who must pass the examination on the Classics or achieve success through military service. Now, in the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance, it is not necessary...

When one's meritorious practice is perfected, by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows, one swiftly ascends to the other shore; this is analogous to being granted an official fief by one’s ancestors, thereby immediately receiving rank and emolument.

Among the various forms of gratitude for the Buddha’s kindness, this is the most extraordinary; indeed, when comparing the recollection of the Buddha to other dharma-gates, it is certainly a singular grace. And yet—
The single gate of Buddha-remembrance (*nienfo*) further comprises many varieties, such as contemplating the image, contemplating the visualization, and contemplating the true aspect (*dharmatā*).

In contemplating the image, once the image has departed, it is no longer present, resulting in interruptions. In contemplating the visualization, the mind is coarse while the object is subtle; thus, the sublime contemplation is difficult to accomplish.

Regarding the true aspect, only those of superior intelligence can fully undertake it, while those of middling or inferior capacity are unable to receive and bear its weight. Only this practice of holding the name is most simple.

It is exceedingly easy. It universally encompasses all faculties. Like a crane soaring or a great Peng bird taking flight; like a steed galloping or a dragon leaping—this is the most exceptional grace among all exceptional graces.
The Preface: Regarding the gateway of the forty-eight vows, it refers to the Bhikṣu Dharmakara, who, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja...
He made forty-eight vows. The Buddha then drew each one forth individually to point them out to sentient beings; therefore, it is said that he "pointed to the forty-eight.
For example, there is the vow that within his land there shall be no three evil realms, up to the final vow that one shall immediately attain the ultimate stage of all patiences (*kṣānti*).
As for the term "vow-gate" (*praṇidhāna-mukha*), each gate differs from the others, for this is not that.
Regarding the exposition of the sixteen contemplation methods (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-dharma*): these were proclaimed because of the request made by Vaidehī.

Since they were first established on this day, it is said that "the sixteen contemplations are opened. These begin with the contemplation of the setting sun like a suspended drum and end with the contemplation of rebirth through the three grades.
They are called "methods" (*dharma*) because each possesses its own specific rules and modes of cultivation, which are not uniform.
Regarding "returning to universal salvation": as with the four teachings and the four great vows, each has its own four aspects;
here, however, it refers exclusively to the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings. "Universal" means vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive.
"Returning" means that although there are forty-eight different types [of practices], when one considers their ultimate destination, they all without exception lead to universal salvation.

"Taking the wondrous mind as the fundamental principle": "fundamental principle" (zong) here means "master. This means that although there are sixteen different types [of contemplation], when one investigates what they fundamentally master, they are none other than the wondrous mind.

The "wondrous mind" refers to the fact that within the sixteen contemplations—whether regarding the environment (*ni*) or its inhabitants (*zheng*)—one always contemplates the realm of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) by means of the mind of the dharma-realm, thereby giving rise to the form and mind of the dharma-realm environment and inhabitants.
Commentary: Regarding the statement that "all are the perfect stillness of the single mind of emptiness, conventionality, and the Middle Way," there are two types of contemplation of phenomena:

contemplation of phenomena as events (*vastu*) and contemplation of phenomena as principle (*tattva*). As for contemplation of events: take, for instance, the contemplation of the sun. The practitioner sits facing west and contemplates the sun as it is about to set, appearing like a suspended drum.
Whether with eyes closed or open, the image of the sun appears before them; this is called contemplation of events. Contemplation of principle is further divided into two [types]. There is...

The sequence is as follows. Regarding the three contemplations performed with single-mindedness: first, one contemplates that this disk of the sun is produced through conceptualization and is entirely empty of intrinsic nature;
this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Furthermore, one contemplates that the appearance of this disk is established through causes and conditions;

thus, one does not destroy its conventional appearance—this is the contemplation of the conventional (*saṃvṛti-vipaśyanā*). Using these two contemplations as skillful means, one next contemplates that the locus of the conventional is entirely empty. This is the contemplation of emptiness.

The realm of phenomena is entirely provisional (*prajñapti*). That which is neither empty nor provisional is the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). This constitutes the sequential threefold contemplation (*krama-trisamādhi*), wherein one first contemplates emptiness, next the provisional, and finally the middle.
Regarding the threefold contemplation within a single mind (*ekacitta-trisamādhi*): the object of contemplation is simultaneously the True (*tathatā*), the Conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and the Middle;

the contemplating observation is simultaneously emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. By means of the threefold contemplation within a single mind, one contemplates the three truths as a single realm. And...
There is no object outside of contemplation; there is no contemplation outside of the object. When both object and contemplation are forgotten, there remains only the single wondrous mind.
This is the practice of contemplating the sun that is one's own mind with the mind that is the sun itself, so that the sun of the original nature may manifest before one.
This is the contemplative method of the perfect wonder of the One Mind.
Preface. "Extensive" (*guǎng*) takes the meaning of being vast and manifold, as well as broad and comprehensive.

"Vast and manifold" refers to the wondrous functions inherently present within the Tathāgata-nature, which arise in concealment and respond in secrecy without end. "Broad and comprehensive" refers to these inexhaustible vows, each of which is identical to the awakened nature (*jue-xing*) and possesses no boundaries or limits.
"Great" (*dà*) takes the meaning of vertically exhausting the past and horizontally pervading all directions. "Vertically exhausting" means that these vows exhaust...
It shall continue without cessation until the end of the future. As for "pervading horizontally," this vow fills the ten directions without limit.
