Now, by skillfully demonstrating rebirth, one truly awakens to non-arising. There are two ways to awaken to non-arising: either in this land, one achieves the single mind through principle (*li*), or...
One immediately awakens to non-arising; or, after being reborn [in the Pure Land], one sees the Buddha and hears the Dharma, thereby awakening to non-arising.
Among the paths within paths, none surpasses the recitation of the Buddha’s name. This is already a path of cultivation;

yet, through the practice of *nianfo* by holding the Name, one ascends directly to the stage of non-retrogression using only the four characters of the Great Name. The matter is not complex, yet the merit is supreme. Therefore, it is the most direct among all paths.
Direct Path. Commentary:

Regarding "thought entering non-thought," the essence of thought is fundamentally empty; it exists only because of delusion. Now, using delusion to extinguish delusion is like using poison to counteract poison.
When the illness is cured, the body returns to its natural state; when delusion is exhausted, the True is revealed. Thus, "birth attains non-birth."
Birth has no inherent substance; it takes mindfulness as its substance. If mindfulness is not empty, then birth is not empty; if mindfulness is empty, then birth is empty.
Regarding the phrase "to act as a ford and a bridge": a ford is a place for crossing over, and a bridge is a span. By means of the single phrase "Amitābha," one is transported...
To place sentient beings on this shore upon the other shore is what constitutes acting as a bridge and ferry.

Although the text following the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment contains three turns of the wheel and speaks of three aspects of great compassion, the primary intent lies in the Dharma-ending age (*mappō*).
This can be known from the two characters "Dharma-ending" in the title.
Commentary: Regarding the statement that "at twenty thousand years, one enters the kalpa-turbidity": this is because prior to twenty thousand years, afflictions were slight and false views were few;
the multitudes of humans and devas flourished, while those in the three evil realms were rare, and lifespans were long. Thus, the time had not yet become turbid.
Regarding the statement that "when Śākyamuni appeared, human life was one hundred years": this refers to the ninth *kalpa* (aeon) within the current abiding kalpa (*sthiti-kalpa*).
In the *antarakalpa* (minor kalpa), four Buddhas appear. At the beginning of the kalpa, when the human lifespan is eighty thousand years, it decreases to sixty thousand years and Kṛkī Buddha appears.
When it decreases to forty thousand years, Kanakamuni Buddha appears. When it decreases to twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appears.
When it decreases to one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appears. When it decreases to thirty years, the three minor calamities (*upadrava*) arise. This continues until—
At ten years of age, the reduction reaches its limit. Then, for every hundred years that pass, the lifespan increases by one year until it reaches eighty-four thousand years;

this is when a Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel appears in the world, marking the limit of increase. After this, during the tenth minor kalpa, for every hundred years that pass, the lifespan decreases by one year.
When the lifespan has decreased to eighty thousand years, Maitreya will descend to be born. Following this, there are another nine...
One hundred and ninety-five Buddhas appeared in succession until the completion of twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*). Then, the three great calamities arose and destroyed the world.
As for the scriptures whose teachings were extinguished, they began with the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* and the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*, and ended with the [twelfth]...
The various teachings shall all be extinguished, leaving only the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* to remain in the world for a hundred years before finally vanishing.
At the time of the Dharma’s extinction, the *kāṣāya* robes will naturally turn white, and the scriptures in the treasuries will naturally lose their characters.
The sixteen *arhats* will collect all the worldly sūtras and teachings and store them within a bronze stūpa. Walking in circumambulation around the stūpa, they will sigh and say: "Śākya..."
When the Dharma of Kāśyapa perishes, this stūpa will sink down to the adamantine foundation (vajra-pṛthivī), signifying the extinction of the Dharma in the world.
The phrase "when the waters reach the heavens, the great night finally sinks" is a metaphor for the ever-deepening afflictions of sentient beings and the increasingly thick darkness of ignorance.

As it was said of old: "The clouds of delusion gather densely, obscuring the sky of the nature; the fire of consciousness burns in mutual conflict, boiling the cauldron of the mind. This is precisely what it means.

Chapter: Regarding the many gateways for entering the Way, such as the twenty-five individuals in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, each of whom expounds a skillful means for perfect penetration (*pariṣuddha-āyatana*), or the thirty-two practitioners in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, who together discourse upon the Dharma-gate of non-duality (*advaya-dvāra*), and so forth.
"Not meeting a Buddha in the world" means that Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet appeared. There are three meanings for "attaining the constant sight of the Buddha":
first, at the moment of death, the Buddha comes to welcome and guide one; second, after having been reborn [in the Pure Land], one constantly beholds Amitābha;
third, within the midst of meditative contemplation, one is able to perceive the sacred form.

Regarding the skillful means for severing delusions: in the Hinayana, one must completely sever and exhaust both the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) before emerging from the triple world.
In the Mahayana, it is only when the life-faculty is severed and the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*) has withered away that one finally emerges from birth and death.

Thus it is said: "A hair’s breadth of lingering thought is a karmic cause for the three miserable realms; a fleeting arising of emotion results in shackles for ten thousand kalpas. Now, this practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha's name) can merely suppress them.
[By] merely [reciting the name], one immediately attains rebirth.
As for those who do not cultivate other practices or skillful means—for example, in giving (*dāna*), it must be characterized by the emptiness and stillness of the three spheres;

in maintaining precepts (*śīla*), they must be neither deficient nor broken; and so on, up to being fully endowed with meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—only then can they be called *pāramitās*. Truly, these are not easy to practice. Now...
Now, when we contemplate the Buddha, he does not transcend the single mind, for all myriad practices are fully contained therein.

Those who attain liberation through expedient means rely on other dharmas for cultivation; they refine their nature over a thousand lifetimes and discipline their minds for a hundred kalpas before finally attaining liberation.
Although the Chan school speaks of attaining the Way in a single lifetime, this too requires cultivation and refinement over many kalpas, as Yongjia said: [The text continues with Yongjia’s verse].
He said: "I have long ago practiced through many kalpas; this is not a casual fabrication.
Indeed, by reciting the name of Amitābha now, one will swiftly ascend to the other shore."

Commentary: Regarding the term "Dharma-gate" (dharmaparyāya): that which guides and gives rise to understanding is called "Dharma"; that through which noble wisdom universally traverses is called a "gate.

As for the phrase "the essence of the Way is profound and subtle": the Way has no form or appearance, no location or direction; it cannot be approached or settled upon, nor can it be grasped through deliberation.

This is as stated in the *Analects*: "The higher one looks up at it, the higher it seems; the harder one drills into it, the more solid it proves. One gazes for it to be before one, yet suddenly it is behind. This is precisely what is meant.
Regarding "entering through the gate": the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "Suddenly one is granted a magnificent mansion by the Heavenly King; one must enter through the gate.
The *Analects* says, "If one does not find the gate and enter, one will not see the beauty of the ancestral temple nor the abundance of the hundred officials."
To use skillful means to guide others so that they may enter the gate: this gate pervades all places; one may enter it at every turn and take refuge in every dharma. As the ancients said:
"At every place there are green willows where one can tether the horse; in every house there is a road leading to Chang'an. Yet sentient beings do not know this;
wherever they encounter him, they pass by him at every turn. This is what is meant by the path being rugged and difficult to traverse.

"Vast as before, difficult to sustain; profound and deep, beyond comprehension," and so forth. "Winding and difficult to reach" refers to the accumulation of practices through the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* and diligent cultivation over vast eons.
Regarding Vaidehī’s universal observation and her vow to be reborn in Sukhāvatī, the World-Honored One emitted light from the crown of his head, illuminating the worlds of the ten directions;
he then withdrew that precious light and condensed it into a golden platform, within which the ten [directions] were universally manifested.
He caused Vaidehī to observe the Buddha-lands in their entirety; yet Vaidehī alone aspired to be born in Sukhāvatī.

Regarding the Samādhi of True Suchness (Tathatā), there is both correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) and skillful means (*upāya*). Correct contemplation is the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-lakṣaṇa-eka*), wherein all phenomena are equal and non-dual.
As for skillful means, it refers to the investigation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), wherein neither form nor mind can ultimately be [found].
Yes. If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one immediately attains compliance with and entry into the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding the two gates of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight): *śamatha* refers to the cessation of all marks of objective realms; it involves two factors: detachment from objects and the elimination of the mind. *Vipaśyanā*... [text continues]

This refers to the four practices: discerning the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, the characteristic of existing phenomena (*dharmas*), great compassion, and great vows.

These are the dharmas that point toward the cultivation of the five gates, namely: first, giving; second, precepts; third, patience; fourth, diligence; and fifth, calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).
Those who are beginners in these dharmas refer to sentient beings of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) whose cultivation of faith is not yet complete. As for their...
The mind is timid and weak; thus, while the inner mind is already inferior, one does not constantly encounter a Buddha in this Sahā world, and so lacks the external superior conditions.
Therefore, the practice of faith is difficult to accomplish, and one is on the verge of regressing. There are four kinds of faith:

first, faith in the root, which means delighting in mindfulness of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma; second, faith that the Buddha possesses immeasurable merit, and constantly mindful of drawing near to him.
First, making offerings and showing reverence, one generates roots of goodness because of the aspiration for all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Second, having faith that the Dharma brings great benefit, one constantly recollects and practices the various *pāramitās*.

Third, having faith that the Saṃgha is able to practice correctly for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others, one always delights in drawing near to the assembly of Bodhisattvas in order to seek and learn their authentic practice. As for "approaching": [the text continues].

This is the accomplishment; that is, the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith. The Treatise states: "Regarding the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith, what kind of mind is aroused?
Briefly stated, there are three types: first, the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it correctly contemplates the dharma of *tathatā*;

second, the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because it delights in practicing all virtuous deeds; third, the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-citta*), because it desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings."
Regarding the "difficulties": this refers to the practice of the stage of faith, which requires ten thousand kalpas before it is finally accomplished;

thereafter, there is never any regression. This is categorized into three types: first, like a lotus flower that has not yet opened, when the practice of faith is not yet complete, one is not yet called "non-regressive," but because one dwells in a state free from conditions for regression, one is termed "non-regressive. Second, once the stage of faith is fulfilled and beyond, the flower opens.

Upon seeing the Buddha, one enters the stage of the ten abidings (*daśavihāra*) and attains a partial vision of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), thereby abiding in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Third, when the stage of the three types of worthies (*trayaḥ pṛthagjanāḥ*) is fulfilled, one enters from the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) onward, realizing the all-pervading Dharma-body and being born in boundless Buddha-lands.
As the Buddha prophesied for Nāgārjuna and others, those abiding in the first ground are born in pure lands. In this sutra, these correspond to the two phrases concerning the seven days.
He cites the original sūtra as evidence. Regarding the fact that the original sūtra is cited as evidence within all four sections of the text:
this clarifies that the division of these four types is not based on mere conjecture.
Regarding the statement that one attains liberation only when delusions are exhausted: if afflictions of thought (*sahakleśa*) are not exhausted, one does not transcend the Triple Realm;

if delusions as numerous as dust motes are not exhausted, one does not transcend the realm of the Two Vehicles; and if ignorance (*avidyā*) is not exhausted, one does not transcend the realm of the Bodhisattvas. As for those who are born with delusions remaining:

according to the *Contemplation Sūtra*, those of the highest grade of birth have severed the delusions of ignorance; those of the middle and upper grades have severed the delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-sahakleśa*).

Regarding those who produce [the aspiration] at the middle or lower levels: those at the beginning have severed the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). As for the three grades of the lower class, they have not yet severed any delusions at all;

rather, they are merely able to slightly suppress their delusions and achieve a pure body, whereby they are born in that land. Therefore, it is said that they "attain birth while still carrying delusions."

Regarding the six perfections and the myriad practices, there are differences in both phenomena and principle between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. Furthermore, within the principle, there are varying degrees of depth, as elucidated in Tiantai’s Four Teachings.
As for the statement that "the myriad practices are fully present within a single mind," this single mind itself is also divided into phenomena and principle.
If it refers to the single mind of principle being fully endowed with the myriad practices, there is no need to discuss it further; however, as for the single mind of phenomena, although...
Although one has not yet entered into the ultimate principle, regarding the six perfections and the myriad practices within the teachings of the Tripitaka, it may also be said that they are complete.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, "offenses" (*āpatti*) are themselves "obstructions" (*āvaraṇa*); because offenses can obstruct the Path, they are further termed "obstructions.

As for the fact that these [offenses] are extinguished through this recollection of the Buddha, it is because that Buddha possesses inconceivable power of majestic virtue and the power of inconceivable great vows.
Therefore, this mindfulness of Amitābha is itself the Great Prajñāpāramitā; it is like a person who falls to the ground and rises from that very ground again.
This is one proof of attaining liberation swiftly. In the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra*, it is said that one dies here and is born there.
All this is due to desire. Because the Western [Pure Land] is free from desire, one transcends birth and death instantaneously; these are two proofs that liberation is swiftly attained.
For those who exert the power of diligence to listen to this Dharma-gate, there are three ways of listening: listening with the ears, listening with the mind, and listening with the spirit.
The inferior person listens with the ears, like the wind passing by the ear. The middling person listens with the mind and is somewhat able to understand the meaning. The superior...

The spirit of the practitioner listens. One who deeply awakens to the true nature (*dharmatā*) now speaks of listening to the Dharma with diligence; this is not listening with a conditioned mind (*nimitta-citta*), but listening with the spirit.
Regarding "the ant on the mountain" and "the wind and water," the *Lianzong baojian* states: "Pursuing the Way through other gates is like an ant climbing a high mountain;
rebirth through the recitation of the Buddha's name is like a wind-blown sail sailing upon a following current."

Chapter: Stirring and Elevating the Ordinary Beings of Birth and Death. To be born and then to die, and to die and then to be born—through ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there is no end.

Therefore, they are called "ordinary beings of birth and death. "Stirring" (ji) means to incite, causing people to give rise to weariness with the world. "Elevating" (yang) means to drum forth and uplift, causing people to give rise to joy.
Regarding "those who are submerged and deluded in their own nature": "deluded" (mi) means to be in a state of confusion; "submerged" (chen) refers to the extreme of such delusion.
Furthermore, "intrinsic nature" refers to the Dharma-gate of equality mentioned in the commentary. Due to the initial single thought of ignorance, the six coarsenesses and three subtleties arise;
consequently, the mind loses its true nature and acts in inversion, transmigrating within this cycle and taking up its own flow and turning.

Regarding the manifestation of the two lands of suffering and bliss: this refers to the Pure Land and the realm of suffering, gold and jewels versus silt and sand, the lotus pond versus the womb-prison, and the jade tree versus the thorn forest.
This is truly because the mind is divided between defilement and purity, leading to the perception of the ascent and descent of these two lands.
Regarding the opening of the two gates of *śamatha* (calming) and *vipaśyanā* (insight): sentient beings are deeply attached to Saṃsāra, and thus the Buddha [responds accordingly].
He speaks of the sufferings of the Sahā world to subdue them; since sentient beings are unaware of the Pure Land, the Buddha speaks extensively of the bliss of the Pure Land to gather them in.
Thus, within the single practice of *nien-fo*, both methods of subduing and gathering are fully contained.

The "superior mind" refers to a courageous mind and a mind of diligence. That pure karma fails to achieve accomplishment is entirely due to being lax and indifferent, such that the mind lacks vigor and sharpness.
If one can truly exert effort for even a single day, giving rise to great courage and great diligence, there will be no practice that does not reach fulfillment.
Therefore it is said: "Once the superior mind has been aroused, pure karma is thereby accomplished."

Commentary: "The deluded mind pursues objects" means that one does not know the fundamental emptiness of the mind; from beginning to end, it arises and ceases in every thought-moment—this is called a deluded mind.
Not recognizing the fundamental stillness of objects, one follows after the six sense-objects and creates karma in response to them—this is called pursuing objects.
Regarding "the field frog and the well minnow," *Zhuangzi* says: "A field frog cannot be spoken of in terms of the ocean."
They are confined to a dilapidated well. The *I Ching*, in the hexagram of the Well (*Jing*), states in its line-text: "The well-valley shoots at a minnow; what benefit does this bring to the task?

This means that if one were like the great Peng or the golden-winged Garuda, striking the wind for ninety thousand *li* and agitating the waters for three thousand *li*, one might reasonably expect them to soar to the heavens.

But as for a field frog or a well minnow—what is the use of holding them accountable? If it were someone of superior capacity and sharp intelligence, whose mind roams beyond the mundane realm, [then such expectations would be appropriate].
Those who tread upon the Great Way may be taught to directly awaken to their own minds; what use is there in teaching ordinary beings caught in the cycle of birth and death?

Regarding those who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): "non-arising" refers to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); not even the slightest phenomenon arises, nor does the slightest phenomenon cease.

Therefore, it is called "non-arising. As for "patience" (*kṣānti*), this refers to the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣāntijñāna*). By means of the wisdom of initial awakening, one accords with the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

it is clearly understood within the mind, yet cannot be expressed. It is like a person who endures a matter: neither harboring it nor releasing it. This is termed "the patience of non-arising" (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*).

Section: Those of the Two Vehicles who cling to emptiness. There are two types of practitioners of the Two Vehicles: those who cultivate only the primary contemplation (samyag-darśana) merely recollect emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;

and those who also cultivate auxiliary contemplations, who mostly enter the state of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) by means of the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti). Therefore, they all cling to emptiness.
Furthermore, many śrāvakas, having reached the stage of cessation within the Four Noble Truths, rest there and do not advance further, thereby becoming entangled in emptiness.

As for the species of those who follow the path of the Pratyekabuddhas (Pratyekajinas), they generally establish nirvana within the clarity of their awakening and do not proceed further; thus, they produce the seeds of non-transformation.

Consequently, many who cling to emptiness and do not cultivate the Pure Land claim to have already attained nirvana, and furthermore, they feel weary of and seek to escape conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).

Regarding those who have just attained the realization of the emptiness of persons: there are four kinds of emptiness. First, the emptiness of persons; second, the emptiness of phenomena; third, the emptiness of emptiness; and fourth, the emptiness of even that emptiness of emptiness.
At present, one has merely attained the first—the emptiness of persons. As for those who immediately give rise to attachment and stagnation:
this refers to sinking into emptiness and lingering in quiescence, falling into the pit of the unconditioned, and drinking the wine of samādhi.

Regarding the purification of Buddha-lands and the transformation of sentient beings, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "When Bodhisattvas take up pure lands, it is entirely for the benefit of all sentient beings.
The *Ratnakūṭa* further clarifies: "Know, O son of noble family, that a straightforward mind is the pure land of a Bodhisattva;
when that Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who are free from deceit will come to be born in his land. A profound mind is the pure land of a Bodhisattva..."
When one attains Buddhahood, sentient beings endowed with merit come to be born in that land.

As for those whose minds do not find joy in the six perfections, the myriad practices, and so forth—it was because they were previously attached to existence that they underwent saṃsāra; now, having realized the emptiness of persons, their saṃsāra has momentarily ceased.
Yet, they relish the bliss of a biased emptiness, namely nirvāṇa. Upon hearing it said that Bodhisattvas extensively practice the myriad deeds to purify the Buddha-land...
They are born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Naturally, they do not give rise to even a single thought of attachment or delight.

*Commentary:* However, those who realize that there is no self (*anātman*) within the aggregates (*skandha*), yet do not know that the aggregates themselves are also empty, [are incomplete]. There are two kinds of emptiness:

first, the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which refers to the absence of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span; this is what is realized by the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Second, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which refers to the absence of...
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are what the bodhisattva realizes. Now, within these aggregates (skandhas), there is no self;

this is the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The aggregates themselves are also empty; this is the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). In the Hīnayāna, one contemplates the body as impure, sensation as suffering, the mind as impermanent, and phenomena as non-self;
thus, one awakens to the absence of self within the aggregates. However, when one clearly perceives that the five aggregates are all empty, [this is the realization of the bodhisattva].
This is the realm of the great Bodhisattvas; therefore, they do not know it.

Furthermore, that which is empty is such because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are by their very nature unarisen and thus without cessation, being originally in *nirvāṇa*. As stated below, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is cited as proof.
The phrase "the ancients say" introduces ancient sayings as evidence. Regarding the statement that there is no teaching of other Buddhas:

the followers of the Hīnayāna know only of Śākyamuni and do not know of the Buddhas of the ten directions. This sentence is an elliptical reference to the Mahāyāna teaching that there are Buddhas in other lands.

Regarding the discourse on the ocean of lands, such as in the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," there are world-systems numbering as many as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields.
Within each individual world-system, there are twenty layers of inexhaustible worlds.
This phrasing implicitly excludes the Hīnayāna, which knows only the existence of the Sahā world.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess compassion based on three conditions, four kinds of wisdom, nirvana, the five practices, and the four unconditioned vows;
therefore, their [compassion] is vast and inexhaustible. Because the mind is the object, it is not obstructed by objects; because the object is the mind, it is not obstructed by the mind.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The seeing, the objects of seeing, and the perceived characteristics are like flowers in the sky;

they have never existed from the beginning. Therefore, it is said that their fundamental nature is inherently empty. All dharmas do not transcend the two categories of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
Now, sentient beings are the dharma of form, while saving them is the dharma of mind. Since all things are inherently empty, is this not saving sentient beings all day long? All day long...
"Without measure. Thus one knows that these two characters run directly through to the end of "no measure throughout the day. Within this, there are two sections.
The four lines concerning the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas correspond to the preceding passage on being born by transformation in the Pure Land.

The six lines concerning "the mind does not delight in [objects]" and "the mind is not obstructed by objects" correspond to the preceding passage on grasping at objects as real and desiring only to avoid them for the sake of seeking quiescence; this is, for the most part, the fundamental malady of the Hīnayāna.

These two lines—“merely realizing that there is no self within the aggregates, yet not knowing that the aggregates themselves are empty”—mean that because one has only realized the absence of self within the aggregates, one considers only what has been realized to be ultimate.
Consequently, one does not further recognize the wondrous efficacy of the Mahāyāna;

upon hearing of rebirth by transformation in the Pure Land, one’s own mind feels no joy. Today, having turned the mind back [to the Dharma], one finally understands the wondrous efficacy of the Mahāyāna, as follows:

This is vast; it is thus inexhaustible. Because one does not know that the aggregates (*skandha*) are also empty, one fails to realize that all sensory phenomena are illusory transformations, arising in their own place and ceasing in their own place.
Consequently, one clings to objects as being real, desiring only to avoid the world and seek tranquility.
Today, having turned the mind back [to the source], one realizes that fundamentally they do not obstruct one another; in their very essence, they are entirely empty. Thus, one transcends...
There is no limit.
Chapter. Bodhisattvas at the initial stage of mind differ according to the four teachings.

Those of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, as well as those of the Distinct Teaching prior to the first bhūmi, and those of the Perfect Teaching prior to the first abode—all are included. Why is this? Because of the *Amitābha Sūtra* (the *Contemplation Sūtra*), which is of the highest grade.

Only upon reaching the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) does one ascend to the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*). This "first ground" is equivalent to the first *vihāra* (abiding) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).
Thus, this Bodhisattva at the initial mind—prior to the distinct and perfect stages and abidings—is something that can be clearly visualized by oneself.

Furthermore, according to the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, those in the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), fearing that the faculty of faith is difficult to establish, should seek rebirth in the Pure Land; once the faculty of faith is accomplished, it constitutes the fulfillment of faith.
The arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) refers to the simultaneous and perfect arousal of the three minds; this is precisely the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).

Thus, it can be further inferred that this bodhisattva of the initial resolve encompasses all stages prior to the distinct and perfect grounds. Since the distinct and perfect teachings are thus, the *āgama* and *śrāvaka* vehicles are even more evident by comparison.
Although the great resolve has been established, the bodhisattva who has newly aroused the mind seeks the fruit of Buddhahood above and transforms beings below.
Sentient beings differ from those of the Two Vehicles in that they do not seek the Buddha-way and do not teach sentient beings. Regarding "the supreme patience not yet perfected":

supreme patience refers to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Bodhisattvas at the initial stage have not yet eliminated their afflictions (*kleśa*) nor shattered their ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because they have not yet realized the principle of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma*), the "group of those fixed in rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*) refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). This is because the inhabitants of that land all possess the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and are non-retrogressive.

However, if one discusses the severing of afflictions (*kleśa-prahāṇa*), then only those who have generated the mind through the fulfillment of faith (*adhimukti-cittotpāda*) are said to have entered the group of those fixed in rightness. In that land...
This refers specifically to those who attain the highest birth in the highest grade. The phrase "realizing the state of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is an inverted expression.
This is because there are three types of *dharma-kṣānti*: first, the patience of resonance (*ghoṣānugā-kṣānti*); second, the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*);
and third, the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Here, it is said that the patience realized is precisely that of non-arising.

Furthermore, regarding the six types of complacency: if one does not seek rebirth in the Pure Land but instead wishes to deliver sentient beings from the sea of suffering, one must take heed of the cautionary examples of Śāriputra and others.
As for "self-satisfaction," a bodhisattva at the initial stage of mind will inevitably have some attainment;
often, they become self-satisfied with what they have attained. This is just as when a person of the Perfect Teaching reaches the fulfillment of the ten stages of faith.
There still remains the malady of falling from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). This shows that the two characters "self-sufficiency" (*zizu*) are the root of the illness of the beginner.
Therefore, these are specifically pointed out.

[Note: The three citations from the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (or *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) within the commentary, from "the ordinary person bound by self-attachment" (*zijubuo fanfu*) to "falling from this," are provided in full.
The first section serves as a general proof and encouragement of the overall meaning of the entire text.

From "Furthermore, it is like two people rescuing those drowning" up to "is like one who has obtained a boat" constitutes the second section; this specifically proves the two phrases of the main text regarding "riding the great vessel of vows."
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "It is like an infant" (extending to) "to deliver sentient beings" constitutes the third section;
this serves as a distinct scriptural proof for the two lines: "The fledgling wings entwine the branches."
The character "bound" (bó) signifies being bound within by afflictions; it signifies being bound externally by sounds and forms.
Those who have not yet attained the power of patience are bound by sounds and forms. A Bodhisattva who has attained patience regards forms as if blind and hears sounds as if deaf.
This is what is meant by the saying of Master Pang: "Passing through a grove of a hundred flowers, not a single petal sticks to one's robes."
It is said: "If you yourself have no mind toward the myriad things, what prevents the myriad things from constantly surrounding you?
An iron ox does not fear the lion’s roar; it is just like a wooden man watching flowers and birds. But now, that is not so.
Ordinary beings lack the power to descend [to the Pure Land] on their own; thus, one must combine the two metaphors.
That is to say, if one is separated from Amitābha, one will either fall into the pits and wells of the three miserable realms or perish while thirsting for the milk of the Dharma.

Conversely, if one draws near to Amitābha and relies upon the branches of the trees in the Pure Land, one can develop the wings of non-arising and thereby fly through the void of the triple world with ease and without obstruction.

Those who have already realized the sixth stage (*bhūmi*)—according to the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*), it is only upon reaching the seventh stage that one is termed "non-retrogressive" (*avaivartika*). Since he has only now realized the sixth, he still possesses conditions for retrogression.

Consequently, upon encountering a beggar for his eyes, Śāriputra—who had generated the Mahāyāna mind during his causal phase—was prompted by Śakra, who manifested as a *brāhmaṇa*, to beg for his eyes from him.
Śāriputra gave them to him, whereupon the *brāhmaṇa* immediately cast them on the ground and stepped over them.
[The character] "tà" (to tread).
By this, one may lose the Great Resolve (*mahācitta*). Regarding those who gain benefit upon seeing signs, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states:

When Prince Mahātejas saw the Tathāgata Suprabhaśrīcakṣus attain perfect enlightenment, he obtained ten kinds of benefits, the first being the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) called the "Gate of the Boundless Ocean-Treasury."
Ultimately, one attains the light of wisdom, which is called the Pure Treasury of All Buddha-Dharmas.

If worldly people can still have their minds transformed by merely beholding the countenance of a virtuous person, how much more so when seeing the wondrous marks of a Buddha—how could they not derive benefit?

"Truly because of the following" clarifies that taking mindfulness of the Buddha as one's father has two meanings: first, the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*); second, the meaning of the biological seed. Regarding skillful means:
the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states, "The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas; skillful means is their father.
Now, to take the wondrous mind and apply it to the recitation of the Name is precisely the most supreme skillful means; therefore, it is considered the father. As for the biological seed:

This refers to the direct transmission of the true seed. Now, by recollecting that Buddha, one realizes oneself as the Buddha; by recollecting the primordial Buddha, one becomes the Buddha of the present moment.
This is precisely the direct transmission of the true seed, and is therefore called the "Father. Regarding "directly realizing truth while engaging with phenomena":

when one contemplates that the essence is fundamentally empty, then the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are themselves the truth. Thus, one can practice the recollection of the Buddha without hindrance, and engage with phenomena without obstruction. It is through this very realization of truth...
Not engaging with phenomena is a principle, not a skillful means. Engaging with phenomena without immediately realizing the truth is a conditioned dharma;
it remains separated from the unconditioned and is likewise not a skillful means. Now, to realize the truth while simultaneously engaging with phenomena—this is called a skillful means.
Furthermore, "principle" (zhen) refers to the ultimate truth, and "phenomena" (shi) refers to the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.

"Engaging with phenomena while abiding in principle" means that although one contemplates the principle, one proceeds through the various phenomena of mindfulness of the Buddha. This is precisely the contemplation of principle through successive phenomena within the three types of contemplation—contemplation based on the Dharma (*fufa*), contemplation based on entrusting to phenomena (*tuoshi*), and contemplation based on practice (*congxing*).
One who is able to adorn Buddha-lands with pure and wondrous practices knows emptiness yet does not cling to emptiness; this is called "true emptiness.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Though one knows that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, one constantly cultivates pure lands and teaches and transforms sentient beings.
This is proof of the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha and rebirth in the Pure Land at the seventh stage (*bhūmi*). One thoroughly understands that all Buddha-dharmas are merely...

"Mind-only" (*cittamātra*) means realizing that all phenomena are merely the manifestations of one's own mind. "Attaining the Patience of Accordance" (*anulomikī kṣānti*) refers to accordantly accepting and assenting to the wondrous principle of Mind-only.

These three stages of the *śaikṣa* (the Three Stages of Worthiness) correspond to the stage of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*). Upon entering the First Stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one corresponds to direct realization (*abhisamaya*).
Regarding those who were born in the First Stage, Nāgārjuna was told by the Buddha: "In the land of South India, there is one of great fame..."

The virtuous bhikṣu, whose name was Nāgārjuna, was able to shatter the tenets of existence and non-existence. He manifested my Unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma within the world and attained the first stage, the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).
Having attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), he was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

Regarding those who attained the patience of non-arising and were reborn there, the *Bodhisattva-janma-bhūmi-sūtra* states: "At that time, Mādhavamaṇḍala attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas, as did five hundred faithful lay followers."
The men and women all attained the stage of non-retrogression; at the end of their lives, they were reborn together in the Land of the Buddha Amitāyus.

The above constitutes the testimony of those who, having reached the Three Sages and the First Bhūmi, attained rebirth there. As for figures such as Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, they are Bodhisattvas of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
One also desires to be reborn there. As stated in a verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"One who thoroughly realizes that one’s own mind is not without transformation and rebirth. The treatise says:

"If one contemplates the Tathatā-Dharmakāya of that Buddha and constantly and diligently practices, one will ultimately attain rebirth and enter the state of right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma*). If you awaken to this mind, ten thousand oxen cannot pull you back.

This refers to the practitioner who has awakened the mind. Such a person knows that the Pure Land is solely the mind; those who are born in the Pure Land are not born in a land external to themselves, but are born within their own minds.
Although it is said that even one who has attained clear understanding is still far from the Buddha, the ancients have said:

"Though sudden awakening is identical to that of the Buddha, the habitual tendencies of many lifetimes remain deep. When the wind ceases, the waves still surge; when the principle manifests, delusive thoughts still intrude. It is further said: "Recognize the ice..."

This water still relies on the steam of boiling water to melt away its impurities. To awaken from delusion and realize the truth, one must likewise rely upon the Buddha’s wisdom for refinement and tempering.

*Commentary:* Regarding "ceasing to see and cutting off hearing," Qingliang (Zongmi) said: "It is so high it cannot be looked up at; even Bodhisattvas who have accumulated practices for eons would expose their gills [in despair] before it."
The scales [of those] at the Dragon Gate are deep and cannot be fathomed. When those of superior virtue hear of the auspicious assembly, they close their eyes and ears to it.
Those who now release their gills and dry them in the sun are like the fish at the Three Stages of the Yu Gate; those who cannot leap over them return with their gills exposed.
The constant Dharma is precisely to settle offenses according to the Vinaya without disturbing the mind.

This means one should speak directly of the inherent emptiness of the nature of offenses, which do not exist within, without, or in between. Regarding the comparison to the light of a firefly, the *Song of Realizing the Way* says:
There were two bhikṣus who had committed the offenses of sexual misconduct and killing; Upāli’s accumulation of karmic fetters was like the glow of a firefly.
The Great Being Vimalakīrti suddenly dispelled their doubts, just as the blazing sun melts frost and snow. This is it.

Regarding the practice of impurity-counting breath: Śāriputra instructed two disciples, one to cultivate the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and the other to cultivate the meditation on counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).

After a long time, neither achieved success, and their minds desired to return to secular life. They went to see the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One asked the two what their occupations had been when they were laypeople.
The one who practiced counting the breath replied, "I tended graves. The one who practiced impurity replied, "I worked in metal foundries."

The Honored One then instructed the two individuals to practice by shifting their perspectives. Before long, both attained the fruits of the Way. Regarding the "three minds," these are as described in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*:
first, the mind of utmost sincerity; second, the profound mind; and third, the mind of dedication and aspiration.

It is called "perfect" (*yuan*) because it is perfect and sudden, lacking any gradual stages; furthermore, it is perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*) because it lacks the distinction between self and other; and again, it is perfect...
"Full," because it is without deficiency; this refers to the person of perfect integration (*yuanren*). One awakens the mind by means of these three dharmas of perfect interfusion.

It should be understood that the arousal of these three minds constitutes the cause; this is the stage prior to being born in the Pure Land, occurring within the stage of the ten faiths (*shixin*) of the Perfect Teaching.

Direct entry into the non-arising of phenomena is the fruit; it is the event that occurs when one has already been born in the Pure Land, and it is the event that occurs when one realizes the first stage of the Perfect [Bodhisattva Path].

Regarding "direct entry into the non-arising through the perfect arousal of the three minds," this means that for one who is able to perfectly arouse the three minds, at the very moment of being born in the Pure Land, they directly enter the non-arising of phenomena.

Regarding the "ten recitations" (*daśa-smṛti*), there have traditionally been two interpretations. The first maintains that simply calling the name with a sincere mind ten times constitutes the ten recitations.
The second maintains that the number of phrases is irrelevant; rather, exhausting a single breath constitutes one recitation, and exhausting ten breaths constitutes ten recitations.
Furthermore, there are those who practice the ten recitations only at the moment of death, such as Zhang Shanhe; there are also those who practice the ten recitations throughout their entire lives.
The Dharma Master Zhixian was such a person. Success in practice may also be explained in terms of both phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*).

If one merely attains the accomplishment of the power of faith and is able to somewhat subdue delusions, this is success in phenomena. If one possesses great capacity and attains the accomplishment of the power of contemplation, being able to swiftly shatter delusions, this is success in principle.
For the most part, it is simply this single practice that, according to one's capacity and its application, leads to these results.
The mind can be divided into nine grades. Furthermore, one should know that this phrase refers to the cause, while the subsequent phrase—attaining birth in that land—is the fruit.
Moreover, one should know that those who achieve these ten recitations all possess great roots of goodness from past lives, or have habitually practiced meditative contemplation in the present life;
therefore, by exerting effort at once, they suddenly sever the afflictions of worldly toil. If their faculties...
If one's faculties are somewhat inferior, or if one lacks a fundamentally virtuous nature, one must not seek such luck while neglecting the exclusive recitation of the Name.
The five desires, the three poisons, and immeasurable afflictions are the dull fetters; the partial vehicles, external paths, and all views are diseases.

Regarding the "driving forces" (*anuśaya*): those who have exclusively severed the delusions of views through the [Hinayana] vehicles do not call them "driving forces," yet they are still afflictions.
For example, in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the "seeds that entangle emptiness" and the "untransformed perfect seeds"—are these not afflictions of view?

As for "Great Generation" and "Broad Generation," the *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes* says: "As for Qian, when it is still, it is focused; when it moves, it is direct. Therefore, it is Great."
Thus life arises. Now, as for Kun (Earth): when it is still, it contracts; when it moves, it expands. Therefore, it gives birth extensively. "Chapter":
When right mindfulness is clear and distinct, this corresponds to the two modes of upholding—phenomena and principle—in the subsequent text.

Generally speaking, for those of dull faculties, hearing the Buddha’s name, they should constantly recollect and constantly keep it in mind, using the mind to trace each syllable with clarity, so that the preceding phrase and the succeeding phrase continue in succession.

Without interruption—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—one dwells solely in this single thought-moment, with no second thought. This is what is meant by clear and distinct right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

For those of sharp faculties, upon hearing the Buddha’s name, they do not merely recollect it; rather, as soon as they think of it, they turn back to reflect, examining and scrutinizing its very source until the root is fully investigated.
When this investigation reaches its ultimate limit, there is a sudden accord with one's own fundamental mind. This is what is meant by the clarity of right mindfulness.
It was clear. This lucid mindfulness was precisely that which did not falter from right view;
it was precisely the power and majesty of his vows; it was precisely within the great radiance; it was precisely reaching the site of enlightenment.

Who could disturb him? A precious mirror repels demons. One may relate the matter of Wangdu: Wangdu hung the precious mirror upon a tree, and the tree was immediately struck by thunder. A great serpent...
He died beneath a tree. Furthermore, he used a mirror to look at a woman; the woman immediately begged for the mirror, vowing to die after becoming intoxicated.
After she had fallen asleep on her bed in a state of intoxication, she was revealed to be a dead fox.

Commentary: "Zen" (chan) refers to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); "contemplation" (guan) refers to visualization. Here, they are combined as "zen-contemplation" (*changuan*), which serves as the general name for all *samādhis*.
If distinguished individually, there are worldly *dhyāna*, world-transcending *dhyāna*, and the supreme world-transcending *dhyāna*.

As for contemplation, there are the contemplation of analyzing emptiness (*khaṇḍa-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the contemplation of realizing emptiness (*dharmatā-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), the three successive contemplations, and the single-mind threefold contemplation.

Regarding "contemplation" and so forth: the "aggregates" (skandhas) refer to the five aggregates. "Māra" refers to the Māras; this is translated as "the slayer," because they can slay the practitioner's wisdom-life of the Dharma-body.
As for these māras of the aggregates, according to what is taught in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, they are not outside of the celestial māras, the mental māras, and the view-māras.

There are three aspects: "striking" refers to striking and shaking; "arising" refers to manifesting. Sentient beings possess these aggregates (*skandhas*), and thus they possess these demons (*māras*).

Because they do not cultivate contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), [the demons] remain hidden and do not manifest. Now that they have cultivated dhyāna and are about to break through these aggregates, they strike and shake the various demons, and the demons consequently appear.
That which is easily recognized and easily dispelled refers to the clarity of right mindfulness; this is the illumination of *prajñā*-wisdom.
"Recognition" means that wisdom is able to discern, and "dispelling" means that wisdom is able to destroy. As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"There may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness and are thus deluded and disturbed by various māras, non-Buddhists, ghosts, and spirits. While they are sitting in meditation, these beings may manifest forms to terrify them, or..."
When appearances such as handsome men and women manifest, one should contemplate that these are merely mind; then the objective realm will cease, and they will ultimately not cause affliction.
Furthermore, the methods for discerning and dispelling [delusions] are fully explained within the *Tiantai Zhiguan*; examine those teachings and know them for yourself.
That wisdom shines with such brilliant clarity that Māra finds no opportunity is truly due to the distinctness of right mindfulness;
this is the foremost method for dispelling Māra. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If the host is deluded, the guest gains the advantage.
If one dwells in *dhyāna* and awakens without confusion, then those demonic affairs can do nothing to you. You are like boiling water, while they are like solid ice. [Warmth...]"
His vital energy gradually declined, and he passed away within a few days.
[Zhang] said: "The mind is fundamentally without thought; this mind is the true mind, while thought is deluded thought. Within the true mind, there is fundamentally no deluded thought.
To give rise to thoughts to recite the Buddha's name—is this not, in fact, to act in opposition to that mind?"
"Using poison to counteract poison; using military force to stop military force" means that the thoughts of delusive conceptualization can harm my Dharma-body and wound my life of wisdom;

these are the poisons and the weapons. Furthermore, the thoughts of reciting the Buddha’s name—which arise and perish moment by moment and have not yet accorded with *prajñā* (wisdom)—are likewise poisons and weapons.
Yet, without the poison of reciting the Buddha’s name, one cannot counteract the poison of delusive conceptualization. It is not...

The army of mindfulness of the Buddha cannot subdue the army of delusive thoughts; for although both are equally delusive thoughts, they are fundamentally different in that one is distracted while the other is focused, and one is pure while the other is defiled.

Regarding the healing of illness and the pacification of bandits: it is like the dismissal of deluded thoughts; therein, the delusive is itself the real. There is no seeking of a "true mind" apart from deluded thoughts.
Yongjia said: "The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body."
Commentary: Regarding "the essence of mind is free from thought," the *Awakening of Faith* states: "What is called the meaning of awakening refers to the essence of mind being free from thought.
This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is all-pervading, and this single characteristic of the Dharma-realm is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharmakāya."

As for "recollection of the Buddha through the true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-buddhānusmṛti*), one must be free from all marks before it can be called the true mark; this is precisely what is meant by "direct mind and right mindfulness of True Suchness" (*tathatā*).

Regarding the state where coarse thoughts have temporarily ceased but subtle thoughts still persist, this is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as "internally maintaining a state of profound stillness," which is [still considered a form of attachment].
These are but reflected images arising from the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

Furthermore, although the luminous clarity of awareness is empty and still, and the coarse and heavy shadows of external objects no longer exist, the root-source of birth and death remains like a shimmering mirage, flickering and turbid. As the Patriarch said:

"One who sits atop a hundred-foot pole, though they have gained entry, has not yet reached the truth. One must advance further from the top of that hundred-foot pole; throughout the ten directions of the world..."

When the entire body manifests within the realms (*dhātu*), one who takes this as their object of contemplation and advances in cultivation is what the ancients called "one who employs troops skillfully need not separately brandish weapons;
they simply use the enemy to attack the enemy and use thieves to kill the thieves. This is also termed "returning home by way of the very path."
Regarding the statement that "reciting the name of one Buddha replaces those hundreds of thousands of miscellaneous thoughts": miscellaneous thoughts arise from the six sense objects;
if one is detached from these objects, they cease to exist. When every thought grasps at conditions and every mind fails to abide, this is a thought that deviates from the Truth (*tathatā*).

Although the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is likewise illusory, because it arises from faith and focuses single-mindedly on a single object, it is a thought that approaches the Truth. As the ancients said: "It is like using honey..."
"Result" refers to this very bitter gourd.
As for "the false arising from the true," it means that although mindfulness of the Buddha is a fabrication, there is no fabrication apart from the truth; thus, the false arises from the true.
It is like waves following the arising of water. There are two meanings to "mindfulness is itself emptiness": first, when mindfulness reaches its ultimate limit, it becomes empty;
that is, at the peak of mental application, mindfulness falls away. Second, the essence of mindfulness is fundamentally empty;

thus, though one recites the Buddha's name all day long, there is no mindfulness throughout the entire day. Furthermore, the fundamental essence itself has two meanings: first, the sense of reversing delusion to return to the truth.

This means that when delusion is exhausted to its end, the truth is revealed. Second is the principle of "total delusion and total truth," which refers to the observation that appearances are fundamentally delusive and the nature is fundamentally true.
However, within these two phrases, both meanings emphasize the former sense.
This is because the title of the original text specifically indicates that by attaining entry into non-thought, one realizes the state beyond thought.
That "the myriad dharmas are false and illusory, and there is only the one mind" means that all objective realms exist solely because the mind arises delusively;
if the mind is free from deluded movement, then all objective realms cease, leaving only the true mind, which is omnipresent.
Regarding "Awakening at every touch": every single thing is it; every phenomenon is true. Clearly manifest is the tip of the hundred grasses;
clearly manifest is the meaning of the Patriarch. As Dongpo said: "The sound of the stream is entirely the broad and long tongue; the color of the mountains is nothing other than the pure body."
Section: Manifesting Signs. "Manifesting signs" is like the crowing of a rooster at dawn; looking toward the east, one already perceives a subtle radiance.

As for being "merely named" in the seventh stage: although signless contemplation has been accomplished in this stage and discriminative cognition has been abandoned, manifest consciousness has not yet ceased, and one has not yet attained great mastery over all forms; therefore, one merely attains the manifestation of signs.

Regarding the attainment [of this realization] at the eighth stage: because in this stage the manifest consciousness has already ceased, one enters into all phenomena as being of the nature of empty space.
One enters into all phenomena as being originally unborn, without arising, and without marks; the initial, middle, and final limits are all entirely equal.
The sphere entered by non-conceptual suchness-wisdom is called the true attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Those who urgently desire to extinguish arising and seek non-arising have it said by the ancients: "Among great afflictions, none is greater than having a body;

therefore, one extinguishes the body to return to non-existence. Among diligent labors, none precedes having wisdom; therefore, one dissolves wisdom to merge into the void. To enter existence and yet attain...
Regarding the transformation of the ordinary into the sage through emptiness: to seek birth in the Pure Land is to enter existence; to realize non-arising is to attain emptiness.
Entering existence makes one an ordinary person; attaining emptiness brings about the fruit of sagehood.
Commentary: Regarding "purifying the immeasurable body, speech, and mind":
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage, by means of their profoundly pure mind, accomplish physical karma, accomplish verbal karma, and accomplish mental karma.
They have completely abandoned all unwholesome paths of action censured by the Tathāgata, and because they constantly and skillfully practice all wholesome deeds praised by the Tathāgata.
The meaning is roughly the same as this. The Tiantai teachings state that one attains non-arising (*anutpāda*) at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

Qingliang states that from the first ground onward, one merely attains the manifestation of the light of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), yet this is not yet considered the true attainment.
Thus, when Tiantai says that one attains it at the first stage, he is referring to the attainment of the light of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.

Regarding "being free from all conceptualization of mind, intellect, and consciousness": "discriminating" (*vijñāna*) refers to the sixth [consciousness]; "deliberating" (*manas*) refers to the seventh;
and "arising through accumulation" (*citta*) refers to the eighth. Within the eighth, however, there are three aspects: the karmic, the evolving, and the manifesting.
That which is here to be abandoned is the manifesting aspect, which is what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* calls the "manifesting-consciousness" (*khyāti-vijñāna*). Section.
As for "distinction": although these six, seven, and eight stages differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety, each possesses its own various forms of discrimination.
Now, upon reaching the eighth stage, all such discriminations are abandoned.
"Extinction that is not true extinction" refers to the extinction of annihilation; it is not the extinction of quiescent cessation (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).

The extinction of annihilation is a false extinction, whereas the extinction of quiescent cessation is true extinction. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When birth and extinction have ceased, quiescent cessation manifests before one.

This is precisely what is meant. "Ultimately resulting in cyclic existence" refers, for example, to the non-Buddhist practitioners of the Realm of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), whose power of meditative concentration lasts for five hundred kalpas.

Having passed away, he was reborn in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), where he directly slandered an Arhat. Consequently, his body underwent further existence and he fell into hell, transmigrating through the various realms of existence.
It is like a bull that destroys a cart; the bull suffers from pulling the cart and thus destroys it, only for its owner to build another.
Likewise, a person who loathes the body as suffering seeks to extinguish it quickly, yet they do not realize that although this body is destroyed, they will receive another.
Regarding the remaining body seeking birth while not deviating from non-arising, the *Song of Realizing the Way* says: "Who is without thought? Who is without birth?
If there truly is neither birth nor non-birth, call upon the wooden mechanical man and ask him: 'Seeking the Buddha through exertion, when will it be accomplished?'"
Ascending as an immortal, like Xu Xian, whose entire residence was uprooted and ascended; or like Xiao Shi, who rode a phoenix and attained transcendence.
Attaining sudden nobility, like Yu Shun, who emerged from the furrows of his fields; or like Jiao Ge, who was raised from among the fishers and salt-makers.

To abandon secret formulas and cultivate empty words is to claim that not reciting Amitābha’s name is the teaching of seeking out texts and analyzing meanings. To discard divine elixirs and take wild drugs is to claim that... [not practicing the Way].
Seeking the Pure Land is like practicing a Chan that seeks to catch the wind or grasp shadows.
Chapter: Those who travel ten thousand li away gradually sever delusions, gradually realize the truth, and gradually depart from birth and death.

Regarding the crane soaring and the Peng bird ascending: the ancients said, "Where a hundred birds cannot reach, the hawk can reach; where the hawk cannot reach, the crane can reach. Furthermore, the *Nanhua jing* says:
"In the Northern Sea there is a fish whose name is Kun. The magnitude of the Kun is such that one does not know how many thousands of li it spans.
It transforms into the Peng, which flies with a wrathful intensity. Its wings are like clouds hanging from the sky as it strikes against the whirlwind (*fú*)..."
That which rises by shaking itself ascends ninety thousand *li*, for it breathes once every six months.
A galloping horse or a soaring dragon— while ordinary horses cannot travel more than a hundred *li* in a day and even excellent steeds possess the power to chase the wind and pursue lightning—
they still cannot match the transformations, flight, and soaring of the divine dragon, which no human can fathom.

Commentary: There are many kinds of pure practices, such as the cultivation of contemplation according to the *Contemplation Sūtra* or the recitation of mantras such as the *Dhāraṇī of the Drum-Sound*.
When these are compared with the practice of holding the name, they are the direct paths; holding the name is the path within the paths.

In the principal and extensive versions of this sūtra, the reliance on the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the methods of cultivation and practice, are fully detailed. Now, by selecting and distinguishing through the practice of holding the name, it is as follows:
That is the path; holding the Name is the path within paths. As for "vertically exiting the triple world":
first one cuts off the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and only then does one exit the desire realm;

next, one cuts off the thirty-six grades of afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and only then does one leave the form realm; next, one cuts off the thirty-six grades of afflictions of the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), and only then does one transcend them.

Regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): first, one must cultivate the four fundamental dhyānas to emerge from the desire realm; next, one must cultivate the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) to depart from the form realm;

and finally, one must cultivate the absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) to transcend the formless realm. As for those who "emerge transversely," they do not sever their afflictions nor do they cultivate dhyāna;
yet, merely by attaining what is called "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekacitta*), they proceed with their afflictions still intact to be born beyond the three realms.

Regarding those who fall specifically into heavy realms: as stated previously, by the power of generosity and ethical discipline, one may become a king, a minister, or someone wealthy, noble, and autonomous;
yet, having extensively committed various transgressions, one consequently falls [into lower realms], and so forth.

Regarding the passage "The *I Ching* has no thought and no action," etc.: generally, any object that possesses a mind must necessarily have thought. Only the *I Ching* is without a mind; how could it have thought? How could it have action?
When the stalks have not yet been divided and the hexagrams have not yet been sought, the lines, divinations, images, and transformations remain hidden and leave no trace;
it is silent and unmoving. However, when it is stimulated and one divides the stalks to seek the hexagrams, it then receives the mandate.

Like an echo responding to things, it brings about their realization; it penetrates change and exhausts the ultimate numbers, thereby fully revealing the hexagrams and images, and thus thoroughly comprehends the affairs of the world.
Indeed, it is without thought yet without not thinking, without action yet without not acting. Only by reaching the ultimate divinity of the world can one act in this way.
Otherwise, if one remains in stillness, one lapses into quiescence; if one responds to stimuli, one becomes mired in them.
It is in motion. Who could be so still and yet so responsive? Its exertion is somewhat difficult;
thus it is not particularly simple, for one must practice until reaching the goal. Its duration is somewhat long;
thus it is not extremely rapid, for one must be swift to be fast. Not being delayed by years or months is to be extremely rapid—swift without even being hurried.
It is also not dependent on artificial effort; it is the ultimate simplicity, reaching the goal without traveling.

Regarding the detailed exposition of the primary and secondary environments (*niśraya* and *pratishthā*): in the *Smaller Version*, the secondary environment is like the water in a pond, and thus it merely says there are "seven-jeweled ponds with water of eight meritorious qualities.
In the *Larger Version*, however, it extensively discusses the dimensions and number of the ponds, as well as the nature of the water that follows them.

Regarding mental functions and so forth, the *Smaller Version* primarily concerns the direct retribution [of the Buddha], such as his disciples; thus it simply refers to them as "immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples.
The *Larger Version*, however, extensively discusses various superior virtuous persons, including those who expound, recite, listen to, and practice dhyāna meditation upon the sutras.
Regarding those who fully engage in practice: this refers to upholding the Name with a single mind without distraction.

As for the Great Text, it fully explains matters such as leaving home and abandoning secular life to become a śramaṇa, hanging silk banners, scattering flowers, and providing food and drink to the monastic community.

"Elaboration and brevity" are spoken of in reference to the scriptural text; "comprehensiveness and conciseness" are spoken of in reference to the gate of practice. Furthermore, there is no other teaching than this: it points directly and solely to the holding of the name.

This is precisely the honoring of the simple and the removal of the complex. Merely attaining single-mindedness, one is born in that land; this is precisely the citing of the concise to encompass the comprehensive.

Commentary: Regarding those who delight in the extensive and those who delight in the concise, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is not fixed, but accords with the capacities of sentient beings, just as a skilled physician prescribes medicine according to the specific ailment.

As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Just as a skilled physician prescribes various remedies for each and every patient, so do the Buddhas teach sentient beings according to their capacities and in accordance with their measure."
The phrasing is concise yet becomes increasingly clear. To explain by means of the text that conveys [the meaning], the matters are summarized yet become doubly superior.

To explain by pointing toward the meaning being conveyed, there is extensive discourse on various merits, with the three grades analyzed in detail; this is prolixity of phrasing. [In contrast,] merely upholding the Name and merely being born in that land is conciseness of phrasing.
This constitutes many virtues and much merit, whereby one attains non-retrogression from Bodhi in both cases; thus, the principle is even more clear.
Furthermore, to discuss various merits at length involves three grades, which is extensive in its scope. To merely hold the Name and be born in that land is concise in its practice;
yet this constitutes both great goodness and great merit, as one attains non-retrogression from Bodhi in both cases, with the latter being many times more efficacious.
Section. That the first nine are "universal" means that the preceding nine causes are common to all four types of mindfulness of the Buddha.

That the last one is "particular" means that the latter is the path within paths, being specifically the practice of holding the name. To include the general meaning of the preceding [nine] is to recognize that the entirety of the teachings throughout the various periods of the Buddha's life appeared in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition (*ekamahā-kṛtya-hetu-pratyaya*).
Commentary: "To teach sentient beings to practice mindfulness of the Buddha" means not teaching them to cultivate other practices;

this phrase refers to the preceding nine causes, which still encompass the four types of mindfulness of the Buddha. "To teach sentient beings to practice mindfulness of the Buddha by reciting the name" means not teaching them to practice mindfulness of the Buddha by visualizing the image and so forth;
this phrase refers to the final cause, which is exclusively mindfulness of the Buddha by reciting the name.

To teach sentient beings to hold the name and practice mindfulness of the Buddha so that they enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision means more than merely teaching sentient beings to practice mindfulness of the Buddha for rebirth in the Pure Land;
this phrase encompasses the previous general meaning for the purpose of entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Section. Regarding the phrase "within the division of the Piṭakas": *Piṭaka* has the sense of "containing" (*saṃgraha*), meaning it contains all objects of knowledge that ought to be known.
*Śāsana* (Teaching) has the sense of "revealing," meaning it reveals [the truth] to sentient beings so that they may attain right view.
*Bhāga* (Division) has the sense of "portion" (*vibhāga*), meaning the various numerical categories are each distinct. As for what each belongs to, the term "Piṭaka" is used...
The teachings are divided into three categories, each of which has its own distinctions. Now, within the Tripiṭaka, to which collection does it belong?
Within the teachings, to which category of teaching does it belong? And within the divisions, to which division does it belong?
Commentary: Regarding the term "Sūtra" (Kie-king) used here: it means that above, it accords with the principle of all Buddhas, and below, it accords with the capacities of sentient beings.
If it accords with the principle but does not accord with the capacity, then the Dharma does not meet the needs of the capacity; such mere words are not a Sūtra.

If it accords with the capacity but does not accord with the principle—such as the songs of woodcutters or the chants of herdsmen, or worldly speech that does not expound the wondrous principle—it is likewise not [a Sūtra].
"Sūtra" refers to the scriptures. "Vinaya" (Discipline) means the refinement of the three karmas and the subduing of transgressions and faults, so that body, speech, and mind all return to purity.
"Abhidharma" (Metaphysics) refers to two kinds of dharma: first, ultimate dharma, which is nirvāṇa; it is called "ultimate" because it is virtuous and eternal.
Second, dharma of characteristics, which encompasses the characteristics of the four noble truths; this refers to their essential nature and specific attributes.
The "counterpart" (*pratipakṣa*) also has two aspects: first, "orientation," which means being directed toward *nirvāṇa*; second, "contemplation," which refers to contemplating the four noble truths.

That which acts as the counterpart consists of untainted pure wisdom (*anāsrava-śuddha-prajñā*) along with its associated mental factors (*caitta*). Regarding the term that possesses multiple meanings:
in the *sūtras*, it is sometimes called "cord" (*sūtra*), sometimes "woven mat," "well-rope," or "holy teaching" (*āgama*). As for *abhidharma*, it is also named "subduing" (*abhibhava*).
Because it can overcome and subdue the arguments of others, it is called *abhisamaya* (penetration). Because it can thoroughly explain the scriptural texts, it is called *vyākhyāna* (explanation).
It is called *vinaya* (discipline); alternatively, it is called *śīla*, which here means "purity. It is also called *prātimokṣa*, which here means "guarantee of liberation," and so forth.
Regarding the Ten Treasury Sections that reveal the Vinaya: this is the second treasury, the Treasury of Ethics (*śīla-piṭaka*), which extensively discusses the Vinaya.
It begins with the ethics of universal benefit and concludes with the ethics of non-transgression, thereby clarifying ten types of ethical discipline.

The "Chapter on the Questions of Samantabhadra" (*Prajñāparipṛcchā-parivarta*) elucidates the nature of scholarly discourse. Ten bodhisattvas engage in mutual inquiry and response to deliberate upon the sublime principles.

Beginning with Mañjuśrī’s question regarding the various distinctions within the single mind, and Bodhiruci’s response revealing the nature of reality through the emptiness of the essence of all phenomena, the dialogue culminates with Bodhiruci’s further inquiry concerning the Buddha-realm, to which Mañjuśrī replies by means of the realm of sentient beings and the dharma-realm.
There is no separate answer.
The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* is the Mahāyāna Dharma, such as that taught in the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and so forth.
The *Śrāvakapiṭaka* is the Hīnayāna Dharma, such as that taught in the four *Āgamas* and so forth.
Commentary: Regarding those Pratyekabuddhas who do not rely on the teachings, there are two types of Pratyekabuddhas.

First, the *pratyeka-buddha* (individually enlightened one), who appears during the era of a Buddha and attains awakening by receiving the Tathāgata’s teaching on the twelve links of dependent origination. Second, the *vīta-rāga* (solitary awakened one), who appears during an era when no Buddha is present;

dwelling alone upon a solitary peak, they contemplate conditions and awaken to the Way. This refers to what is called contemplating the transformation of phenomena and thereby awakening to impermanence, or observing the withering of autumn leaves and entering [the path].
The True Path. What is indicated here is specifically the Pratyekabuddha.

Regarding "benefiting oneself and benefiting others": at the outset, one seeks birth in the Pure Land for the sake of sentient beings; in the end, having realized patience (*kṣānti*), one returns to deliver sentient beings.
Thus it is said.
Regarding the Avataṃsaka’s encompassing of immeasurable vehicles, the Preface by Qingliang states: "If the thousand gates flow secretly together, it serves as the great source for all scriptures;
