Regarding that scripture which also incorporates various teachings: in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are those who take the unimpeded and profound *dharmadhātu* as the central theme;

there are those who take dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as the central theme, because the *dharmadhātu* and dependent origination are mutually identical and interpenetrating; and there are those who take cause and effect as the central theme.

Because this sutra extensively elucidates both the causes of the bodhisattva’s stages and practices (*caryā-bhūmi*) as well as the fruits they achieve, some take the principle of the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) as its primary tenet, while others take the synthesis of the principles of cause and fruit as its tenet;

for cause and fruit constitute the stages and practices, whereas the principle constitutes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Since each of these previous views is individually incomplete, now Xianshou [Fazang] combines all these explanations.
These constitute the common thesis (*abhiprāya*) and purpose (*prayojana*).

Regarding the statement that the preceding phrase is the thesis and the subsequent phrase is the purpose: in that [other] sutra, cause-and-effect dependent origination is the thesis, while the reality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the purpose.
In this sutra, the purity of the environment and its inhabitants is the thesis, while faith, aspiration, and rebirth in the Pure Land are the purpose.

Section: A Separate Explanation. This involves successive investigation and inquiry. It is precisely where the Great Master exhaustively discusses its vast merits, providing a basis for people to give rise to true faith.
Many in the world doubt that the text and meaning of this sutra are coarse and shallow; the "Instruction and Meaning" (Jiao-yi) pair is sufficient to refute this.
Many fools cling to phenomena while remaining deluded regarding principle; the "Phenomena and Principle" (Shi-li) pair is sufficient to refute this.

The deluded often cling to principle while neglecting phenomena; the pair of "object" (境) and "practice" (行) is sufficient to refute this. Or they may doubt that the practice of nianfo (buddha-recollection) properly involves conditioned existence;
the pair of "action" (行) and "quiescence" (寂) is sufficient to refute this. Or they may doubt that nianfo cannot bring about complete liberation for oneself.
The pair of "quiescence" and "function" is sufficient to refute this.
Regarding the first point, "teaching" refers to verbal instruction, while "meaning" refers to the underlying principle. A wise person can understand immeasurable meanings within even a single word;
a fool, though they may read every volume of the *Paiśācī* script, does nothing more than trace the lines and count the characters. Therefore:
The first pair of doctrinal principles must be elucidated. Regarding the second, "phenomena and principle":
phenomena refer to the objective aspects such as the environment, the body, faith, and vows; principle refers to each of these being resolved back into one's own original nature.
Those who cling to the literal while being deluded regarding the principle do so precisely because they do not understand the underlying intent.
Regarding the "three objects and practices": the object refers to the realm of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is Amitābha Buddha; the practice is the mind of the Dharma-realm.

To single-mindedly grasp and maintain this is precisely what is called "binding the object of focus to the Dharma-realm" (xi yuan fa jie). To exclusively recite the name is the Samādhi of Single Practice (yi xing san mei).

Regarding "the four practices of stillness": "practice" refers to the practice of the single practice; "stillness" refers to the stillness of the serene light (ji guang). This is the cultivation of the Samādhi of Single Practice.
[This refers to] obscurity. It is the desire to realize the unsurpassed fruit of *sambhogakāya* (the Land of Tranquil Light).
Fifth, regarding "quiescent function": quiescence is the eternally tranquil fundamental substance (*dharmatā*), while function is the wondrous activity as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
To realize this fundamental substance and initiate wondrous function in order to deliver sentient beings—this alone is the sublime purport of the Mahāyāna.

Commentary: It is not merely a matter of words and letters. As the ancients said: "You spend your whole day reciting sutras, yet you do not realize that it is the sutras that are reciting all day long.
This is because they treat them as mere words and letters. Therefore it is said: "Reciting a thousand volumes of sutras is not equal to understanding a single verse of the sutras."

There are two meanings for manifesting the ultimate principle inherent within the phenomenal events: first, entering contemplation according to the text, whereby each point is dissolved back into oneself;
second, practicing based on the events to attain rebirth in that land, thereby illuminating the principle that self-nature is mind-only.
To do otherwise is merely to leave behind traces of worldly conditions—what is called "spending one's whole life drilling into old paper," and... [the text ends].
Regarding those who merely mutter and count their prayer beads:
they take the "object" (*viṣaya*) as their primary principle. As for the character "object" (*jing*), if one follows the explanation in the subsequent text, it designates the object of mindfulness;

that is, the four-character name is taken as the object. Thus, in this context, it should be said: the object is precisely the name being recited. And as for the word "precisely" (*ji*), it refers to...
What is the principle of this contemplation? It is simply because the four characters of the name "Amitābha Buddha" that one contemplates are, in their entirety, the Dharma-realm;
they are, in their entirety, one's own mind. And within a single thought-moment of one's own mind, the three thousand natures and characteristics are fully present.
A single thought of one's own mind is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way; is this not the principle that is the object of contemplation?
The wisdom that contemplates it is precisely the mind with which the person recites the name—vivid and unobscured, without interruption.

Regarding the statement that "it is called an object (viṣaya) because it is confronted by the wisdom that contemplates": this means that the Buddha who is the object of mindfulness is termed an "object" in relation to the mind that performs the mindfulness.
In reality, however, there is no object outside the mind, and no mind outside the object.

Furthermore, according to the principle that self-nature is mind-only, the distinction between subject and object is forgotten and absolute relativity is transcended; how then can one speak of an "object"? Therefore, it is said: "Although in principle it is not an object..."

Regarding the wisdom that contemplates, it may also be called the "object. If one intends for this very [wisdom] to be the true object, one should know that these characters are the self-nature of Mind-Only;
they are the principle that is the object of contemplation; they are the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha.
Apart from the nature of mind, there is no name or title; apart from this name and title, there is no nature of mind. It is entirely so.

To take the dharma-realm as the true object means that one initiates the contemplative practice of upholding the name by taking this name itself as the true object, thereby initiating the contemplative practice of upholding it. This is precisely "arising cultivation from the nature."

Since the nature is already beyond words, practice likewise has no abiding; though it is called "maintaining," it is in fact free from the four propositions and transcends the hundred negations—it is the mindfulness of non-mindfulness.
To forcibly suppress the deluded mind is to have concentration without wisdom, which is termed "deluded dhyāna. If one falls into non-conception, then one becomes an outsider.

Thus, although the essence of principle is quiescent, it does not preclude the arousal of practice and the upholding of names. Using illusion to cultivate illusion, and using a wedge to extract a wedge, when illusion is exhausted and awakening is perfected, one returns to true quiescence.
To now rely upon right contemplation is precisely the "upholding through principle" as described in the subsequent passage of the text.
As for "one mind," this refers to the subsequent principle of one mind. "With effort" (*sābhisamskāra*) means conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
It is contrasted with "effortless" (*anabhisamskāra*). "False conceptualization" (*parikalpita*) refers to deluded imagination; it is contrasted with "perfected reality" (*pariniṣpanna*).
This means that if one does not return to empty stillness, it is a practice characterized by conditioning and effort, which will ultimately lead to ruin and decay even after many kalpas.
Those who sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence are attached to the essence of emptiness and stillness, yet fail to give rise to the function of benefiting sentient beings;
this is the realm of the *parinirvāṇa* with remainder of the two vehicles.
Commentary: Equality is life-span; purity is radiance; awakening is the Buddha. Zhi Loujiachen and others were the five translators.
Zhi Loujiachen lived during the time of Emperor Ming of the Han. Because Guangwu had restored the dynasty, it was called the Later Han.
Emperor Ming was the son of Guangwu. Kang Sengkai was a person of the Wei state. Cao Pi usurped the Han.
The state name was Wei. Zhi Qian was a man of Wu; when Sun Quan assumed the title of Emperor, the state name was Wu.
Fa Xian lived during the Song dynasty of the Zhao people; when Zhao Kuangyin became the Son of Heaven, the state name was Song.
Bodhiruci was a man of the Northern Wei; the ruler of Wei’s original surname was Tuoba, which was changed to Yuan, and the state name was Wei.

There are also things not yet exhausted; that is to say, while the beautiful has been exhausted, the good remains unexhausted. Furthermore, regarding the essential points of the old texts, he too failed to fully extract them.

Regarding the loss of order between the high and the low: if the lower grade does not produce [the result], then its non-production constitutes inferiority. Yet the higher grade is never mentioned; does this mean the higher is also inferior?
Since it is never mentioned, its silence would constitute superiority. Conversely, if the lower grade speaks of non-production, does that non-production also constitute superiority?
Therefore, it is said that the order has been lost.
Regarding the essential principle for the correct rebirth through the single resolve: if one does not generate the bodhicitta, one remains at the level of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) alone;
the seeds of the Two Vehicles will not sprout. Therefore, it should be known that the generation of the resolve is the very root of rebirth.
Commentary: *Gāthā* (verse) is here translated as "isolated verse. Regarding the "Ten Great Vows of the King":
first is paying homage to all Buddhas; second is praising the Tathāgatas; and so on, up to the tenth, which is universal dedication.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* teaches with directness and straightforwardness. That both sutras ultimately lead to Sukhāvatī is because those who wish to enter the nature of Vairocana [must do so through that path].

The Sea [of the Dharma] first returns to the Pure Land through the Gate of the Silken Thread. Desiring to awaken to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle, one must first enter the Western Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*).
Since this is the case from beginning to end for these two sutras, it may be known that the same applies to all intermediate sutras.

Thus, we know that the single gate of the Pure Land is the *dhāraṇī* (comprehensive summary) of the entire teaching of the Buddha’s lifetime and the ground of refuge for all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Section: On the Detailed and the Abridged, and on the Same and the Different. "Detailed" refers to the Great Text (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*). "Abridged" refers to this present sutra. "Same" means belonging to the same category.
"Different" means neither of the same division nor of the same category.
Commentary: Regarding "the Qin of the Ying": During the Zhou dynasty, there was a man named Fei Zi, who was a descendant of Bo Yi.
He was skilled at raising horses, and King Xiaowu of Zhou favored him, enfeoffing him in Shan with the state name Qin. Later, he annexed the various states and came to possess the empire.
Because his surname was Ying, it is called the "Ying Qin. Regarding the "Fu Qin": This refers to the Di people during the Eastern Jin dynasty. Fu Jian was powerful...
Sheng (Fu Jian) seized control of Guanzhong, and his state was likewise called Qin; this was the Fu Qin. As for the Yao Qin, they were of Qiang descent.

Yao Chang had served as a general under Fu Jian; later, when Jian was defeated by the Jin forces, Chang subsequently took possession of Guanzhong and passed the throne to his son Xing, who established the Yao Qin.
Regarding those who master the languages of the four quarters according to the *Zhou Li*: in the east it is called Ji, and in the south it is called Xiang.
In the west they were called *diti*, and in the north they were called *yi*; these were all official titles.
*Jiyan* (寄言) was able to convey the differences in customs from this [land], while *xiangyan* (象言) was able to imitate the differences in customs from that [land].

*Diti* was intended to distinguish the differences in their dress and ornaments, whereas *yi* was intended to discern the differences in their speech. In the *Zhouguan* (官), they were collectively termed *xiangxu* (象胥). And...
In common worldly parlance, this is called "translation" (*yi*). Furthermore, it means "to explain. It is synonymous with "transcribing.
This refers to transcribing and explaining the languages of one side to those of the other so as to facilitate mutual understanding. Regarding the dispatch of the general Lü Guang:

in the thirteenth year of the Jianyuan era of Fu Jian of the Former Qin, Lü Guang was sent to conquer the kingdom of Qūzī; having defeated them, he led his troops back to Liangzhou and subsequently took control of the province.
He was titled King Liang. After Guang died, his nephew Lü Long surrendered to the Qin dynasty. Thereupon, the Master was invited to enter the Pass and resided in the Xiaoyao Garden.
Regarding the two sūtras that are "linked and compared": "linked" (lián) means continuous succession, and "compared" (bǐ) means placed side by side.

Master Kumārajīva translated the former, and Master Xuanzang translated the latter; thus they possess the sense of being linked in succession. Furthermore, the meanings and principles of the two sūtras do not contradict one another.
On the meaning of comparison. Commentary:
"Standing out in solitary independence" refers to when the Master was eleven years old. Seeing the novice monks engaged in boisterous talk and laughter, he rebuked them, saying:
"Those who have left the household life do so for the sake of the unconditioned Dharma (*asamskṛta-dharma*). How can you still indulge in childish play? This may be called empty.
He passed away at the age of one hundred. Those who discerned him knew that his spiritual capacity was extraordinary.
(Note: The ten commentaries on sutras by Gushan are: 1. the Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra; 2. the Śālistamba-sūtra [sic];
3. the Prajñā-hṛdaya-sūtra; 4. the Prātihārya-sūtra; 5. the Sūtra in Forty-two Sections; 6. the Acintya-dharmamukha-sūtra.)

The sutras: 1. the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; 2. the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*; 3. the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*; 4. the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*; 5. the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*; 6. the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*; 7. the *Saptabuddhaka-sūtra*; 8. the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*; 9. the *Amitābha-sūtra*; and 10. the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*.
These are the ten sutras for which he is popularly known as the Commentator.

Note: Regarding works such as the *Ratnarāja-śāstra* (Treasure King Treatise), the Dharma Master Feixi of Caotang composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Baowang Lun* (Treatise on the Treasure King of the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection).

The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai composed the *Shi yiqu lun shi* (Commentary on the Treatise Resolving Ten Doubts). The Layman Wang Rixiu of Longshu composed the *Jingtu wen* (Text on the Pure Land).
The Layman Zhang Shangying, known as Wujin, composed the *Qiusheng Jingtu wen* (Text on Seeking Rebirth in the Pure Land). And the Court Gentleman Wang Gu [composed the *Jingtu lun*].
The *Zhizhi jingtu jueyi ji* (Collection for Resolving Doubts Concerning the Direct Pointing to the Pure Land) was composed by the Wuqun śramaṇa Dayou.

The *Jingtuzhigui ji* (Collection on the Destination of the Pure Land) was composed by the layman Wugong Wang Qian. The *Jingtuxinzhen lu* (Record of Self-Confidence in the Pure Land) was composed by the Chan Master Zunsui of Ciyun.
The Venerable Shandao composed a verse, which says: "Gradually the skin becomes like that of a chicken and the hair turns white like a crane; look, look at the steps..."
In these declining times, there is only the direct path of cultivation: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.

This was the intent of Chan Master Yongming Shou, who composed the "Rhapsody on the Spirit Dwelling in An-yang," as well as the various masters of the Pure Land school, such as Zhongfeng, Xizhai, and Chushi.
Commentary: "The branches bend low only to hang the golden altar. A poem says: "My Master ascended to the First Stage in a single thought;
to the land of Buddhas he has come twice amidst the music of flutes and songs. Only the ancient locust tree before the gate bends its branches low, solely to hang the golden altar."
Note: For example, there were Xizhai, Konggu, Tianqi, Dufeng, and others. During the Ming Dynasty, Chan Master Chushi Qi composed the *Xizhai Jingtusong* (Pure Land Poems of Xizhai).

Chan Master Konggu Long compiled the *Kongguji* (The Collection of Konggu). Chan Master Tianqi was styled the "Solitary Elder" (Qiongjue Laoren) and authored the *Qiongjueji* (The Collection of the Solitary Elder).
Chan Master Dufeng Shan’s recorded sayings (*yulu*) are extant in the world.
Section: Regarding the fact that all the stars revolve toward the North Star, the *Analects* states:
"To govern by means of virtue is like the North Star (Beichen) abiding in its place while the multitude of stars revolve around it."
Commentary: Regarding Yongming being one born into the highest grade of the Chan school:

Chan Master Yongming Shou upheld the principle of the single transmission and composed works such as the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) and the *Wanshan Tonggui Ji* (Collection on the Convergence of Myriad Good Deeds). After his passing, there was a monk who circumambulated his stupa for years.

When people asked the reason, he said: "I fell ill and entered the underworld. I saw the image of a monk enshrined to the left of the hall in the palace, and the King paid him diligent and respectful homage."

Li inquired privately and learned that this was Master Shou of Hangzhou. While ordinary people must all pass through the underworld after death, this master had already been reborn in the highest grade of the highest rank in the Western Paradise.
Regarding "Yuanzhao designates the Lotus Realm as his destination": During the Song dynasty, Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben initially attained realization upon first visiting Tianyi.

Later, he devoted himself single-mindedly to the practice of *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha) while residing at Jingci Monastery. There was a Dharma Master named Cai of Leifeng who traveled spiritually to the Pure Land and saw an exceptionally beautiful lotus flower;
when asked about it, he replied, "It awaits Chan Master Ben of Jingci. Furthermore, Master Xi of Zifu visited this master... [text continues].
He prostrated at [the Master's] feet, offered gold, and departed. People asked him the reason for this, and he said, "In my meditative concentration, I saw a golden lotus flower.
Others remarked, "This was surely for the sake of Master Benchan. Later, when his end approached, he passed away while sitting upright; he was posthumously titled Yuanzhao (Perfect Illumination).

Regarding the account of Sengrui’s golden lotus emerging from his couch: Sengrui had received the meaning of the scriptures from Dharma Master Kumārajīva and later joined the Lotus Society at Mount Lu.
In the sixteenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, he suddenly announced to the assembly, "I am about to depart.
Facing west with palms joined, he passed away. The assembly saw a golden lotus flower before Sengrui's couch, which vanished in an instant, leaving behind five-colored [traces].
Fragrant smoke issued from his room.
Regarding Qingzhao’s recitation of a verse upon returning to the West: Master Vinaya-holder Qingzhao Heng of the Song dynasty initially relied on Lingzhi Temple to study the Vinaya.

For sixty years, he exclusively cultivated the practice of Pure Land. At the time of his death, as he recited the Buddha’s name, he spoke this verse: "Amitābha, Amitābha— I call upon Your name, The white tuft between Your brows..."
Contemplate this in every thought. Maintaining this non-retrogressive mind, one will certainly be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

As for the "nine schools," they refer to: the Confucian school, the Daoist school, the Yin-Yang school, the Legalist school, the School of Names, the Mohist school, the School of the Vertical and Horizontal (Sophists), and the Miscellaneous school.
The Nong lineage:
Wen Lugu (styled Yanbo) served as a Chancellor of the Song dynasty and was enfeoffed as Duke of Lu. Su Changgong (styled Shi) served as a Hanlin Academician and styled himself Dongpo.
As for the "Ten Thousand Causes," it refers to those who exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name and recorded their names in the "Lotus Register."

It satisfied the aspirations of one hundred thousand people. Regarding the "Western Paradise Pass" held by the Elder: whenever the Elder traveled between the north and south, he always carried a depiction of the Western Paradise with him.
When people asked about it, he would say, "This is my official pass for rebirth in the Western Paradise."
Regarding those who abandoned the study of immortals and turned their hearts [to the Dharma]: Ge Jizhi of Song was a native of Jurong. He had long devoted himself to the study of immortals.

His wife, Lady Ji, alone maintained singular sincerity in the recitation of the Buddha’s name. In the third year of the Yuanjia era, while she was at her loom, she suddenly perceived a clarity and purity in the air.
He then gazed upward toward the four quarters and saw a Buddha manifesting in the west; precious canopies, banners, and streamers eclipsed the Milky Way.
Rejoicing, he said, "The Sūtra speaks of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life—is this perhaps He? He then prostrated himself on the ground.
When Huizhi approached in astonishment, Lady Ji pointed out the location of the Buddha, and Huizhi also beheld half of the Buddha’s body amidst auspicious clouds of five colors.
His kinsmen all witnessed this. Thereupon, Tanluan changed his mind and began to recite the name of the Buddha.
He burned the *Cinnabar Scripture* (*Xian jing*) and instead practiced the *Contemplation Sutra*. Tanluan of the Later Wei was by nature fond of the pursuit of longevity;

he had received ten fascicles of the *Cinnabar Scripture* from Tao Hongjing, the Master of Seclusion. Later, upon meeting Bodhiruci, he asked him, "Does the Buddha possess a technique for longevity and immortality?"
Hu Zhi laughed and said, "Immortality and eternal life are the Way of our Buddha. I shall therefore bestow upon you the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*.

If you study this, you will no longer be born within the three realms nor pass through the six destinies. Your lifespan would be such that even the kalpas of the Ganges sands or the eons of cosmic stones could not compare to it.
This is the 'long life' of us followers of the Golden Immortal. Tanyue was greatly delighted and subsequently burned his Daoist scriptures.
Yet he cultivated the Pure Land.
Regarding "those who practiced the arts of Qi and Huang while reciting the Buddha's name": Yuan Wu Zizhang practiced medicine and recited the Buddha's name throughout his life.

During the Zhizheng period, he passed away without illness while reciting the Buddha's name. As for "Qi and Huang," this refers to the dialogues between Qibo and Huang Di (the Yellow Emperor) of Xuan-yuan, which form the *Inner Canon* (*Nanjing*).
The *Jingdengshu* (Book of the Lamp-like Sūtras) is the progenitor of medical literature.

Among those who bore the plow and were renowned for their names was Zhang Quan of the Jin dynasty. He was a man of lofty reclusion and great learning; while tilling the soil with his hoe, he never ceased carrying his scriptures.

Later, he entered the Lotus Society at Mount Lu, where he investigated the inner teachings (Buddhist scriptures) with such depth that he attained numerous insights and realizations. This was in the first year of the Jingping era of the Song dynasty.
He passed away without illness, facing west while recollecting the Buddha;
the Lord of the Netherworld paid him respectful homage. This was the Dhyāna Master Shou. As for "the rākṣasa who ceased his wicked ways": there was once a rākṣasa living in a certain village.

The people there daily sent their children with food. Among them was one whose son had returned to place his faith in the Triple Gem and was single-mindedly mindful of the Buddha; consequently, he was unable to eat.
Because of this, he attained the realization of the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). "Attaining" means reaching it. "Reaching" means being present therein.

Regarding the phrase "If there is no doubt, why consult the divination? it refers to when Emperor Taizong of Tang was still the Prince of Qin. He harbored mutual resentment toward Crown Prince Jiancheng and intended to raise an army.
As his subordinates were suspicious and feared they would not prevail, he ordered Zhang Gongjin to perform a divination. Zhang took a tortoise shell and threw it to the ground, saying:
"Divination is used to resolve doubts; if there is no doubt, why consult the divination?"
*The Explication of the Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, Scroll One;
*The Fixed Text of the Explication of the Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra*, Scroll Two:
The Meaning of the Title. First, explaining the general title so that there may be a guiding framework: the presence of a title for a sūtra is like having a net for a fisherman.
There is a "mainstay" (綱). When a garment has a collar, if one grasps its mainstay, all the loops are raised; if one lifts its collar, all the threads follow.

Regarding the *Commentary*’s statement that the Buddha “then pervades” (周): the Buddha is the supreme object of contemplation. By citing his primary retribution (正報), [the text] encompasses [all other aspects].
The "fruition" (niṣyanda-phala) comprises the six contemplations of the sun, moon, pond, tree, and so forth.

To describe the principal teacher of transformation as encompassing his retinue comprises the nine contemplations of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the three grades of rebirth, and so on. Although these contemplations number sixteen, by speaking of the Buddha alone, they are fully accounted for.
Therefore, the title reads: *The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha*.
Regarding the commentary: "The Original Teacher Śākyamuni" refers to Śākya in Sanskrit, which here means "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren);
this is his clan name. Muni in Sanskrit means "Silent Sage" (Jimo); this is his personal name. He is the Buddha realized by Prince Siddhārtha after he left the household life.
Furthermore, because he is the Teacher of the Sahā World, he is called the "Original Master" (benshi).
Regarding the phrase "the distinction between the refined and the plain": the Sanskrit originals are all the language of the Western Regions; they are plain and lack literary refinement.

When translated into the language of this land [China], one employs the style of the Six Classics, Zhuangzi, and Laozi, such that the prose becomes elegant and beautiful, brilliantly forming complete compositions.
Regarding the term "Zhendan" (China): "Zhen" refers to the East; "Dan" means the first light of dawn.
Since this region lies at the extreme eastern edge of Jambudvīpa and is the place where the sun rises, it is named Zhendan.

The three phrases concerning the self-awakening that distinguishes one from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*): Ordinary beings are deluded by the clouds of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsana*) and sink into the ocean of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*);

they lack any self-awareness whatsoever. The Buddha, however, possesses a vast and luminous great awakening; thus he differs from ordinary beings. The followers of the Two Vehicles seek only their own transcendence of the world and lack the mind for universal benefit;

they cannot awaken others. The Buddha, however, universally delivers all through great compassion; thus he differs from the followers of the Two Vehicles. As for Bodhisattvas, their ignorance has not yet...

Exhausted. Because the *dharmatā* is not yet perfected, one cannot attain full awakening. The Buddha, however, has reached the ultimate limit of wondrous awakening (*miao-jue*) and his rank is supreme among the *tathāgatas*;
thus he differs from the *bodhisattvas*.

Furthermore, the three phrases concerning "awakening apart from the mind" are as follows: "mind" refers to the *vijñāna*-mind; "form" refers to that which is transformed by the mind. By means of the mind...
Regarding the observation of forms: when the mind is intimate with form and form is distant from the mind, "intimacy of mind" is called "self," and the "distance of form" is called "other.

Once the consciousness-mind that can transform is seen as empty, it is called "awakening to self. Furthermore, once the delusory forms that are transformed are seen as empty, it is called "awakening to others.
When both mind and form have reached the end of emptiness, and even that emptiness is itself empty, it is called "fulfillment of awakening."
"Knowing the number and non-number of all sentient beings, as well as the permanent and the impermanent. The *Guangming shu* (Commentary on the Light) states:

"Number" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings and the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; because they fall into existence or fall into non-existence, they all remain within the realm of number. "Non-number" refers to the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas;

because they have directly realized the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Dharma-body does not fall into any such numbers. "Permanent" refers to the Perfect and Sudden One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); "impermanent" refers to... [the three vehicles].
Regarding the six classes of ordinary beings and the three vehicles of the teachings, the Buddha knows them all; this is called the *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all aspects).

Furthermore, that which is numerable and impermanent constitutes the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); knowing this is termed the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths). That which is innumerable and permanent constitutes the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
To know this is called "all-knowledge" (sarvajñā). That which is numerical is non-numerical; that which is permanent is impermanent. This constitutes the object of the Middle Truth.
To know this is called "knowledge of all modes" (sarvākārajñā).
The Tathāgata possesses ten titles common to all Buddhas: because he is without falsehood, he is named Tathāgata; because he is a field of merit par excellence, he is named Arhat;

because he knows the dharma-realm, he is named Samyaksaṃbuddha; because he is endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge, he is named Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna; because he does not return [to this world], he is named Anāgāmin.
He is named Sugata because he knows sentient beings and their lands. He is named Lokavid because he is peerless in understanding the world. He is named Anuttara because he tames the minds of others.

He is named Puruṣadamyasārathi because he is the eye for all sentient beings. He is named Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām because he knows the three categories of beings. He is named Buddha because he awakens them.

One who possesses these ten virtues is the sovereign lord of both the mundane and supramundane realms. Since names are the guests of reality, the "Ten Titles of the World-Honored One" refer to the World-Honored One’s ten virtues.
Possessing these ten virtues, he is venerated by the nine dharma-realms; therefore, he is named the World-Honored One (Bhagavān).
These ten titles are specific designations, while the two characters "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān) are general.

They comprise two types of wisdom and five phrases. The two types of wisdom are the fundamental and the subsequently attained. The two obstacles are the afflictive and the cognitive. The two truths are the ultimate and the conventional.
"Awakening from a dream" is like waking from a great dream; "the opening of a lotus" is like the blossoming of a lotus flower. If these are to be distributed accordingly:

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) severs the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), realizes the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and attains the benefit of self-benefit, like awakening from a great dream.

Subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) severs the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), realizes the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and attains the benefit of benefiting others, like the blooming of a lotus.
"Identity from the beginning" (*lishi*) refers to the five phrases; it is called "six" when categorized by phenomena (*shi*), and "identity" (*ji*) when categorized by principle (*li*).
Furthermore, it is called "six" to prevent arrogance, and "identity" to prevent despondency.

Regarding "identity from the beginning," this means that the principle of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by sentient beings is non-dual and undifferentiated from that of the Tathāgata. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One..."
"All sentient beings are Buddhas. This is the Buddha as the Principle (*li*). As the ancients said: "In movement and stillness, the principle is entirely present;

in action and withdrawal, phenomena are utterly non-existent. Obscurely following things as they turn, one wanders on in the distance, unaware of the way home. This is it. Regarding the Buddha as Name-and-Word (*mingzi*):
this refers to hearing [the teaching] from a spiritual friend or obtaining it from within the scriptures, thereby attaining thorough penetration and understanding of all things.
There are no phenomena that are not the Buddha-dharma; this is what is meant by "names are themselves the Buddha. As the ancients said:

"Upon first hearing the melody of non-arising, and just hearing the song of immortality, one finally realizes it is right within this very body, yet turns to regret one's own wasted time. This is precisely it.

Regarding "correspondence through contemplative practice" (觀行即), it means knowing that all things are the Buddha-dharma, which requires that mental contemplation be clear and that principle and wisdom be in accord.

What one practices accords with what one speaks, and what one speaks accords with what one practices; this is "Contemplative Practice as Suchness" (*kuan-hsing-chieh-fo*). This is the fifth stage, the Stage of Meritorious Understanding (*wu-pin-wei*).

As the ancients said: "In every thought-moment, one conforms to the constant principle; in every mind, one quiets the illusory dust. One universally contemplates the nature of all phenomena, which is neither false nor true.
This refers to it. Regarding "Similar Suchness" (*xiang-si-ji*): it means that within the stage of contemplative practice, the more one contemplates, the clearer it becomes. The more...
Cessation becomes increasingly tranquil. Although one has not yet truly realized its principle, one perceives it dimly and realizes the truth in a semblance;
this is "semblance Buddhahood," which refers to the stage of the ten faiths. As the ancients said: "Though the four abidings have already fallen away, the six dusts are not yet entirely empty;
there is still a film before the eyes, so one sees red flowers in the sky. This is precisely that. "Partial realization" refers to...
Regarding the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*), there are forty-two grades. Upon reaching this stage, one shatters one grade of ignorance and realizes one portion of the *dharmakāya*;
this is what is meant by "partial realization as a Buddha. This refers to the stages from the first abode (*prathamabhūmi*) up to the position of Equal Enlightenment (*samudāgama-bodhi*).

As the ancients said: "Suddenly the mind opens and awakens; all things are thoroughly penetrated. Yet the source is not yet fully exhausted; the moon is still seen through a veil. This is precisely it. To investigate...
"Ultimate immediacy" refers to the five abodes and two deaths being completely purified without remainder, immeasurably profound, and forever beyond the reach of thought.
This is what is meant by "ultimate immediacy as Buddhahood. As it was said of old: "In years past, the real was truly delusion; today, delusion is entirely real.
It is merely the restoration of things as they were; not a single dharma is new. This is precisely it.

The ten bodies consist of three phrases: first, the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment (*abhisambuddha-buddha*), because he manifests the attainment of perfect enlightenment; second, the Buddha of Vows (*praṇidhāna-buddha*), because he manifests his body according to his vows;

third, the Buddha of Karmic Retribution (*vipāka-buddha*), because it is induced by myriad practices; fourth, the Buddha of Sustenance (*dharmatā-sthiti-buddha*), because his own relics abide eternally;

fifth, the Buddha of Nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-buddha*), because he manifests parinirvāṇa; sixth, the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharma-kāya-buddha*), because the dharma-realm is of a single characteristic; seventh...
1. Mind-Buddha, because he possesses a heart of great compassion; 2. Samādhi-Buddha, because he is constantly in meditative concentration; 3.
Original-Nature Buddha, because his wisdom realizes the original nature; 4. According-to-Desire Buddha, because he manifests according to the desires [of beings].

There are four groups of nine regarding devas (*deva*). First, the worldly devas (*laukika-deva*): although kings dwell in the world, they enjoy brocade robes, jade food, and palaces of precious gems like those of the heavens;
thus, they are called worldly devas. Second, the devas by birth (*upapatti-deva*):

if one diligently cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karma-patha*) and concurrently attains the *anāgamya-samādhi*, one will be born in the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). If one further cultivates the four fundamental [dhyānas]...

Those who practice meditative concentration (dhyāna) attain rebirth in the heavens of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). If they further cultivate the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samādhi), they attain rebirth in the heavens of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu).
These deities of the three realms do not transcend birth and death; when their merit is exhausted, they fall back down. Therefore, they are called "born in heaven.

As for the "three pure heavens," these are the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas who have severed the delusions of the four abodes, realized the principle of the True Dharma, and purified all afflictions (kleśa); therefore, they are so named.

The Heaven of Purity. As for the Heaven of Meaning (Arthadivaukas), this refers to Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes who advance to sever the afflictions of views and thoughts beyond the realms, thereby realizing the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya);
hence they are called the Heaven of Meaning.
Commentary: "To gladden what one harbors" means that "gladdening" (*yue*) refers to joyful exuberance, and "harboring" (*huai*) refers to the mind’s inner state.

According to this sutra, it refers to the Tathāgata’s long-cultivated and long-realized *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), which he had stored within his heart; having now encountered those with the capacity [to receive it], he speaks, thereby giving full expression to what he has long harbored.

Regarding "proclaiming through the four analytical knowledges": by means of immeasurable skillful wisdom, one gives rise to the four types of unimpeded analytical knowledge and expounds the Dharma using various forms of speech and terminology.
The "twelve divisions" (*dvādaśāṅga*) and so forth clarify the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the teachings expounded.

That is to say, they may be presented as prose (*sūtra*), or as verses in repetition (*geya*), or as accounts of marvelous events (*adbhutadharma*), or as spontaneous utterances without prior inquiry (*udāna*), and so on.
These twelve divisions apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Some say that the Hīnayāna consists of only nine divisions, while the Mahāyāna has twelve; others say that the Hīnayāna...
Twelve. The Mahāyāna consists of only nine divisions; however, some say that both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess twelve. The term "etc.

refers to the eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma (*dharmakośa*), the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), and all other gateways to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*).

"Reaching the four *siddhāntas* clarifies skillfulness in exposition; that is to say, each and every one of the various dharmas taught—such as the twelve divisions of the canon—is made to benefit [beings] through the four *siddhāntas*.
'Reaching' (*zhì*) means that from the various teachings themselves up to the various modes of exposition, there is not a single instance that does not convey the meaning."

"All are those who explain the meaning" refers generally to clarifying the characteristics of their expositions. If we were to rely on the exposition of the present [text], it would concern precisely the practice of *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection), which will be shown in detail in the subsequent passage;
therefore, it need not be set forth here. Consequently, for now, I shall clarify the characteristics of their expositions in a general sense.

Commentary: Regarding the four kinds of analytical eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*): first is the unimpeded analytical eloquence regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), which refers to thoroughly understanding the principles and meanings of all phenomena (*dharma*) with complete penetration and without obstruction.

Second is the unimpeded analytical eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), which refers to penetrating the names and designations of all phenomena, distinguishing them without obstruction.

Third is the unimpededness of dharma-words (*dharmapada-pratisaṃvid*). This means that regarding the names, meanings, and principles of all phenomena, one follows the diverse languages and dialects of all sentient beings to expound them for their sake, enabling each to attain understanding with eloquence free from obstruction. Fourth is the unimpededness of joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
This means that according to the faculties and dispositions of all sentient beings, one expounds the Dharma they wish to hear, in a manner that is perfectly harmonious and integrated.
There is no obstruction.
That which is called "speaking" is that in which all four [faculties] are unimpeded. If there were even one thing that obstructed it, the mind would not be joyful;
if the mind were not joyful, it would not be speaking. This is because speaking is itself joy.

Regarding the statement that "the Buddhas preach the Dharma for sentient beings by relying on the two truths": the two truths refer to the two truths of the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

At times, they sweep away everything entirely, not establishing even a single atom; this is preaching by relying on the ultimate truth. At other times, they establish everything, not discarding a single dharma;
this is preaching by relying on the conventional truth.

Regarding the unimpeded knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), it is explained through the differentiation of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Conventional knowledge is precisely the wisdom that comprehends the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

When the Tathāgata, in accordance with sentient beings, expounds the names, meanings, and principles of all phenomena using various dialects and different languages, he does so entirely by means of the wisdom that comprehends conventional truth, speaking through such differentiation.

Regarding "expounding with eloquence through unimpeded knowledge by means of skillful mastery of the wisdom of the ultimate truth": the wisdom of the ultimate truth is precisely the knowledge that realizes the ultimate truth.
The Tathāgata, in accordance with the dispositions of all sentient beings and the teachings they delight to hear, expounds them for their sake.
This is done with perfect integration and without obstruction, all through skillful mastery of the wisdom that realizes the ultimate truth. This is what is meant by "skillful."
As for "skillful means": the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is fundamentally beyond verbal expression; all that exists as verbal explanation is due to skillful means.
Regarding the "worldly standpoint" (loka-samvṛti-siddhānta): "world" (loka) has the meaning of separation, and "standpoint" (siddhānta) refers to a distinct category.
Because the faculties and capacities of sentient beings are shallow, the Buddha, in accordance with what they desire to hear, provides sequential and analytical explanations for them, so as to...
It generates joy; it functions as the benefit of generating joy.

Regarding the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint for individuals): this refers to when the Buddha intends to preach the Dharma, he necessarily observes the capacity of sentient beings—the magnitude of their faculties and the depth of their past seeds—and only then, in accordance with their specific aptitudes, causes them to give rise to right faith, thereby functioning as the benefit of generating wholesome roots.
The *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remedial counteraction) refers to teaching the contemplation of impurity to those sentient beings who have an abundance of desire,

and teaching the cultivation of a compassionate mind to those who have an abundance of hatred. These Dharma-medicines are taught to counteract these various ailments and are bestowed universally upon sentient beings to achieve the benefit of extinguishing evil.
Regarding the *paramārtha-siddhānta*: "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) refers to the principle (*li*).

This means that when the Buddha perceives that the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of sentient beings have matured, he immediately preaches the Dharma for them, causing them to attain awakening and thereby providing the benefit of entry into the Path.
All dharmas are taught according to what is appropriate, yet they ultimately converge into four types of teaching so as to bring about four kinds of benefit.

All dharmas do not exceed the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates; these eighty thousand and more teachings are subsumed within the four teachings—namely, the eighty thousand of the *utpāda-vyaya* (arising and ceasing), the eighty thousand of the *anutpāda* (non-arising), the eighty thousand of the *apramāṇa* (immeasurable), and the eighty thousand of the *anabhisaṃskāra* (unconditioned). As with the *utpāda-vyaya*, so it is for the others.

Of the eighty thousand [teachings], taking up a single dharma, one must open four gates. Explaining according to the gate of existence (*yǒu-mén*), every thought-moment is impermanent, like the flickering of a lamp’s flame.

Explaining according to the gate of emptiness (*kōng-mén*), the three provisional designations (*sān-jiǎ*) are insubstantial and void, like clouds and mist. Explaining according to the gate of both (*shuāng-yì-mén*), the two characteristics coexist harmoniously.

Explaining according to the gate of neither (*shuāng-fēi-mén*), both characteristics are abandoned. Among these four, because the faculties of sentient beings are matured through one particular gate, there are the four *siddhāntas*.

For those who have not yet planted the seeds [of merit], he provides teachings on the world to inspire joy in them. For those who have already planted the seeds, he provides teachings on rebirth as humans to cause them to generate wholesome roots.
For those whose evil has not yet been destroyed, he provides teachings on antidotes to cause them to eliminate that evil.

For those whose faculties are already mature, he provides teachings on the ultimate truth to cause them to enter into the principle. The Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacities [of beings], and thus his teachings invariably hit the mark; this is known.
It does not enter into ultimate principle. It causes one to obtain three benefits: knowing that evil is not destroyed, it causes one to obtain two benefits.

Since there is no further goodness to be produced, it is spoken of as being for the sake of the world; it merely gives rise to joy. Therefore, it is said that these four explanations—beginning with "ultimately returning to the worldly"—are intended solely to cause one to obtain the four benefits, such as joy.

Regarding the bestowing of the Dharma by discerning the capacities [of sentient beings], as for those whose texts are extensive and vast, it has been clarified above: namely, that the single "Gate of Existence" (yǒumén) serves the four *siddhāntas* according to capacity;

the same applies to the other three gates serving their respective capacities. Since this is the case for one of the eighty thousand [teachings]—wherein the four gates and four *siddhāntas* serve capacities—it follows accordingly for all.

The same applies to the remaining dharmas being applied to sentient beings through the four gates and the four *siddhāntas*. Since the four *siddhāntas* apply to the eighty thousand gates of the One Vehicle teaching, the same holds true for the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, it is said that "one discerns the capacities of beings and bestows the Dharma," though the full textual elaboration is extensive.

Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the Buddha’s merits are inexhaustible," the two characters for "merit" (*guṇa*) encompass the entirety of the three bodies (*trikāya*), the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), the ten eyes, the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates.
They are "inexhaustible" because those on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) cannot fathom their source, and even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) cannot perceive their summit.

Regarding these immeasurables, two matters are briefly cited here: as stated in the eighth stage of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one attains an immeasurable body, immeasurable voice, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable births, immeasurable pure lands, and the transformation and teaching of immeasurable sentient beings.
They enter immeasurable Dharma-gates; they possess immeasurable supernormal powers; they have immeasurable assemblies and distinctions of sites of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa);
and they abide in immeasurable physical, verbal, and mental actions. Thus, how could this life-span and radiance be anything other than a mere mention of two such matters?
Commentary: The two phrases "multitudinous and beyond measure" mean that, like the Buddha’s lifespan, it endures through incalculable kalpas;
and like his radiance, it is of unspeakably many numbers—this is "multitudinous and beyond measure.
Furthermore, this very life-span and light pervade the entire Dharma-realm without limit—this is "vast and without finite measure."
Among the ten great numbers, "immeasurable" (apramāṇa) is still an immeasurable that remains measurable; it is an immeasurable that is not yet infinite.
Only the "immeasurable of true immeasurability" is the ultimate immeasurable.
Commentary: Regarding the statement that the teachings spoken by the Buddha are collectively termed *sūtra*:
these three characters, *sū-tra*, are the general name for the Great Canon and the common designation for the Three Studies (*triśikṣā*).
This is because whether they be *sūtras*, *vinayas*, or *śāstras*, they all accord with the principle of the Buddhas above and accord with the capacities of sentient beings below.

Regarding the phrase "the sūtra has many meanings": because there are seven meanings in that region and four meanings here, it is said to have "many meanings. As for why they do not exceed four meanings:
although there are seven meanings in that region, they do not go beyond the two meanings of "pervasion" (guàn) and "inclusion" (shè). Here [in this region]...
Although there are four meanings, they do not transcend the two meanings of the "Eternal Dharma" (nitya-dharma).

Therefore, it is said that they do not exceed these four meanings. First, "giving birth": because it gives birth to all meanings and the fruits of sagehood. Second, "manifesting": because it manifests the characteristics of phenomena (dharma-lakṣaṇa).
Third, "a gushing spring": because its inexhaustible meaning and flavor flow forth without end. Fourth, "a plumb line": because it establishes the standard with precision.

Because it distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox: fifth, "Stringing Together" (Guan-man) means to thread together all dharmas. That which remains unchanging for ten thousand ages is called "Constant" (Chang).

The rules and regulations of the ten realms are called "Dharma" (Fa). The path traversed by noble wisdom is called "Pathway" (Jing). That which is venerated by both past and present is called "Canon" (Dian).

First, I shall explain the two meanings of "pervading" (guàn) and "encompassing" (shè). These can encompass five meanings; these two characters, "pervading" and "encompassing," are sufficient to exhaust the meaning of that [Sanskrit] term.

Furthermore, regarding the term "constant" (cháng), it next refers to the two meanings of "constant dharma" (chángfǎ); these can encompass the two meanings of "path" (jìng) and "scripture" (diǎn). These are the two meanings of "constant dharma."
The word "character" (zi) fully exhausts the meaning of this section.
Thus, at the end of that section, the four characters in summary are able to exhaust the meaning of the entire sutra; therefore, although there are many meanings, they do not go beyond these four.

Regarding the direct translation as "thread" (*sūtra*): since mats, cords, ropes, and the like are all translated as "cord" (*pāśa*), the sense that a thread has the meaning of "pervading and sustaining" incorporates the two meanings previously assigned to *buddhabhūmi*.
As for these two being sufficient to encompass the five meanings of "arising," they further incorporate the five meanings previously found in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*.
"Pervading and penetrating" can generally encompass all five meanings, as "arising" and the others are equivalent to it.
Because it clarifies the principles being explained, "retention" (*dhāraṇī*) encompasses both the meanings of "stopping" (*śamatha*) and "giving birth to the measuring line" (*sūtra*).

This is because it gives birth to the fruits of sainthood and establishes the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, thereby preventing one from falling into false views. If "pervasive retention" (*vyūha-dhāraṇī*) is understood as encompassing both what is explained and those to be converted, then both types of retention include all five [categories].
Commentary: The single character "sūtra" (經) constitutes the general name, because—with the exception of the Vinaya and Śāstras—all twelve divisions of the teaching are sūtras.
The five characters "Buddha-spoken" (佛說) constitute the specific name, because this is the Buddha’s discourse on Amitābha, and not [a work such as] the *Mahāvaipulya-buddha* and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "the principles of practice according to the teachings are likewise both general and specific": if we refer to the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*, as for the general and specific aspects of the teachings, they are as explained above.
As for the general and specific aspects of practice, because the modes of practice differ—ranging from a single [practice] up to immeasurable ones—this constitutes the specificity of practice.

The principle and the gates are both identical and distinct. Regarding the distinction between the principle and the gates: although the principle itself has no name, one uses the names of the gates to designate the principle;

thus, the principle follows the gates, resulting in sixteen [categories] through the fourfold application of each of the four [gates], which is called the "distinction of principle and gate. When the gates follow the principle, this is called the "identity of principle and gate.

This discussion of identity and distinction is based on the entirety of the Buddha’s teaching (*ekāśāsana*). However, as explained in the *Chao* (the *Zhiyuan Fabao Tanjing Miji*), the discussion of identity and distinction is based on a single title.
Regarding the statement that the merit of hearing the title of the scripture is immeasurable:

since the "title" refers to the secret treasury of the three virtues, when the mind hears this secret treasury, pure wisdom becomes wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and quiescent. How could the resulting merit possibly be measured?
As it is stated in the teachings, the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* says: "First is the greatness of essence (*tài-dà*):

it refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*), because true suchness (*tathatā*) is equal and neither increases nor decreases. Second is the greatness of characteristic (*xiàng-dà*): it refers to the tathāgatagarbha, because it is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits.
Third is the greatness of function (*yòng-dà*): it is able to produce all causes and fruits, both mundane and supramundane, that are wholesome."
Commentary: Regarding the establishment of the teachings based on the fundamental principle: from the *prajñā* of the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*), the *prajñā* of written words flows forth;
that is to say, the twelvefold division of the teachings flows forth from True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Regarding "practicing according to the teachings": from the *prajñā* of words and letters, one cultivates the *prajñā* of contemplative observation; relying upon the twelve divisions of the teaching, one practices the myriad deeds.
Regarding "revealing the principle through practice": by means of the *prajñā* of contemplative observation, one awakens to the *prajñā* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
By practicing the myriad practices, one then accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
As for the teaching being Prajñā, the twelvefold division of the teachings is the Prajñā of letters (*vyañjana-prajñā*);
for while Prajñā is the wisdom that illuminates the objective realm, the twelvefold division of the teachings is the wisdom that illuminates the capacities of sentient beings.
As for "practice is itself liberation": because liberation is the wondrous function of the *dharmatā*, and all myriad practices are likewise the wondrous function that accords with conditions.

Furthermore, since principle permeates teaching and practice, the *dharmakāya* is itself *prajñā* and liberation; thus, the nature is entirely realized as cultivation, and therefore principle permeates [all].

[This is] practice. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) pervades all sūtras; therefore, the principle extends throughout the teachings. It is directly the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), not [merely] the non-Dharma-body.

The Dharma-body must necessarily possess both prajñā and liberation. If the Dharma-body were separated from these two virtues, it would be the principle of partial truth (pratisaṃvid-śūnyatā), and thus not the Dharma-body.

Regarding those who practice the teachings that penetrate the principle: practice is identical to nature; thus, practice penetrates the principle. The myriad practices of the Bodhisattva awaken sentient beings;
thus, practice penetrates the teaching. Direct liberation is not [mere] liberation; liberation must necessarily possess both the Dharma-body and Prajñā.
If liberation were divorced from these two virtues, it would be a solitary liberation rather than the Great Liberation.

Regarding the teaching that penetrates both principle and practice: the nature of words and letters is emptiness, which is itself the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Therefore, the teaching penetrates principle. By following the text, one accomplishes contemplation;
thus, the teaching penetrates practice. This is direct Prajñā, yet it is not [merely] Prajñā; for Prajñā must necessarily possess Dharmakāya and Vimukti.
If Prajñā does not possess these two virtues, it is merely the Prajñā of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā-prajñā), and not the Great Prajñā (Mahāprajñā).

Regarding the statement that "whether general or specific, it is also as in the previous examples": all sūtras possess the three aspects of essence (*tattva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and function (*vṛtti*); therefore, they are called "general.

When referring specifically to this sūtra alone, the Buddha is the essence, longevity is the characteristic, and light is the function; because these are restricted to this [sūtra] and differ from others, they are called "specific.
Furthermore, the essence is the *dharmakāya*, the characteristic is *prajñā*, and the function is *vimukti*. Thus, the essence encompasses both the characteristic and the function.

The Dharma-body is itself prajñā and liberation. Thus, from the ultimate to the conventional, essence and function interpenetrate, and function interpenetrates essence and form. To mention one is to include all three;
this may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

Commentary: Regarding "either single or compound," this refers to the seven distinct categories formed by the three single [elements]—person, phenomenon, and analogy—and the three compounds, together with the one complete [set].

The Commentary states: "The *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Vaipulya) fully possesses the person, the dharma, and the metaphor. "Great" (*mahā*) refers to the Greatness of Essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*). The essence of the dharma is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive;

it is called "great" because it is all-encompassing in accordance with its own nature. "Vaipulya" (Extensive) refers to the Greatness of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*). "Vai" signifies "dharma," in the sense of "guiding and maintaining" (*avasthāpana*).

This is because the ocean-like qualities of intrinsic virtue (*guṇa*) can all be guided and maintained. "Pulya" (Extensive) refers to the Greatness of Function (*kriyā-mahattva*), which is the function of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
It is "vast" because it is expansive and extensive. The Buddha is a person, for he is one capable of realizing the three great [bodies]. *Avataṃsaka* is a metaphor;
it refers to the causal flowers of the bodhisattva’s cultivation of the ten thousand practices, which adorn the ocean-like fruition of the One Vehicle.
Regarding "The Dharma of the Great Expedient Person has no Analogue": the Dharma is the repayment of kindness through great expedients;

the Buddha is the person. "Expedient" refers to skillful means (*upāya*). "Repayment of kindness" is as stated in the sutra: "The Honored Śākyamuni, the Great Filial One, throughout kalpas repays his parental kindness."

Having accumulated causes to achieve perfect enlightenment, it is called "Great Expedient Means" (mahopāya). This expedient means of repaying gratitude is the provisional manifestation of the very essence itself, not a provisional manifestation external to that essence; therefore, it is called "Great."
Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as being without [the distinction between] Dharma and parable: the wondrous Dharma of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) is skillfully likened to the lotus flower.
There are three meanings in the sequence where the flower exists because of the lotus, the flower opens and the lotus appears, and the flower falls and the lotus is realized;

these serve as metaphors for the two gates of the Original and the Traces, and for the three meanings of establishing the provisional based on the real, opening the provisional to reveal the real, and abolishing the provisional to establish the real.
In the *Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa-sūtra*, the person is the metaphor for the dharmas that do not exist. The Bodhisattva is the person; the *ābharaṇa* (ornament) is the metaphor.
Just as an ornament adorns the body, it is used as a metaphor for how the myriad practices adorn the Dharma-body.
Regarding the metaphor of the "single dharma and the absence of a person" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: *prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*).

That the Sanskrit term is retained instead is because wisdom is considered light and superficial, whereas *prajñā* is revered; among the five reasons for not translating [Sanskrit terms], this falls under the category of "not translating due to its reverence."

Regarding the single metaphor of the Brahma-net which lacks [the distinction between] person and phenomena: it was when the Buddha observed the net-canopy banner of Mahābrahmā that he taught that immeasurable worlds are like the mesh of a net;
each and every world is distinct from one another, differing in infinite ways.
The gates of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so. Bodhisattvas adorn their Dharma-body with pure conduct (brahmacarya), just as the Brahmā King [adorns his realm].
The Brahma-net serves as its floral ornament.
When the Dharma is expounded by a person and illustrated through a human example, it is as in this sutra:

the Buddha proclaims the Dharma of the adornments of the primary and secondary realms and of rebirth through faith and aspiration; he employs the analogy of a great cartwheel, and hundreds of thousands of kinds of music play simultaneously.
This is the analogy. [The] *Chao* [states]:
"All merits arise from the Buddha. The Buddha is the grove of merits and the treasury of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
As the Sūtra says: "The thoughts in the minds of beings as numerous as the atoms of all lands may be counted; the water in the great oceans may be drunk up; space may [be measured]."
The wind may be measured and tied, but one cannot fully describe the Buddha’s merits.
To take them briefly, one sets forth those that are most essential; that is, to set forth what is essential means to select and excerpt it.
To take its essentials means to omit what is secondary. To transcribe means to record and clarify it; that is, to annotate so as to make it manifest.
If one copies and records [this] in a commentary, then the text of the notes will become clear, radiant, manifest, and fully evident.
Regarding the phrase "the awakening of self-nature is the meaning of Buddha": this refers to the saying that "to see with the eyes of form or seek with the ears of sound is to walk a deviant path.

If one says that another is the Buddha while oneself becomes a demon, [one fails to realize that] the two types of awakening—original and initial—are inherent in self-nature. As the *Awakening of Faith* states:

The meaning of *original enlightenment* (*prakṛti-awakening*) is spoken in contrast to the meaning of *initial enlightenment* (*ādi-awakening*). This is because initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment.

The meaning of initial enlightenment arises because there is non-enlightenment (*a-awakening*) based upon original enlightenment; and because there is initial enlightenment based upon non-enlightenment.
The essence of self-nature awakening shines universally. As for "those who explain the meaning of the sutra," this refers to those who, because sentient beings are mired in delusion...

Awakened. Therefore, the Tathāgata awakens and illuminates them with the true light of *prajñā*. Now that the essence of awakening universally illumines all, is this not precisely the meaning of the sutras?
As it has been said of old: "The outgoing breath does not engage with manifold conditions; the incoming breath does not dwell within the aggregates or realms.
One constantly recites such sutras, numbering hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of volumes.

The *Chao* states: "That which is phenomena is itself principle," and so forth; this is the gate of the mutual identity of phenomenon and principle (*lǐ-shì xiāngjí mén*). Because phenomena are identical with principle, phenomena necessarily accord with principle.

Furthermore, the five phrases concerning "that which is principle" constitute the gate of the accomplishment of phenomena based on principle (*yī lǐ chéng shì mén*). Accordingly, as the mind becomes pure, one awakens to the fact that the Pure Land is solely the purity of mind.

This is the principle of the true basis; thus, the Buddha-land is pure, evoking the adornment of both the environment and its inhabitants. This is the matter truly accomplished through that principle.
Since the matter is established based on the principle, the matter must necessarily accord with the principle.

"Awakening" (*bodhi*) is the general meaning; it explains the aforementioned "awakening as intrinsic nature," which is the meaning of "Buddha. Regarding the phrase "within the essence of awakening," it explains the aforementioned "immeasurable awakening as intrinsic nature," which is the meaning of "Amitābha.
As for "vast" (*viśāla*), it is named according to its function; "vast" carries the sense of being extensive and broad. Regarding "extensive":
this essence of awakening inherently possesses wondrous functions more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, which arise subtly and operate secretly.
It should be understood that this is without rest and without exhaustion. As for its "vastness," this inexhaustible function is identical in every respect to the nature of awakening;
it has no boundaries and no limitations. As for its being "great," it receives its name from its very essence, with the meaning of being eternally pervasive.

This "essence" does not refer to a "greatness" that is contrasted with the small, where there would be a "small" outside of the "great" to be excluded; such [a distinction] would still be a limitation.
Limitation. Now, the essence of awakening is itself boundless, transcending all measures; it is provisionally named "Great. Regarding "perpetual and pervasive":
"perpetual" means it extends vertically through the three periods of time. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "That which is called 'Great' is termed 'Perpetual.
"Pervasive" means it encompasses horizontally the ten directions. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "That which is called 'Great' has a nature as vast and expansive as empty space."
Regarding their chronological order: Amitābha Buddha is the ancient Buddha, for it has been ten kalpas since that Buddha attained Buddhahood;
this Buddha is newly accomplished, for Śākyamuni Tathāgata only recently attained the Way during the time of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty.
Thus, "that is the fundamental and this is the beginning" means that the one who attained Buddhahood first is the fundamental, while the one who attained it now is the beginning.
In terms of cause and effect, this Buddhist teaching that causes one to be reborn there is the cause; that one thereby attains the vision of Amitābha Buddha is the fruit.
Regarding the statement "this is the root and that is the beginning": the cultivation of the cause is the root, and the realization of the fruit is the beginning.

Regarding the mutual fusion of the original and the initial: when the essence of awakening is within the bonds of affliction, it is called "original awakening" (benjue); when the essence of awakening has emerged from those bonds, it is called "initial awakening" (shijue).

Since the nature of ignorance is empty, being within the bonds is itself emerging from them; thus, the original fuses with the initial. When ignorance is completely severed, initial awakening becomes identical to original awakening;
thus, the initial fuses with the original.
Those of dull faculties who are satisfied with guarding at the level of phenomenal characteristics merely know to seek Buddhahood through birth;

they abandon this for that, not knowing the principle of Mind-only. It is because of the principle that one finally realizes that within phenomena there exists the ultimate truth, and that it is not merely phenomenal characteristics.
This refutes the delusion of those with dull faculties who cling to phenomena and are confused about the principle. Those of sharp faculties revere the rational nature...
Those who cling to emptiness merely know that self-nature is mind-only; they become addicted to a stubborn void and do not believe in the Western Pure Land.
Because they claim to follow principle, they finally come to realize that the ultimate principle does not depart from phenomenal appearances and does not fall into a stubborn void.
This refutes the delusion of those with sharp faculties who cling to principle while remaining confused about phenomena.

Furthermore, following this sutra, one might fear that someone could ask: "Since the teachings of the Pure Land all ultimately converge upon the principle of true nature (li-xing), practitioners need only directly awaken to the principle of their own mind;
why must they necessarily practice nianfo and seek rebirth there?

Therefore, it is said that this sutra fundamentally relies upon those [Pure Land] names and titles to manifest the principle of one's own mind, which is identical in intent to the *Sixteen Contemplations Sutra*. This is because [the latter] observes...

The *Jing shu chao* states: "The practitioner should know that, based upon the nature of the mind, one contemplates the environment and its inhabitants; thus the environment and inhabitants become manifest.
By relying upon the environment and inhabitants, one contemplates the nature of the mind; thus the nature of the mind easily manifests. Now, this sutra relies upon those names and titles."
This reveals my own mind; it is precisely in agreement with that [previous] intent.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva should still descend [to a lower level], for he may fear another question being asked: "Those who have not yet awakened to the mind should practice the recitation of the Buddha's name and seek rebirth [in the Pure Land]."
For one who has already awakened to the mind, this may not necessarily be required; therefore, it is said that a bodhisattva should still remain close to the Buddha.
This can be understood from the citation of evidence regarding those who have already awakened seeking rebirth, found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
An ancient said that below the Avataṃsaka Sūtra lies the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), which consists of contemplating the mind so that it accords with principle (*li*).

Because the Avataṃsaka is a discourse on the manifestation of nature (*xing*), all phenomena can be contemplated as the mind in accordance with principle. From the Vaipulya (Pafangdeng) sūtras downward, however, phenomena and principle remain distinct.

If the mental dharmas have not yet been immediately realized, how can one be said to accord with principle? For this reason, this sutra is judged to belong to the Vaipulya (fangděng) class; it should not be said to accord with principle.
The ancient masters answer below: "Definitive meaning" refers to the Avataṃsaka, while "indefinitive meaning" refers to the Vaipulya and below.

As for "only the one mind," within the mind of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), one perceives neither the refined nor the coarse, neither the large nor the small, because all are identical within the wondrous mind.
Commentary: Regarding the title "Mother Buddha" used in the sutras, this refers to Lady Māyā.

Because she gave birth to all Buddhas through the illusory dharma-gate, before the World-Honored One had descended to be born, the Buddhas of the ten directions three times each day preached the dharma-gate of receiving birth within Lady Māyā’s womb.
When the ten months were complete, he was born from her right side. And it is said: "How much more so for Śākyamuni alone?"
"I was her mother. In the future Bhadrakalpa, the thousand Buddhas shall likewise have me as their mother;
in every life where a Buddha is born, I shall be his mother. As for the son who is a Buddha, he is Rāhula. [The Buddha] said:
'Not only was I the son of Śākyamuni, but I shall also be the eldest son of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.'"
Commentary: Because they are multilayered and unimpeded, they are called "interpenetrating. "Profoundly" describes the manner of this interpenetration;
it refers to the principle of the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses.
The Sub-commentary (*Chao*) states: "That which is Sanskrit can immediately become Chinese" means that every sentence is in Sanskrit and every sentence is in Chinese.

"Revealing what is not outside of the esoteric" means that Chinese is explicit and easy to understand, whereas Sanskrit is cryptic and difficult to know. That it is both Sanskrit and Chinese reveals that it is not outside of the esoteric.
This should be understood by analogy with the section below on "Chinese and [Sanskrit]."
Regarding "when there is brightness within darkness," the *Cantong qi* states: "When there is darkness within brightness, do not encounter it with darkness;
when there is brightness within darkness, do not behold it with brightness. Brightness and darkness face one another, like preceding and following steps."
Beyond the limit of majestic sound, one does not depart from the gate of this very day; at the gate of this very day, one does not depart from beyond the limit of majestic sound.
At midnight it is perfectly bright, yet at dawn it is not revealed.

They mutually reflect and conceal one another. This is explained in terms of two dharmas penetrating each other: for example, when the eastern mirror enters the western mirror, the eastern mirror reflects the western mirror, while the western mirror conceals the eastern mirror;
it is the same when the western mirror enters the eastern mirror. Their interpenetration is layered and manifold. This is explained in terms of layered mutual reflection:
