Prajñā purifies and refines clinging attachments; once one possesses the correct wisdom of the Mahāyāna, and having possessed that correct wisdom, one will necessarily understand true emptiness.
One does not repudiate the Pure Land. If the teachings concerning the Pure Land were not addressed to Śāriputra, to whom else were they addressed?
Commentary: Regarding Maudgalyāyana’s transformation of his body into various sizes: The dragon brothers Nanda and Upananda dwell on the slopes of Mount Sumeru.
Whenever the Buddha flies through the air up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, the dragons become resentful.

They spit forth black clouds and dark mists to obscure the three luminaries, and they coil their bodies around Mount Sumeru seven times, dragging their tails through the ocean waters while resting their heads [upon the mountain].

At the summit of the mountain, Maudgalyāyana then manifested his body twofold; he circled Mount Sumeru fourteen times, with his tail trailing beyond the outer seas and his head resting upon the Brahma palace.
The dragon remained exceedingly wrathful and rained down vajra-sand. Maudgalyāyana transformed the sand into precious flowers, light, soft, and lovely to behold.
Still not ceasing his anger, Maudgalyāyana then transformed himself into a minute body and entered within the dragon’s body, passing from its eye into its ear.

The breath issued from his mouth, entered his ears, and exited through his nose. The dragon suffered intense pain, and his mind was finally subdued. As for the heretics who sought to move the mountain:
there were five hundred members of the heretical sect who used incantations to shift the mountain. After one month had passed, the base of the mountain began to tremble.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "If this mountain moves, it will cause great harm. Thereupon, at the summit of the mountain, he performed a *dhyāna* concentration...

He sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), yet the mountain remained unmoved. The non-Buddhists said to one another, "Our doctrine moves the mountain; we calculated that it would surely shift by now.
How is it so firmly fixed? If it returns to its original state, it must be this śramaṇa who has caused it to be thus. Realizing their own power was weak, they took refuge in the Buddha’s Dharma.
Regarding "lifting it to the Brahma Heaven": When the Great King Virūḍhaka exterminated the Śākya clan, Maudgalyāyana wished to save them.

The Buddha, however, declared that their karma was fixed and unavoidable, and did not grant his request. Maudgalyāyana then used his supernatural powers to place five hundred members of the Śākya clan in a bowl and entrusted it to the Brahma Heaven.
After the Śākyas had been destroyed, he lifted the bowl to look at it; there was nothing but blood and water. Thus one knows the power of karma. The Buddha...
Nor can he save them. As for the one who stopped the chariot:
Jīvaka was a skilled physician who had already been reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; because the bhikṣu Lianyin was ill, he mounted his vehicle and went there to inquire after him.
It happened that the devas were out on an excursion. Jīvaka, riding in his carriage, did not alight but merely joined his palms in salutation.

Maudgalyāyana used his supernatural powers to bring the carriage to a halt; only then did Jīvaka descend from the carriage to pay his respects. When asked what he intended to do, Jīvaka explained his purpose in detail.
Maudgalyāyana replied, "Abstaining from food is essential. Only after Maudgalyāyana released him was Jīvaka able to proceed.
Regarding "burning the hall": Śakra Devānām Indra had constructed the Hall of Victory (Vaijayanta), which was adorned with extraordinary beauty.

When Maudgalyāyana went to see it, all the celestial maidens hid themselves away and would not come out. Maudgalyāyana thought to himself, "Śakra is attached to pleasure and does not cultivate the root of the Path.

Thereupon, by means of his supernormal powers, he set the Hall of Victory ablaze until it collapsed in a brilliant blaze. He then spoke words concerning impermanence and other such truths to Śakra. Śakra rejoiced.
The rear hall is solemn and majestic, free from the color of smoke and ash.
"Shaking off" (dǒu sǒu) means shaking off the dust of worldly toil; this refers to the sweeping away of accumulated burdens below. "Winnowing" (táo tào) means winnowing away habitual tendencies;
this refers to the clarifying and purifying of body and mind below.

The Commentary states: "Skillful in the horizontal and vertical" refers to horizontal exposition, vertical exposition, exposition that sweeps away [delusions], and exposition that establishes [truth], and so forth.
"Shattering the heat and rebuking the crookedness" means that through its dialectical arguments, it can shatter the heat of false views and rebuke the crookedness of false views.

Regarding "the child binding the mother": the Venerable One lost his father while still young; his mother wished to remarry, but because he was bound by [filial] affection for her, she did not [do so].
To fulfill one's intention is like a cord tied to a fan; hence it is called "the cord of the fan.

Skillfully discerning meanings constitutes the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid). Elaborating upon the path of the teachings constitutes the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid).
He attained great eloquence; therefore, he was foremost in debate.
*Shu* (Commentary): "Tending cattle" means the sense of herding oxen.
*Chao* (Excerpts): Regarding "Kāśyapa’s Praise": after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Ānanda ascended the seat, and Kāśyapa, together with the assembly, praised him, saying:
"His face is like the pure full moon; his eyes are like blue lotuses. The great ocean waters of the Buddha-dharma flow into Ānanda’s heart"—this refers to that.
Regarding the retribution of eating horse-barley: the Buddha and his disciples stayed for three months in the village of Vairaṇyā and subsisted on horse-barley.
To repay past karmic retributions. Only Gālavana received offerings in the heavens.
Regarding the term "ji-heng" (璣衡): it refers to the *xuánjī* (璇璣) and *yùhéng* (玉衡). [Commentary: *Xuán* means beautiful pearls; *jī* means mechanism.
Pearls are used to adorn the mechanism to represent the revolving body of heaven. *Héng* means horizontal; it refers to the horizontal tube (*héngxiāo*). By means of...
Jade was used for the tubes; these were set horizontally to observe the *ji* (the central axis) and to align the movements of the seven celestial bodies, much like the modern armillary sphere.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the stūpa still rejected the cowries": King Aśoka paid homage to the various stūpas of the Arhats.
When he reached the stūpa of Bakula, he spoke this verse: "Though you have personally refined away ignorance, you have brought little benefit to the world.
Because of his offering of twenty cowrie shells, the cowrie shells flew out from the stūpa and landed upon the King's feet. The ministers were astonished and marveled at why this was so.
This is truly because throughout his life, the Venerable One was secluded, tranquil, and possessed few desires;

that his stūpa still possesses such power that its provisions are fully sufficient—this is the first meaning of its name. That it remains undiminished to this day—this is the second meaning of its name.

That whatever is sought is obtained as desired—this is the third meaning of its name. As for those compared to conch shells, during the sequence of the Venerable One’s listening to the Dharma, they were mostly...

He was dozing. The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why are you sleeping? You are like a snail, a clam, or an oyster; once asleep for a thousand years, you shall not hear the name of the Buddha."
Regarding "Delighting in Seeing the Illuminating Vajra Samādhi": it refers to focusing the mind with the desire to see the seeing-nature that illuminates all phenomena;
this is called "Delighting in Seeing the Illuminating. This samādhi can destroy all phenomena, yet all phenomena cannot destroy this samādhi.
Therefore it is named "Vajra.

The commentary states: Regarding the "difficult elder brother and difficult younger brother," Chen Shi, the Taichu Chang of the Eastern Han, had two sons. The elder was named Yuanfang, and the younger was named Jifang;
both possessed brilliant talent. When the sons of these two brothers each discussed their respective fathers' virtues, they went to see their grandfather.
To determine their relative superiority, it is truly said that Yuanfang is difficult to be the elder brother, and Jifang is difficult to be the younger brother.

Regarding the statement that "the King and numbers are mutually pervasive": outside the King there are no numbers, and outside numbers there is no King. Because the One Mind is all-pervasive, that which the King pervades is [the Mind].
Commentary: That which governs the cycle of good and evil is as follows: the first six consciousnesses encompass the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral;
they are capable of creating the three types of outflowing karma and can summon the two retributions of suffering and pleasure. The seventh consciousness is of the nature of obscured-neutral;
it is constantly associated with the eight afflictions—self-delusion, self-view, self-love, and self-pride—and in every moment it clings to the [ālayavijñāna] as its object.
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses is taken as the self; however, only the eighth consciousness is of an unobscured-neutral nature (*anivṛta-avyākṛta*).
It does not create karma such as good or evil, because it is the sovereign lord of the collective retribution for the duration of a single lifetime.
Regarding the fifty-one mental factors (*caitasika*), there are five universal (*sarvatraga*), five object-specific (*viniyata*), eleven wholesome (*kuśala*),
six root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*), twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and four indeterminate (*aniyata*).
The three meanings of "always arising in dependence upon the mind" constitute the explanation of the term *caitta* (mental factors).

"Always arising in dependence upon the mind" means that when the mind-king (*cittarāja*) does not arise, the mental factors do not arise. "Associated with the mind" means they are always associated with the mind-king and never separate from it.
"Belonging to the mind" means that the mental factors belong to the mind-king, just as the eight consciousnesses have five universal (*sarvatraga*) factors.
The seven consciousnesses comprise eighteen [factors]; the first five comprise thirty-four; and the sixth consciousness comprises all fifty-one.
"Wisdom-awakening" refers to Chan Master Yongming Shou. Regarding "desire, perception, and so forth": desire (*chanda*) is among the specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-bhūmika*);
its nature is the longing for an object of pleasure, and its function is to serve as the basis for diligence (*vīrya*). Perception (*saṃjñā*) is among the universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*).
Its nature is the grasping of signs within an object; its function is the establishment of various names and expressions.

Contact (*sparśa*)—which is the same as *sparśa* among the universal mental factors—is characterized by causing the mind and mental associates to come into contact with an object; its function is to serve as the basis for sensation, perception, volition, and so forth. Wisdom (*prajñā*).

This refers to *prajñā* (wisdom) among the object-specific mental factors (*viśeṣa-viṣaya-ka*). Its nature is the discernment of the objects under investigation, and its function is the severing of doubt.

*Smṛti* (mindfulness) refers to *smṛti* among the object-specific mental factors. Its nature is causing the mind to clearly remember objects previously experienced, and its function is serving as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*). *Cetanā* (volition)...
Volition (*cetanā*) is that among the universal mental factors whose nature is to cause the mind to engage in activity; its function is to direct the mind toward wholesome categories and so forth.
Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is that among the object-specific mental factors whose nature is to maintain a firm conviction regarding a determined object; its function is to be unshakeable by others.
Attention (*manaskāra*) is that among the universal mental factors whose nature is to alert the mind; [its function is to direct the mind] toward the focal object.
Its function is to draw the mind [toward its object]. Samādhi is the concentration (*samādhi*) among the five particular mental states;

its nature is to cause the mind to focus intently on the object of observation without distraction, and its function is to serve as the basis for wisdom (*jñāna*). Vedanā is the feeling (*vedanā*) among the five universal mental states;
its nature is to experience objects that are disagreeable, agreeable, or neither, and its function is to give rise to desire (*chanda*).
Kāśyapa, as for those who wish to count with the mind: Kāśyapa practices the twelve dhūta ascetic virtues;
he delights in transcending the three realms and delights in realizing nirvāṇa; he abandons the five worldly desires as if discarding snot or spittle.

Pūrṇa, as for those who count with mental conceptions: Pūrṇa is foremost in preaching the Dharma; he expounds suffering and emptiness and deeply discusses the true mark (dharmatā); he takes only conceptions as [his object].

First, regarding *saṃjñā* (perception): because he is able to observe the capacities of sentient beings and preach the Dharma, proclaiming it through the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
Regarding *sparśa* (contact) and *saṃkhyā* (calculation): Kātyāyana is foremost in debate;

when engaging in discussion, as the guest and host exchange questions and answers, various sublime meanings arise upon contact with the objects of experience, mutually interpenetrating so that both parties attain the joy of the Dharma. Regarding *prajñā* (wisdom): Śāriputra is... [the foremost].
Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom and had attained the liberation of being free from doubt; thus, it is precisely appropriate that his function is to sever doubt.
As for the recollection of Upāli: Upāli was foremost in the observance of the precepts because he constantly maintained right mindfulness, clearly recording and never forgetting them.
Only then can one restrain body and mind so as not to commit transgressions or violations. As for Rāhula, he was foremost in secret practice (*raho-guhyacaryā*);
because such secret practice cannot be accomplished without right reflection (*samyak-manasikāra*).

As for Subhūti, he was foremost in the excellence of understanding emptiness (*śūnyatā-adhimukti*); his resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) was firm and could not be led astray, and he was liberated from all existence (*bhava*).
Regarding "making an effort" (*manasikāra*): Aniruddha was foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). By means of the divine eye of the Hīnayāna, he attained supernormal power through mental effort;
by making an effort, he could see the great trichiliocosm, but if he did not make an effort, he could not even see through a needle's eye.

Regarding "samādhi": Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). These powers are produced from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for his purity and extreme radiance were penetrating.
"Painful! Ānanda is foremost among those of great learning; he has attained the *dhāraṇī* of syllables and receives teachings without loss.
These two [the King and Ānanda] support one another to bring about awakening. If the King were not there, from whom would it be initiated? With whom would it correspond? To whom would it belong?
It would be like a minister who has lost his sovereign or a disciple without a teacher; having nothing to rely upon, by what means could awakening be achieved?"

Awakening must necessarily be supported by the mental factors (*caitta*). If the King [the mind] were not accompanied by these factors, then the factors such as the ten wholesome dharmas would not arise;

the mind could not be led to contact objects, nor could it apprehend those objects before it. Furthermore, everything from right mindfulness to meditative concentration and wisdom would be absent, and awakening could not be achieved.
Thus, the King must necessarily be supported by the mental factors.

Whether it be the King (the *ālayavijñāna*) or its enumerations (the mental factors), they all initially arise from a single thought of ignorance, which, by deluding the source of one's own mind, gives rise to the eight consciousnesses.
From these eight consciousnesses—the sovereign minds (*cittarāja*)—the mental factors (*caitta*) are induced, just as clouds and mist arise from the sky, or waves and surges emerge from the sea.

Now, when the King and its enumerations mutually support one another to awaken to their own mind, then thick clouds and thin mists will altogether become a clear sky, and great waves and ripples will subside.
All become still waters; throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*, there is but the single true mind, wherein no further categories or distinctions can be found.

The *Chao* states: Do not say that the Pure Land is something Bodhisattvas disdain. "Dishonoring" (*xie*) here means "to cleanse. To "not cleanse" means not regarding that Dharma as pure and thus distancing oneself from it.
There are those who claim that seeking rebirth through mindfulness of the Buddha is merely for the sake of deluding the ignorant, and is not [for the wise].
If this present sutra were merely a matter for Mahayana bodhisattvas, then it would not have been heard by the bodhisattvas together with the others.
Since they did indeed hear it together, how could one claim that the Pure Land is something bodhisattvas would find unworthy of pursuit?
Furthermore, there are three meanings: first, both are discussed in terms of the two benefits [of self and others]; second, it is discussed solely in terms of self-benefit;
third, it is discussed solely in terms of benefiting others.
Regarding "the objects of compassion and wisdom": compassion refers to the three types of compassion; wisdom refers to the ten kinds of wisdom.

Compassion and wisdom are the subjective faculties that perceive, while the Buddha-way and sentient beings are the objects perceived. As for the previous statement, "seeking upward through wisdom," without wisdom one cannot seek upward.

There is no lack of compassion; there is no such thing as "descending" [to the world] without it. This means that one first awakens to the Dharma-realm of Vairocana and subsequently cultivates the practice-gate of Samantabhadra;
first one mobilizes great compassion of identical essence, and only thereafter does one universally enter into the realms of worldly toil.

Regarding the combination of subject and object: sentient beings (*sattva*) are the subject, and awakening (*bodhi*) is the object. By combining this subject and object and naming them accordingly, one says "Awakened Sentient Being" (*bodhisattva*).

The mind is the wisdom that acts as the perceiving subject, and thus belongs to the category of the subject; principle (*tattva*) is the objective sphere that is perceived, and thus belongs to the category of the object.

Therefore, regarding the category of those for whom benefiting sentient beings is the priority: at the very moment they first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], they universally intend to act for the sake of all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm.

Even after they have realized the fruit [of Buddhahood], they still retain afflictions to sustain rebirth and do not enter parinirvāṇa. This is what it means for a bodhisattva to prioritize benefiting sentient beings.
To universally awaken all beings means that because sentient beings are inexhaustible, my vows are inexhaustible;
as long as there is even one sentient being who has not attained Buddhahood, I vow not to realize perfect enlightenment myself, and so forth.
Those who hasten toward quiescence for their own peace claim they have already attained *nirvāṇa*;

they are incapable of further responsibility and merely contemplate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, having no joy or delight in the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas. Those of great and powerful diligence are as it is said:
"Even if a wheel of glowing iron were to spin upon the crown of my head, I would never, because of this suffering, fall back from *bodhi*."
The mind:
one who seeks great bodhi does not seek the karmic rewards of humans or devas, nor those of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;

rather, they vow that all sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm shall simultaneously attain bodhi together with them. Regarding the "three incalculable eons": this does not belong to the Hīnayāna (Zàng) teachings.
There are three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. According to the *Awakening of Faith*, one must pass through ten thousand *kalpas* before the mind that has achieved faith (*śraddhā-siddha-citta*) arises.

Furthermore, after passing through another three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, one reaches the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva and so forth, becoming fully endowed with all merits—such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
coolness and immutability; true knowledge and awareness; and even the ten powers and the four [fearlessnesses].
The eighteen unshared [qualities] and so forth, which are free from fear.

At the end of the sixth section of the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Those who believe in the Great Dharma" means they believe in the dharma of the single mind and true suchness (*tathatā*). "Those who understand the great meaning" means...
To understand the meaning of the one mind and the three great aspects: to "arouse the great mind" is to arouse the aspiration to seek the supreme above and transform those below;
to "proceed toward the great fruit" is to proceed toward the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi; to "practice the great conduct" is to practice the conduct of benefiting oneself and others.
"To realize the Great Way" means to realize the unsurpassed, wondrous Way of the One Vehicle.

"To believe, understand, and give rise to this vow of great inclusion" means that when a bodhisattva gives rise to a vow, they must first believe in and understand the wondrous principle, and only then resolve their mind by making the Four Great Vows before the objects of the Three Jewels. "To proceed toward this timing of the Great" means...

Because one does not pass through the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and does not produce the unsurpassed fruit of the One Vehicle, that which is realized and subsumed within this Greatness of Virtue is the wondrous path of the One Vehicle;
for the One Vehicle is itself all the merits of the One Vehicle.
"Great in number" means that his vows are vast and profound, such as the *Innumerable Non-action Vows* (Amitābha’s) and even the *Vow-King of Samantabhadra*.

"Great in virtue" means that his myriad virtues are perfected, such as the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the ten concentrations (*samādhi*), and even the ten patiences (*kṣānti*) found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Karma is great, meaning it is the fulfillment of the myriad practices, such as the Ten Practices and Ten Transferences of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, up to the ten thousand practices of Samantabhadra.
As for the number being the vows, they are like the twelve great vows of Bhaisajyaguru and the forty-eight vows of Amitābha;
the vow-power of Vairocana pervades the entire dharma-realm. Since the dharma-realm is inexhaustible, the power of his vows is likewise inexhaustible.
The five grades refer to the stage of five grades of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) in the Tiantai school: 1. **The Grade of Rejoicing**: The beginner accords with principle;

they rejoice for themselves and rejoice for others. 2. **The Grade of Reading and Reciting**: Ancient teachings permeate the mind, and the sprout of the Way grows. 3. **The Grade of Preaching the Dharma**:

Furthermore, one adds the preaching of the Dharma, expounding and disseminating it according to reality. 4. **The Grade of Concurrent Practice of the Six Perfections**: Through the power of correct contemplation, the six perfections are practiced concurrently.
[This concludes] the fifth section on the correct practice of the six perfections. Regarding the contemplative practice of the six perfections, there are no two distinct characteristics.
Commentary: As for "the fusion of self-nature, truth, and delusion": awakening is truth and sentient beings are delusion. "Fusion" means thorough integration.
Furthermore, it means "melting and integrating. To "integrate" means that there is no delusion outside of reality, and no reality outside of delusion;
for afflictions are themselves bodhi, and the defilement of the three delusions is itself the secret treasury of the three virtues.

Thus, an ancient said: "To sever and eliminate delusive thoughts is to increase one's illness; to strive toward suchness is likewise an error. As for "melting," since delusion no longer exists, reality...
Nor does it stand; for when the stages of the Bodhisattva are exhausted, the eight consciousnesses dissolve and vanish, and both awakening and non-awakening are completely merged and transformed.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The conditioned nature of true reality is empty, for that which arises from conditions is like an illusion.
The unconditioned has no arising or ceasing; it is as unreal as flowers in the sky. To speak of the false is to reveal the various truths, yet the false and the true are equally both false."
The Sub-commentary states: "The True that is unchanging yet follows conditions. "True" refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Unchanging" means that it possesses no alteration and cannot be destroyed.
"Follows conditions" means that it accords with the conditions of the nine dharma-realms. It is called an "enlightened sentient being" because it is delusion within the very midst of the True;
this is explained from the perspective of the unchanging following conditions.

Regarding "delusory phenomena are established while their essence is empty": "delusory" refers to the single thought-moment of ignorance (*avidyā*). "Establishing phenomena" means bringing about the three subtleties and the six coarsenesses—the various manifold phenomena.
"Essence is empty" means that these afflictions, karma, and suffering are, in their very substance, entirely empty.
This is called the "awakening of sentient beings," because delusion is itself the real. This is explained in terms of "unchangingness amidst following conditions. Since it is already delusion...

Yet, if it were truly real, then reality itself could not be established. Since delusion is identical to reality, then delusion cannot be established. From the very beginning, it is free from all names and characteristics;
thus, neither reality nor delusion can be established. Since both reality and delusion are unestablished, there is only wondrous, enlightened clarity.
To perfectly illumine the Dharma-realm is nothing other than this single mind. To reach the state of being solely this single mind is the true fulfillment of the Great Bodhicitta;
who else could it be but a Mahāsattva?
*Shu*: "The Buddha is the King of the Dharma" means that the Buddha is the king among all dharmas, and furthermore, because as the Dharma King he [rules] over the three realms.

*Chao*: "Faith is the foremost of the virtues of practice" means: "practice" refers to the gates of practice (*xingmen*), and "virtue" refers to actual virtue (*shide*). The myriad practices (*wanxing*) are like...

The ocean of the Buddha-dharma consists of generosity and ethical discipline, up to and including the ten thousand practices of Samantabhadra and the ten thousand virtues—such as the eternal, blissful, self, and pure;
the ten powers and fearlessnesses; the eighteen unique qualities; and even the immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dhāraṇīs.
Faith is that which enables entry. As a sutra says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit; faith can nurture all roots of goodness;
faith can ensure one reaches the stage of the Tathāgata. Therefore, faith is the foremost of all practices and all virtues.
To approach, make offerings to, and praise all beings is the practice of Subhūti’s moving of things.

To treat enemies and kin with equality and not cause them harm or distress is the practice of great compassion’s impartiality. That at the time of his birth there were ten kinds of auspicious omens is the practice of the response of supreme merit and auspiciousness.
That these are the practice itself which is liberation, and liberation itself which is practice, is the explanation of the wondrous word "Subhūti. Thus it is.

Regarding the practice of understanding: as with the various practices mentioned above, all are cultivation arising from the complete nature (*dharmatā*); they are not practices that involve conditioned existence or deliberate effort.

Sublime Virtue (*Sudhana*) is one who possesses wisdom; if the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) were not perfected, one would not achieve sublime virtue. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One sees the Buddha clearly."
His nature is like that of Samantabhadra and others; thus, Samantabhadra represents wisdom (*jñāna*). Regarding him being the mother of all Buddhas, a sutra states:
"The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas, and skillful means (*upāya*) is their father. Among all teachers of the multitude, there are none who are not born from these.
As for his being the teacher of Śākyamuni, the sutras refer to Mañjuśrī as the teacher of the seven Buddhas. Thus, he is the realization of practice.
Regarding the interpretation above: "cultivating the whole as identical to nature" is not a conceptual understanding that knows emptiness through emptiness.
The phrase "the Tathāgata relies on the ultimate meaning of the Middle Way" extracts the character *fa* (dharma) from the phrase "the dharma of the *Chūtòu* [Commentary].

The phrase "wherein the Bodhisattva enters this stage" extracts the character *rù* (enter). These two phrases, "thereby continuing and flourishing the Buddha-seed," are extracted from the [original] text.

Regarding the two characters for "correct position" (*zhengwei*), the character "correct" (*zheng*) has not yet been made explicit; therefore, it is explained through analogy: the essence fundamentally abides in correctness. As for "relying on the Middle Way":
the Two Vehicles rely on the Truth (*zhen*), while the Provisional Vehicles rely on the Conventional (*su*); both constitute partial positions.
The Tathāgata relies on the Middle Way, which is to abide in the correct position of the Dharma. When a Bodhisattva enters this stage, they enter the correct position of the Dharma.
"The Great Lord embodies the Origin and dwells in Rectitude" means that the Son of Heaven embodies the virtue of the Qian Origin and occupies the correct position of the ninth and fifth lines.
"The Prince resides in the Eastern Palace" means that the East corresponds to Zhen; Zhen is the eldest son of Qian, and furthermore, it is from Zhen that the Sovereign emerges.
Therefore, it is called the Eastern Palace.

Furthermore, regarding the discussion by way of distinction: since the preceding text was still a general exposition and had not yet made distinctions, if one were to discuss it through further differentiation, then wisdom (*jñāna*) would also differ in terms of being provisional (*upāya*) or ultimate (*tattva*).
Provisional wisdom is the partial emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
This wisdom does not accord with the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena); therefore, it is called "expedient" (*upāya*). True wisdom, however, is the wisdom of the Middle Way within the Mahāyāna;

it accords with the *dharmatā*, and is therefore called "real. Expedient wisdom clarifies the existence of birth: expedient wisdom does not penetrate the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), nor does it realize that all is but mind (*cittamātra*).

Consequently, sentient beings and Buddhas appear remote from one another, and the pure and the defiled remain distinct. Taking one's own birth as the means to seek the Buddha of the other shore, one abandons this [world].

The five turbidities. To go to that Western Land means that one whose true wisdom illuminates non-arising truly understands the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), awakens to the clarity of mind-only (*cittamātra*), and realizes that the arising of beings and Buddhas are not two, and that purity and defilement are interfused.
Although one speaks of "reciting the Buddha's name," there is no Buddha outside the mind;
although one speaks of "rebirth," it is in truth non-arising. Regarding the latter two lines for those of dull faculties, there may be a question: "If it is the same purity..."

Regarding the two categories of "with birth" and "without birth": why is this distinction made? It is because there are those with sharp and dull faculties; thus, one cannot help but differentiate between them.
When entering the ultimate from the provisional, one first maintains the practice according to phenomena (*dharma*) and gradually enters into principle (*li*).
When the provisional and the ultimate are fused as one, then one is neither deluded regarding principle nor does one neglect phenomena.
If one were to discuss this by tracing it back to its source, the preceding passage would still be an analysis based on differentiation; it would not yet be a discussion tracing back to the source.
If one were to discuss it by tracing back to the source, then it is the same profound wisdom.
Commentary: "Compassion is unsurpassed. There are three kinds of compassion. First is compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).
Though there is no intentional effort to take sentient beings as an object, benefit spontaneously manifests for them. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "I truly do not go."
First is the power of the roots of goodness of charity, which enables sentient beings to witness such matters. Second is the compassion that takes phenomena as its object;

though it is without a mind that deliberately contemplates phenomena, it naturally illumines all phenomena universally, like the sun shining upon objects without making any distinctions. Third is the compassion without an object.
Without deliberate mental observation of principles, one naturally abides within the equality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
With unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), one gathers in all sentient beings; this compassion is unsurpassed. This refers to these three types of compassion.

Among the citations in the text, there are three instances of the different ways in which the two benefits (of self and others) are realized across the three periods of time. First, while in the mother’s womb, he already possessed a mind of loving-kindness;
this is present-time loving-kindness and is also loving-kindness for one's own benefit. Second, during a past life; third, when he was formerly a brahmin;
and fourth, during the time of Puṣya Buddha—these are all cases of past-time loving-kindness, and they are all likewise [for one's own benefit].
The fifth is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which is present compassion; this is compassion for the benefit of others.
The sixth is the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, which is future compassion; this is likewise compassion for the benefit of others.

The Commentary states: Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*’s description of ancient Buddhas emitting light to preach this sūtra—when the World-Honored One was at the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, he emitted light from the white tuft between his eyebrows, illuminating eighteen thousand lands in the eastern direction.

Within that light, the phenomena and characteristics of the dharma-realm, as well as the beginning and end of the arising of Buddhas, were perfectly manifested. Thereupon, Maitreya raised a doubt, and Mañjuśrī provided the answer. In that answer, it says:
In the past, after the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa had emitted this light, he immediately preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Now that the present Buddha has manifested this light, he likewise ought to preach this sūtra and others.

Commentary: To "thoroughly understand that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally neither good nor evil" means that that which accords with and benefits the two worlds [the present and future] is considered good, while that which opposes and harms the two worlds is considered evil.
Yet, the nature of phenomena is fundamentally devoid of both opposition and accord, as well as harm and benefit. Furthermore, regarding good and evil:
Regarding the method of duality: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) transcends all dualities; therefore, it is neither good nor evil.

Although it is said that one should cultivate goodness, to "cultivate" while not actually cultivating is because the nature of phenomena is fundamentally without goodness. To have goodness that can be cultivated is to violate the nature of phenomena;
this is the cultivation of evil, not the cultivation of goodness. One should know that there is no goodness to be cultivated—this is the true cultivation of goodness.
Although it is said that one "removes evil," that which is removed does not depart; for the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without evil.

To think there is evil that can be removed is to turn one's back on the nature of phenomena; this is to remove good, not to remove evil. To realize fully that there is no evil to be removed is the true removal of evil.
That not a single thought arises is true vigor (*vīrya*). As the ancients said: "If the mind of vigor arises, it is delusion, not vigor."
"Advancing. If one can keep the mind free from delusion, diligence will be boundless.
The Sub-commentary states: "Diligence represents the practice of aspiration. One aspires after having attained faith; thus, aspiration is the diligence born of the power of faith."
One acts after having made a vow. "Acting" refers to the diligence born of the power of one's vows. [Commentary:
Mañjuśrī’s wisdom is the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) that illuminates everything without exception.

Now, his self-nature shines through heaven and reflects upon earth, glorifying the past and resonating through the present; there is nothing it does not illuminate. Maitreya’s compassion is the great compassion based on the three conditions.
Regarding "there is nothing it does not contain": now, the self-nature encompasses empty space and embraces the entire dharma-realm; there is nothing it does not contain. The *Chao* states:

"That the vastness of self-nature is the meaning of Samantabhadra" means that its practice pervades the dharma-realm, hence it is called "Universal" (*Samanta*), and its rank is adjacent to the ultimate sages, hence it is called "Worthy" (*Bhadra*).
It thus possesses the sense of vastness. Now, this self-nature extends vertically through all time and spreads horizontally across all space, for it has no boundaries.
That the self-nature’s perfect penetration is the meaning of Avalokiteśvara refers to the fact that by cultivating the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, the conditioned mind attains mastery;
this is the meaning of "perfect penetration. Now, because the self-nature’s perfect penetration is thoroughly realized and free from all obstructions, it is so named.
If each possesses [the others] such that their names are mutually interpenetrating, then as there is nothing that does not illuminate, there is nothing that is not accommodated.
Thus, Mañjuśrī interpenetrates Maitreya; the vast and complete universal penetration interpenetrates Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and the others.
As for "the mind itself is the name," the Bodhisattva has no name. As for "name," it is the individual's own mind.
To seek the Bodhisattva apart from one's own mind is to follow a deviant path; such a person does not perceive the Bodhisattva.
Regarding "seeing all bodhisattvas within the mind through correct contemplation": when one realizes that one's own mind has nothing it does not illumine, Mañjuśrī appears before one.
When one realizes that one's own nature has nothing it does not embrace, Maitreya appears in the world. When one realizes the vastness of one's own nature, Samantabhadra is constantly beheld.
When one realizes the perfect penetration of one's own nature, Mahāvairocana is ever-present.

Regarding the statement that we now see ordinary beings but do not see Bodhisattvas: it is because we spend our days with deluded minds chasing after external objects, thereby creating various evil karmas and lacking the power of contemplation.

Even if we should cultivate the goodness of precepts or various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), these merely involve conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and are not right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
Right contemplation consists of directly aligning the mind and maintaining right mindfulness of True Suchness (*tathatā*); according to this sutra, it is precisely "binding the object of focus."
The Dharma-realm is exclusively designated by name; this is what is called "Buddha-remembrance that transcends the four propositions.
If one attains this correct contemplation, then Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteśvara are all fully present. This is seeing all Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it is seeing all sentient beings as universally attaining perfect enlightenment; this is not seeing ordinary beings. Now, seeing ordinary beings...
Indeed, it is because they have failed to maintain right contemplation that they do not see the Bodhisattva.
As for those who attain sudden and perfect realization through being touched by the Buddha’s light:

when the Tathāgata was a bodhisattva, forty kinds of light issued from beneath his feet; from among the marks and signs of perfection, he emitted this light downward to illuminate the hells, whereupon those in hell encountered it.
As for Guang, he was immediately reborn in Tuṣita Heaven. Having heard the sound of the celestial drum and performed repentance, he instantly attained the rank of the tenth bhūmi.
The reason for this is that sentient beings have previously perfumed the seeds of the One Vehicle.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this Dharma is equal, with no high or low," "this Dharma" refers to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Within this nature of phenomena, the holy and the ordinary are equal.
Above, it penetrates through the four propositions. This means that if the dharma-nature possessed high and low, it could not penetrate through high and low;
because it has no high or low, it is able to penetrate through high and low.

From the noble ones downward, there are the Four Truths, which comprise the Dharma of the Śrāvakas; the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, which comprise the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas; the Four Immeasurables and the Six Perfections, which comprise the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas;
and the Five Precepts and Ten Wholesome Paths, which comprise the Dharma of humans and devas. Although the myriad practices are diverse, they collectively encompass the four types of noble beings.

Although the eighty-four thousand afflictions are manifold, they collectively encompass the six classes of ordinary beings. Though the four noble beings and the six ordinary classes differ, they are in truth...
This is the one mind. It is the convergence of the practices of the ten dharma realms back into the one mind. Why is this?
Because within the true nature of the one mind, there is no differentiation among the ten dharma realms. Since there is no differentiation among the ten dharma realms...
Thus, he was able to penetrate the ten dharma realms.
Regarding the phrase "dragons and snakes are intermingled": when Chan Master Wuzhuo paid homage at Mount Wutai, he encountered Mañjuśrī, who had manifested as an old man.
The man asked, "How is the Buddha-dharma maintained in the South? Wuzhuo replied, "In this age of the Final Dharma, monks and nuns rarely uphold the precepts. Immediately—
Question: How is the Buddha-dharma maintained here? The Elder replied: "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary beings and sages intersect. He divided it into four sections.
The first, the Section on the Orthodox Lineage, details the primary and secondary environments to inspire faith and joy;

this belongs to the provision of faith. The second correctly demonstrates aspiration and practice so that one may know how to cultivate and realize; this belongs to the two provisions of aspiration and practice. The third... [intersects].

Regarding the citation of the Buddha’s words to cause the severing of doubt and confusion: although the preceding sections have caused the arising of faith and joy, there remains the fear that doubts may persist and the power of faith remain unsteady;

therefore, the six directions are cited as collectively praising [the practice] to strengthen that faith. Regarding the mutual manifestation of difficult matters to evoke a sense of urgency and inspiration:
although the preceding sections have correctly demonstrated the vows and practices, there remains the fear of complacency, such that one might fail to give rise to them; therefore—
To cite both [the *Sūtra* and the *Śāstra*] in mutual praise serves to encourage the arousal of the vow.
Regarding the distinction between "testifying to faith" (*samyak-pratyaya*) and "arousing the aspiration" (*nidāna*): testifying to faith is universal, for it applies to all sūtras;
arousing the aspiration is particular, for the introductory narrative of each sūtra differs.

Regarding the emission of light from the *ūrṇā-kośa* to inaugurate the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*): at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Tathāgata first emitted the light from the mark of the white tuft of hair, illuminating eighteen thousand lands.
Thereafter, he addressed Śāriputra: "The wisdom of the Buddhas is profoundly deep and immeasurable.
Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Dharma of the One Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third, except for the stage of the Buddha."
Regarding the passage beginning with "Then he spoke," etc.:
when Vimalakīrti manifested illness in the city of Vaiśālī, the World-Honored One dispatched the great *śrāvakas* and the great *bodhisattvas* to inquire after his health; thereafter...

The thirty-two great beings each expounded the gate of non-duality: for instance, the non-duality of arising and ceasing, the non-duality of defilement and purity, and the non-duality of the single mark and the absence of marks;
even to the point that there are no words or speech—this is the true entry into the gate of non-duality.
In the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*), there are many instances where the questions precede the teaching.

Regarding *Complete Enlightenment*, Mañjuśrī requests from the Tathāgata the Dharma-gate of the stages of practice (*yīndì fǎmén*) and the bodhisattvas' methods for distancing themselves from various afflictions. Regarding the *Diamond Sūtra* (*Jīngāng jīng*), Subhūti requests:
"How should one abide? How should one subdue the mind?"
Liberation and meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) constitute two of the five constituents of the Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*).

While there are differences between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna regarding these, meditative concentration further comprises both the phenomenal (*saviṣaya*) and the noumenal (*nirviṣaya*), as well as mundane and supramundane varieties.
Regarding "life existing in a single breath," the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* states: The Buddha asked a śramaṇa, "In how much time does human life reside?
He replied, "For several days. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way. He asked again, "In how much time does human life reside?"
[The Master] said, "During the interval between meals. The Buddha said, "You do not yet know the Way. He asked again, "In how much time does a person's life reside?
[The Master] replied, "In the interval of a single breath. The Buddha said, "Now you know the Way."
The following is an analogy for correlating with the Dharma. Suppose there is a person—this represents sentient beings of the six realms—who suddenly suffers from a malignant ulcer;
their life hangs by a thread, representing how the cycle of birth and death for sentient beings is impermanent and swift.

There is an excellent prescription consisting of five phrases—representing other Dharma gates—which are not easily accomplished and whose practice has not yet reached completion, yet impermanence has already arrived. Herein lies a medicine ready at hand.
"Entering the mouth and immediately becoming alive" is a metaphor for how the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha swiftly transcends birth and death.

The four lines beginning with "One who possesses a benevolent heart" are a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s great compassion. One should respond promptly; why wait until after repeated and earnest entreaties before speaking?

The Commentary states: "Profound wisdom" refers to that which is not the analytical wisdom of emptiness of the Hīnayāna practitioners, nor the wisdom of the universal person's contemplation of the emptiness of the body, nor the wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the two truths. It is the wisdom of equality;
it is only when one uses the inconceivable mind to illuminate the inconceivable realm that it is properly termed profound wisdom.
Regarding those who discern the capacities of purity and defilement: lands are fundamentally neither pure nor defiled; purity and defilement arise from one's own mind.

When the mind is pure, the land is pure; when the mind is defiled, the land is defiled. Regarding those who harmonize the boundaries between phenomena and principle: they wish to behold Amitābha and attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
Yet, there is no principle apart from phenomena, and no phenomena apart from principle; at the boundary between phenomena and principle, they are fundamentally fused.

Because it is pervasive. (Another interpretation states: "Opportunity" (*ki*) refers to the subtle trigger and the mechanism. All that is pure and defiled arises through the transformation of one's own mind;
therefore, one's own mind is the opportunity for purity and defilement. "Thoroughly penetrating" (*tōkan*) means to achieve complete awakening.

To thoroughly awaken to the wondrous mind and deeply realize the dependent origination of a single thought-moment is to penetrate the opportunity of purity and defilement. "Limit" (*sai*) refers to the point of intersection. To engage...
Regarding the point of entry: all phenomena and principles are fundamentally rooted in one's own mind; therefore, the self-mind serves as the juncture between phenomena and principles.

"Fusion" refers to perfect awakening. To perfectly awaken to one's own mind and thereby enter the non-obstructive dharma-realm of phenomena and principles is what it means to fuse at the juncture between phenomena and principles.

Only those who can truly believe without doubt [can do so]. Because they do not realize that purity and defilement arise from within one's own mind, they must say that the same buddha-land is both pure and defiled;
how could there be both purity and defilement? Thus, when they hear of the Pure Land, they inevitably doubt and do not believe it.

This is because they do not realize that phenomena and principle are fundamentally one and the same. Consequently, those who cling to phenomena do not believe in principle, and those who cling to principle do not believe in phenomena.
Furthermore, for one who does not believe in principle, phenomena lack a foundation; after a long time, they will likewise cease to believe in phenomena.

For one who does not believe in phenomena, principle lacks a basis; after a long time, they will also cease to believe in principle. Only by penetrating these two aspects can one truly believe with clarity.

(Another interpretation states: If one does not possess profound wisdom to penetrate the juncture between phenomena and principle regarding the capacities of beings for the impure and the pure, then purity and impurity will obstruct one another, and phenomena and principle will remain separated.
In that case, the Pure Land would be something accomplished through cultivation external to principle, and the myriad dharmas would not be inherently possessed by the mind.
To point toward the causes and effects of that Pure Land as being merely expedient means external to the essence—how could such a person believe and accept [the teaching]?
I suspect this must be profound wisdom that realizes the purity and impurity of the ten directions, condensing them all within a single kṣaṇa;
wherein in one thought-moment, form and mind are arrayed and fully encompassed within the dharma-realm.

Only then can one understand that the transmigration of the spirit across billions of lands truly arises from within one's own mind, and that the formation of a physical body within the nine lotuses does not escape the interior of a single kṣaṇa. Therefore it is said: "Only then can one believe."
"I accept this without doubt.
It is the nature of things that it should be so: when a ruler has business, he must inform his great ministers; when a father has business, he must inform his eldest son;
likewise, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he must inform his chief disciples."
Regarding the *loka-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the tenet established according to worldly convention): "world" (*loka*) carries the meaning of differentiation.

This teaching necessarily possesses specific dharmas, intended to make sentient beings understand the distinctions among the various dharma-gates; it is orderly and systematic, without confusion, so that they may obtain the benefit of joy.

Regarding the *pudgala-prasiddha-siddhānta* (the tenet established for the sake of individuals): Śāriputra’s wisdom was revered by the assembly. Because Śāriputra believed, the entire assembly did not fail to believe; each [person]...

Arouse a wholesome mind so that the benefit of generating goodness may be attained. As for the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of remediation), it is like the wisdom of the great assembly, which is not equal to that of Śāriputra.
When Śāriputra turned his mind [toward the Dharma], there was none who did not turn their minds; they abandoned their false attachments and attained the benefit of extinguishing evil.
Regarding the *paramārtha-siddhānta*: having already turned away from the Lesser Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, it causes one to never regress and to ultimately attain Buddhahood;
by awakening to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it provides the benefit of enabling entry into the principle.

Commentary: To generate faith through wisdom constitutes right faith. This means knowing with faith that the Buddha and sentient beings are non-dual, and that by recollecting the Buddha, sentient beings will certainly attain Buddhahood;
only then is it right faith. Without sublime wisdom, this faith does not arise. Even if one possesses a degree of faith, it is not right faith.

To take wisdom as the basis for making vows constitutes a "great vow. This means clearly realizing the realm of the four truths of non-action and thereby giving rise to the four great vows, vowing to be born in the Western Land;
only then is it a great vow. Without wondrous wisdom, the great vow will not arise; even if one possesses the aspiration for a vow, [it remains incomplete].
It is not because of great vows.
To take the arising of practice through wisdom as the sublime practice means first awakening to one’s own nature (*svabhāva*), and then arising from that nature to cultivate.

Only by recollecting the Buddha while remaining free from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*) is it the sublime practice. Without sublime wisdom, the sublime practice does not arise; even if there is cultivation, it all falls into existence (*bhava*).
Because it is not a sublime practice. [The] Commentary states:
"To illuminate without conditions" means that to illuminate only after having conditions, or to know only after deliberation, is wisdom obtained from without;
it is wisdom produced by effort, not spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*). Without any external攀缘 (pán-yuán—conditions or attachments), there is nothing that is not illuminated. Not...
To exert one's thoughts and reflections yet know nothing—this is "unlearned wisdom" (*aśikṣita-jñāna*), "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*), which is not obtained from another.
Since one already possesses this wisdom, why is it necessary to strike the bells and beat the drums, making three earnest requests, before finally being informed? Therefore, it is said:
"Before the *gandi* has even been struck," and so forth.

Commentary: It is called "Peaceful Bliss" (*Anle*) because it is free from the oppression and affliction of birth and death. It is called "Peaceful Nourishment" (*Anyang*) because its provisions are natural and do not depend on human effort.
It is called "Pure Tranquility" (*Qingtai*) because it is beyond the reach of the three calamities, both great and small.
It is called "Sublime Intention" (*Miaoyi*) because all sublime objects of the six sense-fields accord with the mind.
Commentary: Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*’s clarification of the vastness of the worlds in the eastern direction, the sūtra states:

"Suppose, for example, there were all the earth-elements within a trichiliocosm; and suppose a person were to grind them into ink and, having passed beyond a thousand lands to the east, drop a single dot as large as a minute speck of dust.
Having again passed beyond another thousand lands, he drops another dot. In this manner..."
Suppose these were all filled with ink until the very ground was exhausted. What do you think?
Could a mathematician or a mathematician’s disciple reach the limit of those lands and know their number? “No, World-Honored One.
The multitude of worlds is inconceivable.”
Regarding the "all-world-seeds" of the *Avataṃsaka*, the Sūtra states: "The Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean is supported by wind-circles as numerous as the atoms of Mount Sumeru.
The supreme wind-circle is able to support the Universal Radiance Maṇi Fragrant Water-Ocean.
Within this ocean is a great lotus named 'Various Radiant Filaments and Fragrance Banner. This is the Flower Treasury Adorned World..."

The ocean of realms dwells therein. Within this ocean of worlds, amidst all the great earth inside the Great Cakravāḍa Mountains, there are ten times the number of incalculable buddha-field atoms of fragrant water oceans.
Within these ten times the number of incalculable fragrant water oceans, there are ten times the number of incalculable buddha-field atoms of world-systems established; in each and every world...
As for the world-systems: there are further world-systems numbering as many as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
In the very center of these is a sea of fragrant water named Boundless Light of Exquisite Flowers, from which a great lotus emerges; upon it rests a world-system.
There are worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields arranged therein.

The lowest among them is named Most Victorious Light Pervading Illumination. Reaching the thirteenth world from there, it is named Sahā, surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in thirteen buddha-fields.

Regarding the mind remaining in meditative concentration at the time of death, Tiantai says: "The mind remaining in concentration at the moment of death is precisely the mind that receives birth in the Pure Land.
At the very moment one raises this thought, one is reborn in the Pure Land; thus, being in concentration at the end of life, one receives birth in the Pure Land."
One does not depart from this mind; the mind has no "this" or "that. How could it ever go from here to there? To speak of "rebirth" is merely a single movement of thought.

It is like a person in a dream who goes from one place to another; in reality, they do not depart from the dreaming mind, yet to say they "go from here to there" is simply the dreaming mind manifesting itself.
Regarding "Vairocana pervades all places": Vairocana means "pervasive illumination.
Because he pervades all sentient beings and all lands and so forth, it is said that the Dharmakāya is omnipresent in all places—namely, in all sentient beings and lands.

As for that Buddha’s dwelling place named *Cang-ji-guang* (Constant Quiescent Light): "Constant" (*chang*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "Quiescent" (*ji*) is liberation (*vimukti*); and "Light" (*guang*) is wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is the true pure land of the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-rahasya-kośa*). This is the abode of all Buddhas alone.

Although it is said to be the abode of all Buddhas, in reality, the environment and its inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*) are non-dual; the environment and the inhabitants are not separate. Therefore, it is said: "The physical marks of Samantabhadra are like space."
Emptiness abides in accordance with the Truth and is not a land. If this is so even for Bodhisattvas, how much more so for the Buddhas?
Those who practice the True Dharma are Bodhisattvas at the stage of Worthiness (*kalyāṇa*). Although they correspond to contemplative observation, they have not yet realized the Dharmakāya;
because they cannot fully integrate their nature into cultivation, they are not called "True. Only Dharmakāya Bodhisattvas correspond to manifest observation and directly realize the Dharmakāya.

"Realizing the nature through cultivation" means practicing the true Dharma; this explains the character "real" (*shi*). "The resulting retribution is extraordinary" means that since internal practice is superior, the resultant retribution is likewise superior;
the body of transformation becomes increasingly subtle and wondrous; this explains the character "retribution" (*bao*).
Regarding "adorned with the seven treasures and possessing the pure and wondrous five sense objects," the *Śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva’s five [sense objects]..."
Desire can cause Kāśyapa to dance. The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Immeasurable towers of fragrant clouds. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"Upon each tree there are seven layers of nets; within each net, there are five hundred billion palaces of exquisite flowers.
This refers to the pure and wondrous five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) of that land. As for "the non-duality of form and mind," it is because form...
Externally there is no mind; outside of the mind there is no form. Form is itself the mind; the mind is itself form.

This means that within each and every atom (dust) are all minds, and within each and every mind are all atoms. Each mind and each atom further mutually pervade one another, layer upon layer, inexhaustible and without obstruction.
As for "a single hair and a land of atoms containing one another," this refers to all [atoms] within each and every atom.
Dust. This refers to manifesting a Jewel-King Land upon a single hair-tip. Because the Bodhisattvas of this land have partially realized the Dharma-body, there are no phenomena external to the mind;
by raising a single hair-tip, the entire Dharma-realm is fully revealed. Thus, every phenomenon interpenetrates with every other phenomenon, pervading and containing all.

Regarding the severance of the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa-bhūmi*) which belong to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*): the four abodes are precisely the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*). Taking views as one, they are termed the "abode-ground of all views" (*sarva-dṛṣṭi-vāsa-bhūmi*). The delusions of thought are divided into three:
first, the "abode-ground of desire-attachment" (*kāma-rāga-vāsa-bhūmi*), which consists of the nine grades of thought-delusions in the desire realm;

second, the "abode-ground of form-attachment" (*rūpa-rāga-vāsa-bhūmi*), which consists of the nine grades of thought-delusions in each of the four stages of the form realm; and third, the "abode-ground of formless-attachment" (*ārūpya-rāga-vāsa-bhūmi*), [which consists of the nine grades of thought-delusions in the formless realm].

The nine grades of thought within each of the four stages of the realms—these four abodes—are all already severed by the two vehicles of the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings, as well as by Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching;
however, they have not yet realized the Dharma-body and thus belong to the Path of Expedient Means. This explains the "Expedient Means."
"Unwisdom that is not yet exhausted is called 'with remainder'" means: Unwisdom refers to the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) outside the [three] realms, which consist of forty-two categories.
Since these have not been severed at all at present, it is called "with remainder. This explains the term "with remainder."

It may also be said that each can be divided into pure and impure. Regarding the lightness and heaviness of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (afflictions), there is purity and impurity within the *sahā-loka* (the realm of shared dwelling).

For example, if ordinary beings have light *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, they experience the purity of the *sahā-loka*; if they are heavy, they experience its impurity. Regarding the skillfulness or clumsiness of "substantiality" (*tǐ*) and "analysis" (*xī*), there is purity and impurity within the *upāya* (expedient means).

In the Three Vehicles of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiào*), to realize emptiness by taking the substantiality of form as the basis is skillful, and thus one experiences the purity of the *upāya*. In the Three Vehicles of the Treasury Teaching (*zàngjiào*), to realize [emptiness] by analyzing form...

The void is crude; it gives rise to the defilement of expedient means (*upāya*). The sequential single mind perceives the defilement of the *sambhoga-kāya* (recompense body). Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) cultivate the three contemplations in sequence and realize the principle of the *dharmakāya*; they perceive the defilement of the *sambhoga-kāya*.

Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) cultivate the three contemplations within a single mind and realize the principle of the *dharmakāya*; they perceive the purity of the *sambhoga-kāya*.

Regarding the partial realization and ultimate realization of the *tathatā-prabhāsvara-loka* (the world of tranquil light), as for the Separate Teaching: [The text continues: ...as for the Separate Teaching... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary excerpt from a commentary on the *Fahua wenju* or similar Tiantai/Tendai scholastic literature concerning the distinctions between the teachings regarding the perception of the pure and impure realms by practitioners of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.)
The *Pratyekabuddha* comes; he severs twelve grades of ignorance, partially realizes the three virtues, and manifests the *śāntaprabhāsa* (tranquil light) with impurities.
The Tathāgata of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) severs forty-two grades of ignorance, ultimately realizes the secret treasury of the three virtues, and manifests the pure *śāntaprabhāsa*.

Here, earth, stones, and thorns constitute the environment, while the turmoil of the four miserable destinies constitutes the primary inhabitants; the eight qualities and seven treasures constitute the environment, while the multitudes of humans and devas constitute the inhabitants.
This is correct.

Regarding the principle that "as the capacities [of beings] differ, what they perceive also differs": if one can exhaustively sever ignorance (*avidyā*), one perceives the *Sambhoga-kāya* (Blissful Light) while remaining in the *Nirmāṇa-kāya* (Shared Dwelling);

if one has partially severed ignorance, one perceives the *Dharmakāya* (Reality Reward) while remaining in the *Nirmāṇa-kāya*; if one has severed the delusions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*), one perceives the *Prayoga-kāya* (Expedient Means) while remaining in the *Nirmāṇa-kāya*. Not yet... [text fragment].
They sever the afflictions of views and thought, and while remaining in the shared realm, they perceive their own original land.

As cited from the *Lotus Sūtra* below: "My land here is peaceful and secure. The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "When the great fire burns, my land here remains peaceful and secure. That which is burned by the great fire refers to the shared realm (*sahā-loka-dhātu*).
That "my land is peaceful and secure" refers to perceiving the provisional within the shared realm. Or, one may perceive this very place as such.
When one perceives mountains, forests, earth, soil, sand, and gravel, this is the perception of the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (Shared Residence) as the original land (*mūla-bhūmi*).

When one perceives the seven treasures, this is the perception of the *sāmbhogika-kāya* as the land of skillful means (*upāya-bhūmi*). Or, when one perceives these as the dwelling places of all Buddhas, this is the perception of the *sāmbhogika-kāya* as the land of true recompense (*vipāka-bhūmi*).

This is because the land of true recompense is where the true Dharma is practiced and where extraordinary rewards are realized; it is the place where all Buddhas cultivated their practices during the causal stage. Or, one may perceive...
This is precisely the inconceivable realm. It is the realization that within the same land, one perceives the Dharma-realm of serene light;
it is like a single body of water appearing differently to devas, humans, ghosts, and animals.
Regarding the further division of the Land of Enjoyment (*sambhogakāya*) into that for oneself and that for others, which is identical to the Land of True Reward (*vipākaphala*):
the Land of Self-Enjoyment is enjoyed solely by the Buddha alone and is not shared with others; the Land of Other-Enjoyment is enjoyed by the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.
Although these two are divided into self and other and differ accordingly, both result from practicing the true and real path throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Because they experience the fruition of karmic retribution, they are identical to the Land of Real Reward (*sambhoga-kāya*). Regarding the "Transformation [Land] identical to the previous three and four, the Land of Expedient Means Co-residing":

this Land of Expedient Means Co-residing is the land where the sages of ultimate fruition manifest great, non-localized functions, transforming according to the capacities of beings to benefit them through expedient means.

Regarding the statement that although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is a transformation land (*nirmāṇa-kṣetra*), it can also be a land of enjoyment (*sambhoga*) and a land of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*): although the Land of Ultimate Bliss is indeed a land of cohabitation (*sahā-vāsa*),

when compared to the aforementioned third [land], the land of transformation, if one can advance in practice to realize clear observation (*abhisamaya*), partially sever ignorance (*avidyā*), and eventually exhaust all ignorance,
then it becomes a land that encompasses both enjoyment and the dharma-nature.
Regarding the ten types of provisional and real [lands] as categorized by Fazang, the *Huayan helun* states: First is the Pure Land of the *Amitābha Sūtra*;
second is the Pure Land of the *Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life Sūtra*. These two are provisional and not real. Third is the Pure Land of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*;
fourth is the Pure Land of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*. Both are real but not yet extensive. Fifth is the Pure Land of the *Mahāmāyā...* (text continues).
1. The Pure Land of Śūla-deva; 2. The Pure Land of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; 3. The Pure Land of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*—these are all provisional and not ultimate.
4. The Pure Land indicated by the assembly on Vulture Peak is ultimate and not provisional.
5. The Pure Land of Mind-Only is the ultimate Pure Land. 6. The Pure Land where Vairocana resides is the ultimate Pure Land.
Furthermore, these four lands above are also naturally and inherently complete; one must not merely cling to the Land of Tranquil Light (Sakyām-prabhāsa).

Fearing that people, upon hearing that the Land of Tranquil Light is the reality while the preceding three lands are provisional, might cling exclusively to the Land of Tranquil Light and thereby deny the existence of the other three lands, it is said:
"These four lands are inherently complete within the principle of Dharma-nature. For within the minute minds of sentient beings, there exist the ten realms and a thousand... [worlds].

Thus, the three thousandfold nature and characteristics are fully present without exception. If one clings to the *sāmbhogika-kāya* (the reward body) as the ultimate reality and denies the existence of the preceding three [bodies], this refers to the provisional principle of pure *tathatā* (suchness) as expounded in the Separate Teaching (*prthaktīrtha*) of Tiantai; it is not the true *sambhoga-kāya*.

Regarding the phrase "if one realizes the Land of Quiescent Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*)": if the fruit is truly realized as the Land of Quiescent Light, one may, according to the mind’s inclination, lodge it within any of the three lower lands.

For example, if one wishes to transform *dharmakāya* bodhisattvas, one lodges it in the Land of True Reward (*niṣyandabhoga*); if one wishes to transform the noble ones of the provisional vehicles, one lodges it in the Land of Skillful Means (*upāya*);

and if one wishes to transform ordinary beings, one lodges it in the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahāloka*). This is because the wondrous principle of the Land of Quiescent Light is not [identical to] pure *tathatā*.
Since it does not depart from the previous three [lands], one would personally deny their existence.

If one has not yet realized the Land of Tranquil Light (Sukhāvatī), yet denies the existence of the other three lands, then since all four lands are negated, where does one currently reside? This constitutes falling into a vacuous emptiness and giving rise to the view of annihilationism.
The company of obstructors and the ranks of heterodox teachers have gone far astray. Thus, [the text] states "do not believe" and below provides an illustration.

It is as stated in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* in the passage refuting the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): "They all point to the present moment itself as the Buddha-land; there is no separate Pure Abode (*śuddhāvāsa*), nor is there the golden-hued physical form. This is it.
Regarding those who have forever escaped the burden of form from the eighth stage upward: in the eighth stage, they transform the *xiang-xiang* (aspect-aspect) and attain mastery over form;

in the ninth stage, they transform the *zhuan-xiang* (transforming aspect) and attain mastery over mind; in the tenth stage, they transform the *ye-xiang* (karmic aspect) and ultimately achieve Buddhahood.

These bodhisattvas of the three stages gradually empty the *ye-shi* (karmic consciousness), becoming detached from their very substance and having no basis for reliance. Internally, there is no root-body (*indriya-kāya*); externally, there is no world-system. How much more so for the ultimate fruit!
"Does a Sage possess a land? [The Commentary] states:
In the West, there is a specific reference to the Land of Ultimate Bliss for two reasons. First, because it consists entirely of bliss;
as the subsequent text says, "there is no suffering, only bliss. Second, because its causes and conditions are all sublime; as stated in the *Sūtra on Rebirth* (Wǎngshēng jīng).
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "losing the sheep on many paths," *Liezi* records that a neighbor of Yangzi lost a sheep.

He led his own followers and also requested Yangzi’s young servant to join them in searching for it. Yangzi said, "A single sheep—why so many pursuers? They replied, "Because there are many diverging paths.
After they returned, they had not found the sheep at all. Yangzi remarked, "At the center of each forked path, there were yet more forks."

This is because one does not know where the path leads. Therefore it is said: "The Great Way causes one to lose their sheep through many diverging paths; the student loses their life through many methods.
Regarding the phrase "singly aiming at the *he*": the *he* is a target made of leather. In archery, the *hou* (the outer fringe of the target) is made of skin.
Among these, a crane is painted to serve as the target.
Now, regarding those who universally make offerings to the ten directions, one might fear that a difficulty could be raised:

"Since it is said that one points toward a direction, establishes a sign, and dwells the mind upon grasping an object, why does the sutra further state that one makes offerings to hundreds of thousands of myriads of buddhas in other directions? Therefore, it is said: "This is merely..."
Regarding the West: having seen the Buddha and heard the Dharma, and having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), these are matters for after [that realization];

they are not something that ordinary people who have not yet been born in the Western Land can accomplish now. As for "seeing the egg and seeking the cock at night," *Zhuangzi* says: "Moreover, you are far too premature in your calculations;
seeing the egg and seeking the cock at night, seeing the crossbow bolt and seeking the roasted owl. "Cock at night" refers to the rooster. Seeing...
To expect the crowing of a rooster immediately after it has laid an egg is an extreme expression of the desire for haste.

Furthermore, in the section following the question: "In that case, the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra] speaks of a single body manifesting bodies as numerous as the atoms of all lands (*kṣetraparamāṇu*), each universally prostrating before Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of all lands.

This is not something that occurs only after one has been born in the Western Land; why then do you not fix the mind upon the object? In the response, this is addressed from the perspective of a single...
The "Mutual Identity of One and Many" is answered as follows: it is the Gate of Sovereign Mutual Identity of One and Many within the Ten Gates.

Because the One has no substantiality of its own and takes the entire Dharma-realm as its substance, there is no remaining phenomenon outside of the Dharma-realm; therefore, the One is identical to the many. The same applies when viewing the many from the perspective of the One;
thus, the One and the many are mutually identical. Regarding how they are either universal or partial, and how they are constantly different yet eternally the same—this is the Universal Prostration.
Regarding "dust motes of lands": it may be universal; it may be focused on a single Buddha; it may be both focused and universal;
it may be constantly distinct, as the one and the many are mutually identical; or it may be constantly identical.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "That which takes the distant as near" refers to the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*; "that which takes the near as distant" refers to the present sūtra.
