Furthermore, the "Great Mind" may also be the Bodhicitta. Since there is no other mind subsequent to this mind, it constitutes the sudden entry into the samādhi of non-mind;
it is the sudden departure from the marks of discursive thought. How could this not be great?
How could this not be the Bodhicitta itself? This is because the causes of practice in the nine grades permeate each grade of practice, just as the five heinous crimes do.

Regarding the transgression: ten recitations at the moment of death are sufficient to eliminate its power and belong to the lowest of the lower grades (*adhamādhamā*). If one can subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*), it belongs to the middle grade.

If one possesses great spiritual capacity (*indriya*) and is able to suddenly sever the afflictions—such as King Ajātaśatru, who through profound repentance attained rootless faith (*amūlikā śraddhā*)—this is subsumed within the three higher grades.
Is this not because the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are themselves divided into nine grades according to the power of their repentance? Furthermore, regarding the ten recitations...
Those who attain birth [in the Pure Land] are all those who possessed spiritual roots (*linggen*) from former lives. The *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shiyi lun*) states:

"Those who encounter a virtuous friend (*shanzhishi*) at the moment of death and achieve the ten recitations are all those whose past wholesome karma was powerful, such that they first encountered a virtuous friend. The *Commentary on the Miaozong* (*Miaozong chao*) states:

"Although these individuals committed evil, they had previously practiced contemplation; therefore, when a virtuous friend exhorted them to recite the ten names at the time of death, their minds became settled."

This is accomplished; it is also the practice of the Dharma for those whose zeal for the Vehicle is swift while their observance of precepts is lax. Because their zeal for the Vehicle is swift, they encounter virtuous friends.
Even if they do not cultivate samādhi in the present life, this is due to seeds planted in the past ripening now; thus, they attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Therefore, this is the Great Resolve.
To say that this is precisely the Great Mind of Bodhi is not at all incorrect; how much less so in light of the text of the *Benchao* (Original Commentary).

One should know that this refers to the single mind being undistracted. If it is the single mind in terms of phenomena (*shi*), it is still not yet "Great"; if it is the single mind in terms of principle (*li*), is it not precisely the Bodhicitta?
For this reason, it is called the Great Mind.
Commentary: Because it arises within one’s own mind, it is "going without going. Since it is said to be one's own mind, there is no going;
since it is said to arise within one's own mind, it is going without going. In this "going without going," arising is necessarily arising.
To go while there is no going—when one departs, in reality one does not depart. How could the present act of going to rebirth conflict with the people of the past?
The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "The Huayan’s multilayered Dharma-realm does not transcend the single mind. The multilayered Dharma-realm does not transcend the four Dharma-realms;
the four Dharma-realms do not transcend the One True Dharma-realm. This One True Dharma-realm is precisely the self-nature of the person."

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the mind has no boundaries," this mind is vast and expansive; it has no fixed location, no distinction between self and other, and there is nowhere to which it goes.

This explains the aforementioned "not going. Regarding the description of its ease in becoming defiled and so forth, this refers to departing from impurity to go toward purity, and departing from the old.
"Going to the New" does not mean going from here to there. It means "going beyond" by way of liberation.
Regarding what was explained: the youth Sudhana, in the sixth stage, visited the elder Vimokṣa in the city of Upavartana.
The elder then entered the samādhi called "Universally Encompassing All Buddha-fields. Emerging from that samādhi, he addressed Sudhana, saying:
"I have seen such Tathāgatas as these, numbering as many as the atoms within the Buddha-fields of each of the ten directions.
Those Tathāgatas did not come here, nor did I go to them; rather, they were seen at will, through the coming and going of the Buddhas."
Because they manifest according to the mind, a sutra states: "If one wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm:
all is created solely by the mind. This is it.

Commentary: Regarding those of former times who also aspired to be reborn in the Inner Court of Tuṣita: Tuṣita is the fourth heaven of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is divided into an outer court and an inner court.
The outer court is where devas and humans dwell; the inner court is where Bodhisattvas dwell.
Even the three calamities (*trividha-vipatti*) cannot cause it harm. As for those of former times who aspired to be born there, Bai Xia Shan (Han Yu) said: "The seas and mountains are not my home."
As for the place of refuge: if one must go to a place of refuge, it is indeed Tuṣita Heaven.

According to the *Chao* (Commentary): "One who possesses the merit of wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) is fit to join the ranks of the sages. Wisdom and abandonment refer to the merit of realizing wisdom and abandoning delusions.
The Inner Court is the dwelling place of those sages who have realized wisdom and abandoned delusions; without this merit, one is unfit to participate in the assembly.

Therefore, regarding those who seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss regardless of their afflictions or karma: if one seeks rebirth in the Pure Land and achieves success through the practice of "single-mindedness of the phenomenal" (*shishin-ichinen*), one will attain rebirth while still carrying one's afflictions and karma.
By relying on the inconceivable power of Amitābha’s vows, it is like placing a massive boulder upon a boat—it will not sink.
He drowned in a deep pool, as described above.
Regarding the Master Xuanzang’s statement that it is easy to be reborn in the Inner Court (Maitreya’s Tuṣita Heaven):

since the Master was a preeminent master of the Yogācāra school and Maitreya is the patriarch of that school, the Master frequently beheld the sacred form of Maitreya within his meditative concentration. At the time of his death, he returned to Tuṣita.
Daoshu frequently exhorted others to cultivate the Samādhi of Mind-Only Consciousness; therefore, it is said that rebirth in the Inner Court (Tuṣita) is easy to attain.
As for Maitreya still dwelling at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), this is because he remains in the causal state and has not yet attained the ultimate fruit.

This is precisely what is meant by Qingbian’s assertion that the present Maitreya is not yet an All-Knowing One (sarvajña), and that one must wait until after the Way of the Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa) before seeking his guidance once more. This is the matter at hand.

Regarding those who will be born at the time of the Dragon-Flower (Nāgapuṣpa): the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* states that on the very day Maitreya Bodhisattva leaves the household life, he shall immediately attain Buddhahood. Seated beneath a Dragon-Flower tree within the Flower Forest Garden (Puṣpavana), he will preach the Dharma in three assemblies. In the first assembly, he will deliver ninety-six koṭis of beings—specifically those who fashioned Buddha images during the era of Śākyamuni Buddha’s Dharma. The second assembly... [text continues] ...will deliver eighty-four thousand koṭis of beings—specifically those who made offerings to stupas during the era of Śākyamuni Buddha’s Dharma. The third assembly will deliver sixty-eight thousand koṭis of beings—specifically those who made offerings to the Three Jewels during the era of Śākyamuni Buddha’s Dharma. At that time, the lifespan of sentient beings will be eighty-four thousand years. After the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, his True Dharma will remain for forty-two thousand years, and the Semblance Dharma will remain for forty-two thousand years. During these periods, there will be no kings, ministers, or officials; there will be no cities, villages, or towns; there will be no houses, fields, or granaries; there will be no men or women; there will be no parents, children, or grandchildren; there will be no husbands or wives; there will be no male or female slaves; there will be no servants or laborers; there will be no teachers or students; there will be no ascetics or laypeople; there will be no śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas; there will be no Buddhas, no Dharma, and no Sangha. There will be no white-robed laypeople, no monks or nuns, no upāsakas or upāsikās, and no practitioners of the Way. There will be no offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, or food. There will be no recitation of mantras or dhāraṇīs, no chanting of sūtras, and no cultivation of the Way. There will be no precepts, no observance of the eight precepts, no fasting, and no practice of the ten good deeds. There will be no cultivation of the four immeasurables, no practice of the six pāramitās, and no cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. The second assembly: he delivered ninety-four koṭis of beings; these were those who, during the time of Śākyamuni Buddha, were Dharma-preachers of the five kinds who recited Mahāyāna sūtras.
The third assembly: he delivered ninety-two koṭis of beings; these were those who, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, made offerings to the Saṃgha.
In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, regarding the comparison of buddha-fields, the Bodhisattva Cittarāja addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"O Sons of the Buddha, one kalpa in the realm of Śākyamuni Buddha within this Sahā world is but a single day and night in the realm of Amitābha Buddha in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
One kalpa in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is [but a single day and night] in the realm of [Buddha] Kāśyapa..."
One kalpa in the world-system of the Buddha Vajradṛḍha in the world of Dhvaja is a single day and night in the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja.
One kalpa in the world of Kāṣāyadhvaja is a single day and night in the world of Avaivartikarutacakravatī.
O Son of the Buddha, proceeding in this sequence, even up to a world beyond a million asaṃkhyeya worlds, one kalpa in that final world is [a single day and night] in the world of Varalokadhātu.
In the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Suvimalaprabhāsa, one day and night is equal [to the duration of the kalpa in our world].
It is filled with Samantabhadra Bodhisattva and all the great bodhisattvas who practice together with him.
Commentary: One may not obtain the precepts [in the usual way], yet one can still obtain the increase of receiving them. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:

"If within a thousand li there is no master capable of conferring the precepts, it is permitted to receive them before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva. One must repent until one beholds a 'good sign' (*lakṣaṇa*); then one immediately obtains the precepts.
As for "beholding a good sign," it refers to the Buddha coming to touch one’s head, or seeing light, flowers, and so forth. If one does not behold such a good sign...
In such cases, although repentance offers no benefit and one does not obtain the precepts, one nonetheless gains the benefit of having received them.

Those who attain a thousand awakenings upon hearing a single word are like the one who struck a fist against the ribs, the one who beckoned across the river, the one who saw Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in person while reciting the name of Bhaiṣajyarāja,
and the one who suddenly transmitted the Mind-Seal upon encountering the blowing of a lamp— these are examples of this.
Commentary: "The self-nature is formless; this is the meaning of non-perversion. Regarding "form," it refers to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

All characteristics are the deluded objects of a perverted mind. Now, the self-nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is not a single characteristic, not a diverse characteristic, not a characteristic that is neither one nor diverse, nor a characteristic that is both one and diverse.
It is free from all differentiated characteristics of phenomena. How could there be any perversion or delusion?
The meaning of "the self-nature is stainless, which is the sense of being born in Sukhāvatī" is as follows: "Stainless" means free from defilement.

All defiled phenomena are causes of suffering and fruits of suffering. Now, this stainless *dharmakāya* transcends the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), is free from compounded characteristics, and is purely luminous.
Thus, it constitutes the mirror of the Dharma of transcendence; how could this not be Sukhāvatī?
Commentary: "Thus, even when seeking the true characteristic (*samyak-lakṣaṇa*), it cannot be found," and so forth. "True" (*samyak*) is said in contrast to "inverted" (*viparīta*).
If there were a true characteristic, how would it differ from the inverted? Where there is neither truth nor inversion, this is called being truly non-inverted.
This means that even when seeking for signs of purity, they cannot be found. "Purity" is spoken of in contrast to "defilement.
If there were signs of purity, how would they differ from defilement? Where there is neither purity nor defilement, this is called the true Pure Land.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states: Regarding "pointing at the palm," the *Analects* says: "Is it not as if he were pointing at what is right here? It points to his own palm, and the commentary notes that this means it is easy to see.

The *Chao* further states: "That Amitābha and the assembly of sages appear before one all day long upon the substance of enlightened awareness" means that when the self-nature is quiescent, they are non-existent.
"Amitāyus" (Infinite Life): its self-nature is illumination, which is Infinite Light; "Maitrī" (Compassion) is Avalokiteśvara; and "Jñāna" (Wisdom) is Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and so forth.
Regarding "never not going into the Constant Quiescent Light": "Constant" is the Dharmakāya, "Quiescent" is liberation, and "Light" is Prajñā.

These are the secret treasury of the three virtues, for they are never separated from one another whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining. The phrase "How can it be... concludes with an exhortation.

Commentary: "Rare among humans and devas, difficult to encounter throughout kalpas" means that before the Buddha appeared in the world, in the human realm there were only wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*) who taught the ten wholesome dharmas, and in the heavens there were only Śakra and others who taught treatises on transcending desire;

these all pertain to the causes and effects of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and do not transcend saṃsāra. Even when a Buddha appears in the world, he first teaches the minor teachings for humans and devas, continuing until the Vaipulya [period].
At this time, there has only now appeared this wondrous Dharma that transcends birth and death and emerges from the cycle of saṃsāra. Thus, a sutra says:
"The appearance of Buddhas in the world is extremely rare and difficult to encounter; even if they appear in the world, it is likewise difficult for them to preach this Dharma."

The supramundane causes refer to the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination of the Hīnayāna. These teachings enable one to transcend the triple world and avoid falling into saṃsāra;

however, because they involve practicing based on phenomenal consciousness (*vṛtti-vijñāna*) and perceiving phenomena as existing outside the mind—failing to realize that all is but mind—they remain within the realm of conceptual thought.

Furthermore, this includes the Four Noble Truths of Non-arising according to the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*), and the Four Noble Truths of Immeasurability according to the Distinct Teaching (*viśeṣa-yāna*). These...
This Dharma can transcend the Two Vehicles and does not fall into biased emptiness; however, it is only realized after the Path, for cause and effect are not fused.
In the Pure Land school, cultivation occurs outside of principle, and the myriad dharmas are not considered to be intrinsically possessed by the mind.

Thus, even if one cultivates the Path for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust and travels extensively through Buddha-lands, pointing toward that Pure Land is merely an expedient means external to the essence. Because this is not the definitive meaning, it remains subject to conceptual thought.
This is the deliberation.
As for the supreme cause of the supramundane, the spirit is turned toward billions of lands, yet it truly arises within one's own mind;

the physical form is conceived within the nine lotuses, without escaping the span of a single *kṣaṇa*. Thus, the pure and impure realms of the ten directions are all encompassed and contained within a single land.
In that single moment of form and mind, all things are arrayed and universally encompassed within the Dharma-realm.

If phenomena and principle were separated, or purity and impurity obstructed one another, how could ordinary beings who have committed the five heinous crimes ascend to the Treasure Land through ten recitations, and how could the worthy ones of the Two Vehicles reach the Golden Pond upon turning their minds?
This is the Mahāyāna among Mahāyānas, the definitive meaning among definitive meanings. Thus it is said by the Buddha:
The subtlety of the Dharma transcends this point; beyond it, one knows not how to delimit it. This is the inconceivable merit, the supreme cause for transcending the world.
[The] *Chao* [states]:
"Immeasurable Life, Immeasurable Light, the Three Jewels, the Path-Items (*mārga-pakṣya-dharma*), and various others"—this refers to that which is bestowed.
This is the Dharma. This Dharma is sometimes expounded through the emission of sounds, and sometimes pointed out by the manifestation of signs.

Because the sentient beings of that land possess the purity of the six sense faculties and have attained great dhāraṇī, all six sense objects are the teaching and all six sense faculties hear it; for in every phenomenon and at every moment, there is nothing that is not the wondrous Dharma.
The four lines concerning the water birds and the groves of trees represent the supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*) of Amitābha.
That all sentient beings possess the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and supernatural transformations represents the supernatural transformations of sentient beings.

Although the various wondrous functions of that land are accomplished through the supernatural transformations of Amitābha, if sentient beings do not themselves attain supernatural transformations, they cannot enjoy them. As the Sūtra says: "Skillful means (*upāya*) is the Bodhisattva."
The Pure Land. When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who possess skillful means regarding all dharmas without obstruction come to be born in that land.
This refers to the three phrases concerning the Dharma difficult to believe. The Sūtra says: "If one has not cultivated merit and wisdom in the past, one will not [believe] in this True Dharma."
One is able to hear it because one has already revered the various Tathāgatas in the past; thus, through these causes and conditions, one hears this meaning. As the Prajñāpāramitā says:
"If a person gives rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment, you should know that this person has planted roots of goodness under not just one Buddha or two Buddhas, and so forth."

That the "co-resident world" (*sahā-loka*) is itself the "world of tranquil light" (*śānta-prabhāsa-loka*) means that while those of the lower grade of rebirth perceive only the co-resident world, the Bodhisattva of the Perfect Mind perceives it as the world of tranquil light.
Here, the ponds, pavilions, and lotus flowers are none other than *prajñā*; the railings, nets, and rows of trees are all *tathatā*.
As it is said: "When the mental preoccupations of the practitioner have ceased, everything encountered by the eye is the radiance of the mind."

That the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is itself the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) means that those of middle and lower capacities who are born [in the Pure Land] see only the response-body, whereas the bodhisattva of the perfect mind sees the dharma-body.
Every single ray of light is the secret treasury of the three virtues; how could every single mark and excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) not be the perfect and ultimate one mind?
This is what is called the subtle and pure dharma-body, endowed with the thirty-two marks.

Regarding those who vainly seek out commentaries and treatises, thereby wearying their bodies and minds, the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* states: "If one seeks to hear much and loves the Way, the Way will surely be difficult to realize;
if one maintains one's resolve and serves the Way, that Way is exceedingly vast. Yongjia said: "In my early years, I accumulated learning and inquiry."

"Furthermore, I have once investigated commentaries and sought out sutras and śāstras; I have distinguished names and characteristics without knowing when to stop. Entering the sea to count its sands is but a weary toil for oneself"—this is indeed so.
Regarding the phrase "the self-nature is free from mind, words, and signs": it is because all dharmas are ineffable and inconceivable.
This is what is called *tathatā* (Suchness).

Regarding "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*): it refers to that which dwells in a state of profound obscurity and darkness, being unable to distinguish between the wholesome and the unwholesome; thus, it is called indeterminate.
Now, to seal the mouth and forget the workings of the mind is precisely to be without discrimination; thus, one falls into the state of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

This is that which cannot be attained through thought, nor can it be attained through deliberation; yet even by neither thinking nor deliberating, it is still not attained. This is truly the inconceivable. As the ancients said:
"It cannot be sought with a mind possessed of intention, nor can it be fashioned by a mind devoid of intention; it cannot be communicated through either speech or silence. Its...
This is what is meant by that. [From the] *Chao*:
"Neither arising nor ceasing" means that fundamentally there is no arising; how could there be cessation? "Neither going nor coming" means there is nowhere from which it comes; to where could it go?
"Neither increasing nor decreasing" refers to the perfectly luminous essence of the resultant Buddha. That is...

Because it is the Buddha of the inherent virtue of the nature of sentient beings; "serenely and eternally abiding" means that it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, and illuminating yet constantly quiescent;

"suchness unmoving" means that the aforementioned such wisdom and the aforementioned such object correspond as mind and environment, thereby attaining the unmoving dharmas of emptiness and existence and so forth.
Existence and non-existence, annihilation and permanence, are all conceptualizations of the deluded mind; if one departs from the deluded mind, [these do not arise].
In themselves, all dharmas are devoid of any marks of differentiation.
The east belongs to the spring of generation; as for its association with the hexagram Zhen, the *Yi Jing* states: "The myriad things emerge from Zhen; Zhen is the eastern direction."
Furthermore, it is said that "Zhen (the Trigram for Thunder) represents thunder; its ultimate manifestation is strength. It is also said that "Zhen signifies movement.
That which is both moving and still, remaining eternally quiescent despite responding to myriad transformations—this is what the *Treatise on Non-Transmigration* means when it says:

"One does not abandon movement to seek stillness, but seeks stillness within all movements. Therefore, even as whirlwinds topple mountains, there is constant stillness; and though the rivers compete in their torrential flow, [therein lies the same].
Yet it does not flow. Wild horses gallop and drums beat, yet they do not move [the mountain]. The sun and moon traverse the heavens, yet they do not circle [it].
Regarding "that which is produced by a hundred merits": when the World-Honored One was practicing on the causal ground, he attained one mark and one sign as the fruit of a hundred merits.
By cultivating immeasurable merit, he brought forth immeasurable marks and signs. As for "a hundred merits," it is as if all sentient beings of a great trichiliocosm...
The blind could not see; they were all treated by the physician and restored to sight, which was called the first blessing.
According to the *Chao* (Excerpts), the seven golden mountains are: first, Yugandhara; second, Īṣādhara; third, Kālaparvata; fourth, Sudarśana; fifth, Aśvakarṇa.

Sixth are elephant trunks; seventh are fish mouths; all possess golden radiance. These seven tiers encircle the exterior of Mount Sumeru, their height and breadth decreasing by half in successive order.
For example, if Mount Sumeru is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height, Yugandhara is forty-two thousand *yojanas*. This is how it is.
His fame is lofty and far-reaching, surpassing Mount Sumeru. There are those who are lofty but not far-reaching, and those who are far-reaching but not lofty;

now he possesses both qualities. Vertically, he emerges from the three lands; horizontally, he pervades the sands of all worlds. The higher one looks up, the loftier he appears; the further one gazes, the more distant he seems.
There are no sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu* who do not look up to him in reverence. [Commentary:
The Buddha’s light shines extensively, comprising both the light of the body (*kāya-prabhā*) and the light of wisdom (*jñāna-prabhā*). Regarding the light of wisdom, as the Sūtra says:

"By means of the light of my wisdom, I shine extensively throughout boundless realms. Regarding the light of the body, as stated in the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance": "He emits light that illuminates the entire world."
The realms: ten worlds, up to unspeakable worlds, which cannot be exhausted, and so forth.
According to the *Jiyao*: "Pure, ultimate, luminous, and pervasive" means that ignorance has been completely swept away and *prajñā* is perfectly manifested; this is precisely the light of wisdom.
"Immeasurable radiance" refers to the light of the body itself.
The commentary states that these two phrases—mentioning the cause while encompassing the fruit—are such that the cause does not encompass the fruit, nor does the fruit penetrate the cause;

this is the cause and fruit of the provisional vehicles (*upāya-yāna*), not the cause and fruit of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). The cause of the One Vehicle is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; the fruit of the One Vehicle is... [omitted].
This is also the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

Regarding the two phrases "wisdom without compassion" and "compassion without wisdom": "wisdom without compassion" refers to the partial truth-wisdom of the Hīnayāna; "compassion without wisdom" [refers to the same].
The compassion of ordinary beings arises from craving and views; it is not the Great Vehicle’s compassion that is the wisdom of all-knowledge.
Compassion without an object is precisely the compassion that is wisdom.
The two phrases "practice not arising from aspiration" mean that practice not arising from aspiration is feigned practice; aspiration without practice constitutes empty aspiration.
This is not the Bodhisattva’s wondrous practice of non-action, which is an aspiration that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

Regarding Yao’s benevolence, the *Tongjian* states: "Yao’s benevolence was like that of Heaven. Regarding Shun’s filial piety: his father was obstinate, his mother was garrulous, and his brother Xiang was arrogant;

yet he was able to bring harmony through filial piety. Regarding Yu’s frugality: he used coarse food and drink yet offered the utmost filial devotion to the spirits; he wore simple clothing yet displayed the most magnificent beauty in his ceremonial robes and caps;

he kept his palace and chambers humble yet exerted all his strength in the construction of canals and ditches. Regarding Tang’s magnanimity, Yi Yin praised him: [the text continues with the praise of Tang].
Tang said: "Replace cruelty with leniency.
[The commentary] quotes two lines: "Seeking wisdom externally can be exhausted. An ancient said: "That which enters through the gate is not the family treasure."
It flows forth from within one's own breast; only then does it truly cover heaven and encompass earth. This is it. Furthermore, Xiangyan heard one and answered ten;
when asked ten, he answered a hundred; yet he died under the phrase "before the parents were born," as well as under the question regarding the striking of the bamboo.
Fangyun said: "With a single blow, one forgets all that is known; there is no further need for cultivation.

The *Chao* (Commentary) states that each of the four phrases beginning with "constantly [abiding in] reality" possesses both a phenomenal and a principle aspect. Yongjia said: "There are two kinds of upright speech:
first, speaking in accordance with the Dharma, which causes those who hear it to attain clear faith and understanding; second, speaking in accordance with principle, which causes those..."
Those who hear it have their doubts removed and their delusions dispelled. There are also two types of gentle speech (*mṛdu-vāk*):

first, words of consolation, which cause those who hear them to rejoice and draw near; second, speech with refined and elegant tonal qualities, which causes those who hear them to cherish and practice it.
There are also two types of harmonizing speech (*saṃdhi-vāk*): first, harmony of action, wherein one sees those engaged in strife and exhorts them to desist; and not praising oneself.
Being humble and respectful toward all things; the harmony of these two principles; seeing those who have regressed from the bodhicitta and earnestly exhorting them to advance;
being skillfully able to distinguish between bodhi and afflictions as being of one identical mark; and truthful speech, which is also twofold: first, that which accords with reality.
If it exists, one says it exists; if it does not exist, one says it does not exist. If it is so, one says it is so; if it is not, one says it is not. Regarding these two principles of reality:
all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is eternally abiding and unchanging.

The Commentary states: The ten inexhaustible treasuries are the treasury of faith, the treasury of precepts, the treasury of shame, the treasury of remorse, the treasury of learning, the treasury of giving, the treasury of wisdom, the treasury of mindfulness, the treasury of retention, and the treasury of eloquence.
When he preaches the Dharma, his broad and long tongue fills the world;
this refers specifically to the tenth, the treasury of eloquence.

As for the Bodhisattva being thus: because a Bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) attains the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Physical Body (puxian seshen sanmei) at the very first stage (chuzhu).
The commentary states:

"Realizing the small" refers to the causes—both outflowing (leu) and non-outflowing (wuleu)—that result in the small fruits of humans and devas. "Great matters" refers to opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
According to the *Yao* (Excerpts): the "Samādhi of the Form Body" is precisely the "Samādhi of Universally Manifesting All Form Bodies.
Having attained this samādhi, one manifests as one or many, and manifests as small or large, with sovereign mastery according to one's will.

This constitutes the Great Matter shared with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. In the "Chapter on the Supernatural Powers" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the Buddha extends his broad and long tongue until it reaches the Brahma-world to praise the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and certify the single Great Matter of the causal conditions (*nidāna*).
Now, that the Buddhas of the six directions manifest this tongue-sign to praise the Pure Land—how could this be anything other than a matter of no small causal conditions?

Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the bodies of all Buddhas are identical, and thus their minds are equal," the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body;
they are one body and one wisdom, and likewise for their powers and fearlessnesses. Now, since their external forms are already identical, why should their internal minds not be so as well?
Furthermore, mind, wisdom, and vows constitute the three bodies—the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa—which are precisely the Prajñā of the Dharma-body.
Regarding the "Three Virtues of Liberation":
the *Chao* states, "The sound of the brook is itself [the Dharma]. This refers to the poem by Dongpo (Su Shi), which says: "The sound of the brook is itself the broad and long tongue;
the mountain colors are none other than the pure and serene body. This is it.
That which fuses the sentient and the insentient into a single tongue is the single characteristic of the Dharma-realm; it is ultimately equal.
Within this equality, how can one differentiate between Buddhas and sentient beings, or between the myriad phenomena?
"The tongue is the dharma-realm, and the dharma-realm is the tongue. This is because, in every single instance, there is not a single phenomenon that is not fully present.
That which is called the tongue as the dharma-realm is such that all phenomena converge upon the tongue. This refers to every single atom within the Flower Treasury World.
Within each and every atom, one perceives the Dharma-realm. This means that it manifests all at once and simultaneously, without concealment or manifestation;
everything is perfectly accomplished, without superiority or inferiority. When speaking of its universal pervasion, how could there not be two separate parts?
The Commentary states: "To cause them to be at peace and free from all obstacles and difficulties" means, as the *Guanjing shu* says:
"If one is protected by the Buddha’s compassion, one will ultimately leave suffering behind and forever attain peace and joy. This is it.
This means to cause them to be diligent so that they do not fall back or regress. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) says: "It is like fish eggs;
if the mother does not attend to them, the eggs will rot and perish. It is the same for sentient beings: if the Buddha does not attend to them, their roots of goodness will perish. This is it.
Regarding the natural resonance of mindfulness of the Buddha and the Buddha’s mindfulness of sentient beings, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions cherish and mind sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child has run away, what can the mother's remembrance accomplish?

But if the child remembers the mother, just as the mother remembers him, then throughout successive lives the mother and child will not be separated or far apart. If the minds of sentient beings remember the Buddha and mindfully recite his name, then before their very eyes..."
"Upon coming, they will certainly see the Buddha," and so forth.

The *Yi-chao* states: "A Bodhisattva of the eighth stage is constantly protected and remembered by the Tathāgata because this Bodhisattva has already entered the stage of effortlessness (*anabhoga-bhūmi*) and abides in the practice of retribution (*vipāka-caryā*). If the Tathāgata were not to protect them, at that moment they would immediately enter ultimate *nirvāṇa*."
Having abandoned all activities for the benefit of sentient beings, the Buddhas personally appear before them to preach various dharmas,
bestowing upon these bodhisattvas immeasurable and boundless gateways to the arising of wisdom, and they are constantly protected and remembered by the Tathāgatas.

Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the Dharma-gate of the Universal Eye pervades the entire Dharma-realm," there are two aspects to the Universal Eye: first, the Universal Eye of Great Wisdom, which universally illumines the Dharma-realm;
second, the Universal Eye of Great Compassion, which universally illumines sentient beings. Although both are included here, the intent emphasizes Great Compassion.
Since sentient beings pervade the Dharma-realm, Great Compassion pervades the Dharma-realm. Since Great Compassion pervades the Dharma-realm, then this...
The Dharma-gate likewise pervades the entire Dharma-realm; it is the single teaching that encompasses all teachings. The *Chao* states:
"Pure truth transcends delusion" consists of four phrases. This means that True Suchness (Tathatā) is fundamentally devoid of delusive defilement; this is the ultimate reality.
It is not correct to say that non-Buddhist teachings are sincere simply because they maintain that the six consciousnesses do not arise and they focus single-mindedly on a single flavor;
for these consciousnesses exist only because of sense objects and cease to exist when separated from them, being entirely illusory in nature.
Regarding "one seeing and one hearing, etc.," the ancients said: "In daily activities there is no distinction; it is only that I naturally accord with them.
At every turn there is neither grasping nor rejecting; in every place there is no discord. Who assigns the titles 'red' and 'purple'? Hills and mountains are utterly free of a speck of dust.
Putting on clothes and eating meals, carrying water and hauling firewood—this is it."

Furthermore, that which accompanies every act of seeing, hearing, speaking, and moving is what is meant by the fact that in our eating, resting, rising, and sitting, there is nothing that does not rely upon the power of others' grace.
That which has protected and sustained us from antiquity to the present, without interruption, is what is meant by the unceasing internal permeation of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
That which is never absent whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down is what is meant by "night after night, one embraces the Buddha."
Asleep, one still rises together with them every morning. The former [passage] explained non-separation in terms of the self-nature as it emerges from entanglement;
this explains non-separation in terms of the self-nature while remaining within entanglement.
Commentary: Regarding the "inexhaustibility of great wisdom," there are two interpretations. The first meaning explains it in terms of its vertical profundity and horizontal pervasiveness.
The second meaning explains it in terms of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) and the three knowledges (*tri-jñāna*). As for the correspondence between virtue and knowledge:

the "knowledge of all things" (*sarvajñatā*) is the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, because *prajñā* sweeps away all phenomena; the "knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*) is the wisdom that contemplates the conventional; and as for liberation...

Because it establishes all phenomena, the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) is the wisdom that contemplates the Middle Way. The Dharma-body transcends the two extremes, as it is utterly free from all dualistic oppositions.
Commentary: "Truly great and profoundly renowned," and so forth. A name is the guest of reality.
Because the Buddha cultivated immeasurable practices throughout an ocean of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, his fame is universally heard throughout the ten directions.
The Commentary states: "As for 'the provisional wisdom illuminating phenomena,' it refers to extensively practicing the myriad practices and extensively delivering sentient beings;
knowing the Dharma and knowing their capacities, observing their faculties to bestow the Dharma, and so forth, such as the ardent discernment [of distinctions]."
As for "actual wisdom illuminating principle": it is to maintain right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness), giving rise to no conceptual discrimination.
With the path of language severed, one directly accords with the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), such that wisdom and [its object] are non-dual, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the phenomena and principles are vividly manifest, and the dual illumination is unobscured": when the provisional wisdom (upāya-jñāna) illuminates phenomena, the ultimate wisdom (paramārtha-jñāna) simultaneously illuminates principles;
it vigorously discriminates all dharmas while remaining unmoved within the primary truth (paramārtha). When the ultimate wisdom illuminates principles...
This is the illumination of phenomena through provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*); outside the mind, there are no dharmas.

With green mountains filling one's eyes, those who shoulder all Buddha-dharmas do so because all Buddha-dharmas do not transcend the two truths (*satyadvaya*). It is the two wisdoms that can shoulder them;
thus, he is called the Buddha "Great Flame Shoulder" (*Mahājvālāṃsa*).
Commentary: Regarding the South being Li (Fire/Clarity), the *I Ching* says: "Li signifies clarity; therein all things see one another.
It is the hexagram of the South."
That fire is dark within and bright without represents the *li* (clinging). One *yin* line clings between two *yang* lines;
its image is fire, which is *yin* in substance but *yang* in function.
"Original Light" (*honkō*) means that sentient beings inherently possess this radiance from the beginning.

Regarding the *Shō* (Commentary): "To guide sentient beings and cause them to give rise to a superior intention"—because the wisdom of sentient beings is shallow and they do not know the realm of the Buddha, if one does not praise it, a superior intention will not arise.
Therefore, wishing to guide sentient beings and cause them to give rise to a superior intention, one must first [establish it] oneself.
This is a form of self-praise. For instance, Śākyamuni Bhagavān also praised himself, saying: "I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat;

I am the Knower of the Way, the Opener of the Way, and the Proclaimer of the Way," and so forth. He did this to universally summon all sentient beings with varying capacities and cause them to give rise to superior resolve.
Regarding the Master Guanyin being Guanyin: the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, "In the past, I encountered the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvara.
That Buddha taught me the Vajra-samādhi of hearing-perfuming and hearing-cultivation, which is like an illusion."

"I alone am the Honored One. When Prince Siddhārtha was first born, he pointed one hand toward heaven and the other toward earth, took seven steps in every direction, gazed at the four quarters, and declared:
"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the Honored One."
Commentary: Regarding Master Zhigong’s manifestation as the Eleven-faced One: Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty once summoned the painter Zhang Sengyou to paint an image of Master Zhigong.

As Zhigong parted his face with his fingers to reveal the form of the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara—alternately compassionate and majestic, serene and wise—Sengyou was ultimately unable to set down his brush.
Commentary: Regarding the establishment of meaning: above, one establishes bodhi through great wisdom; below, one establishes sentient beings through great compassion. Commentary:
As for "the Buddha’s light eclipsing all," the light of devas and humans merely eclipses the sun and moon, while that of the śrāvakas...

The light [of the Pratyekabuddha] eclipses that of the devas and humans; the light of the Pratyekabuddha eclipses that of the Śrāvakas; the light of the Bodhisattva eclipses that of the Pratyekabuddha;
and only the light of the Buddha eclipses all other great lights.

Commentary: Regarding the "afflictions of views and thoughts" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*): as for "views," if one says that these afflictions can be severed when one perceives the principle (*tattva*), then the name is derived from the understanding (*jñāna*).

If one says that "viewing" simply means [seeing] that things are provisional (*prajñapti*), where "provisional" has the meaning of being unreal, then the designation is applied according to the essence of the thing itself.

As for the "afflictions of thought," they enter the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) and are eliminated through repeated contemplation of the truth; thus they are called "afflictions of thought. This is derived from the understanding.

They receive their names accordingly. If one speaks of "delusion through conceptualization" (*vitarka*) and "delusion through craving" (*tṛṣṇā*), these are designations based on their essential nature. However, delusion through views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) arises from the object-field of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and is able to obstruct true reality;
delusion through conceptualization (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) arises from the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and is able to draw one into the three realms (*tridhātu*).
These explanations are all given primarily with reference to the majority of cases in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); in detailed analysis, they are not restricted to this.

"Dust-and-sand delusions" refers to the fact that the number of the *darśana-heya* (delusions abandoned through insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (delusions abandoned through cultivation) of sentient beings is as vast as dust motes and grains of sand;

these are the delusions belonging to the sphere of others. Since the practice of a Bodhisattva is specifically for the sake of transforming others, if one enables sentient beings to sever the delusions of *darśana* and *bhāvanā*, this constitutes the severing of "dust-and-sand delusions" for the Bodhisattva themselves.
They are also called "distinctive delusions," because they are distinctively severed by the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, regarding the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*): it refers to the lack of clear understanding regarding all phenomena; hence it is called "ignorance.

This delusion is the seed of the *karmic-consciousness* (*karma-vijñāna*) and the root of afflictions. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas do not know its name, for it is specifically addressed in the Mahāyāna.
A Bodhisattva cultivates both concentration and wisdom and fulfills the myriad practices before they can sever these delusions; therefore, these are also called "distinct delusions.

When one is within the Dharma, it is called an internal phenomenon (dharmas); when outside the Dharma, it is called an external phenomenon. To be able to know and understand them is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvajñā).
To be able to know all the various distinctions among the paths and to discern them without error is called the knowledge of the paths (mārgajñatā).
Within the Buddha-knowledge, there is necessarily the simultaneous illumination of these three knowledges in their entirety; this is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).

These three types of wisdom are the fruit; the three contemplations are the cause. The *Shizhong xinyao* states: "As for the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), it destroys the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), realizes the wisdom of all modes (*sarvajñatā*), and accomplishes the virtue of prajñā.
As for the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*), it destroys the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust, and realizes the wisdom of the paths and their varieties (*mārgajñatā*)."

One accomplishes the virtue of liberation. The Madhyamika practitioner destroys the delusions of ignorance and realizes the wisdom of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby accomplishing the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
However, it is not that wisdom does not involve severance, nor that severance is not wisdom. One must first state that the mind destroys delusions, and subsequently state that it realizes wisdom;

this means that if there is no severance, wisdom is not accomplished. Now, in this excerpt, because wisdom is mentioned first and the destruction of delusions is mentioned later, it is not [the case that] wisdom...
It cannot be severed.
The *Chao* (Commentary) states: "Regarding the eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
'Because I have attained the wondrous and subtle faculty of hearing, I am able to manifest many wondrous forms, even with two eyes, three eyes, four eyes, or nine eyes.'"

The eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes—whether manifesting as compassion or majesty, meditative concentration or wisdom—bring salvation and protection to sentient beings, attaining great sovereignty.
As for the *ūrṇā* mark resembling a tube of lapis lazuli: when the Tathāgata manifested this sign at his birth, it extended five feet in length. [This was during his] ascetic practice.
At that time, it was one zhang four chi in length; when he attained enlightenment, it was one zhang five chi in length. It was hollow within and luminous without, like a tube of lapis lazuli.
According to the *Chao*, those whose stained wisdom does not emit sublime light include the heterodox wisdom of non-Buddhists and the partial wisdom of the two vehicles. All [of these]...
Its essence is ignorance; it does not emit wondrous light. Only when a Buddha has reached the ultimate exhaustion of the five abodes is there "purity to the extreme and the penetration of light.
(Commentary: Regarding "intrinsic purity," it is because the nature is free from the defilement of afflictions; from the very beginning, it is incompatible with all defiled phenomena.

The Commentary states: "Profoundly still like empty space" means that within the reality of emptiness, one is free from all differentiated characteristics of phenomena and devoid of false mental conceptions.
"How could there ever be any boundaries? means that those who are free from the marks of thought are equal to the realm of empty space, as they are omnipresent and nowhere not pervasive.
The Commentary states: Regarding the "eight qualities of sound," the first two are as in the text. Third is the harmonious and appropriate sound; fourth is the reverent and wise sound;
fifth is not feminine; sixth is not erroneous; seventh is deep and far-reaching; eighth is as in the text. As for the phrase "Will Wu become a moat? this refers to the words of Zi Xu:
"In ten years we shall accumulate our population, and in ten years we shall provide instruction; after twenty years, will Wu not have become a moat [for its enemies]?"

Regarding "stopping and obstructing": the Buddha has realized the Dharma-body and attained the inexhaustible treasury; thus, all his supernatural powers and wondrous functions cannot be stopped or obstructed.
The former meaning refers to the essence (*tǐ*), while this meaning refers to the function (*yòng*).

Commentary: "For example, like the descent of the Sun Deity" refers to the analogy of the solar disk universally illuminating. This illustrates that one does not cease benefiting others even when encountering evil.

The scripture explains the application of this principle as follows: "One does not abandon sentient beings simply because their nature is corrupt and evil, or because they are difficult to subdue due to wrong views and turbid anger;
thus, one does not fail to cultivate the dedication of merit. One does not retreat from Bodhi simply because sentient beings do not know how to repay kindness."
Regarding the practice of the bodhisattva (*sādhana*): one does not dwell in the same place as the foolish and ignorant; one abandons all roots of merit that are contrary to reality;

and one does not give rise to a mind of weariness or aversion toward sentient beings, even when their faults and evils are frequent and difficult to endure. Commentary: (Note: The term *sādhana* here refers to the bodhisattva's spiritual practice or conduct.)
Defilement and evil combine to produce the congenitally blind; false views combine with the city of the Gandharvas, causing people to falsely claim it is real.
Hatred and turbidity combine with the hands of the Asuras; the sun serves as the vanguard for Śakra, yet because of that hatred, it is obscured and blocked. Thus, one does not recognize kindness.
The Jambū tree merges with its lofty crags and deep valleys; the foolish and ignorant dwell together in one place.
Dust, mist, smoke, and clouds merge together because clouds and mist can pervade all of space, just as those fools dwell in the same place.

Sentient beings repeatedly give rise to faults and evils, merging with the changes of the seasons—meaning they frequently commit errors, being sometimes good and sometimes evil, like the alternation of day and night and the shifting of shadows.
Yang Yi-du et al., *Chao*:
Regarding the "Thousand-Stringed Net of Brahmā," in the palace of Mahābrahmā there is a net-canopy banner. Red light radiates from one another, and colors shine in mutual brilliance.
At that time, the Buddha observed the various nets and, on that account, spoke of immeasurable worlds being like the mesh of a net.
Each is distinct, and their differences are immeasurable; the gateways of the Buddha’s teaching are likewise so.
Furthermore, regarding the various dharma-gates that mutually penetrate one another: a single gateway enters into immeasurable gateways, and immeasurable gateways enter into a single gateway.
The former principle was explained in terms of universal pervasion; this principle is explained in terms of mutual integration.
Commentary: Regarding "the self-nature contains and encompasses [all things] inexhaustibly": it means that pure dharmas are fully perfected with nothing lacking;
it is profound and boundless, transcending all measures and limits.
Commentary: That which constitutes the end and the beginning of all things is, in terms of time, the point when the myriad yin lines are completely stripped away and the single yang line is reborn;
in terms of phenomena, it is the state where the fundamental principle is fully present, the source of generation and growth;
and in terms of humanity, it is wisdom, the trunk from which all affairs proceed.
The hundred thousand dharma-gates are the virtue of *prajñā*. Boundless virtuous functions are the virtue of *vimukti*.
That they all return to the single square inch [of the mind] and are unified within the source of the heart is the virtue of the single *dharmakāya*.
When sought, it is without characteristics and without form. This is because its intrinsic nature is neither with characteristics nor without characteristics;

neither neither-with-nor-without-characteristics; neither both-with-and-without-characteristics; neither a single characteristic nor diverse characteristics; neither a combination of both nor a negation of both.
It is because it is utterly remote from all characteristics.
That which emerges as infinite and inexhaustible is this nature of Perfect Enlightenment (Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra).
It inherently possesses wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, arising secretly and responding subtly without rest or end. Therefore, it is without exhaustion.
"Originally complete and not requiring seeking from others" means that while the deluded mind seeks externally through discursive thought without end,
the nature of pure virtue is full and requires no external seeking.
The mind of sentient beings is the fundamental nature and virtue (xingde) inherent in ordinary people; it is the *tathāgatagarbha*, the essence of the perfect luminosity of the resultant Buddha.
This Buddha of the sentient beings' inherent virtue is neither self nor other, neither cause nor effect;
it is precisely the essence of the perfectly constant Great Enlightenment. Therefore, it is named the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Furthermore, the mind of sentient beings is precisely the meaning of non-awakening within the gate of arising and ceasing. Based on a single moment of ignorance, the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) is thereby established;
from this karmic consciousness, in turn, the phenomenal consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*) arises. Following after objects and grasping at conditions, it discriminates the six sense-fields.
This is the characteristic of the minds of sentient beings. Furthermore, the *tathāgatagarbha* (womb of the Tathāgata) is the meaning of "awakening" within the gate of arising and ceasing;

that is to say, the essence of mind is free from thought and is the single mark of the *dharmadhātu*. This is precisely the equal *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata, and it is what is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
As for why the mind of sentient beings is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, it is because the unawakened mind does not depart [from it].

Because it is original enlightenment (*prakṛtistha-gotra*). The treatise states: "If one were apart from the nature of enlightenment, there would be no non-enlightenment; if one were apart from the mind of non-enlightenment, there would likewise be no true enlightenment whose own-characteristic could be described.

It further states: "For example, just as various earthenware vessels all share the same nature and characteristics as fine dust, so too do the various karmic illusions of outflow-free ignorance all share the same nature and characteristics as True Suchness (*tathatā*). This is the meaning.
Commentary: Regarding "entering and exiting the three realms with sovereign non-obstruction": ordinary beings enter the three realms and are bound by birth and death, thus they lack sovereignty.
Those of the two vehicles exit the three realms but are bound by nirvana, thus they also lack sovereignty. The Buddha, however, practices both compassion and wisdom simultaneously;
because he comes and goes with ease, he possesses sovereignty.
Regarding the phrase "The lion’s single roar strikes terror into the hundred beasts," Yongjia said: "The lion’s roar is spoken without fear;
when the hundred beasts hear it, their brains are split asunder. The fragrant elephant flees in haste, losing its majesty, while the devas and nāgas listen in silence, giving rise to joy."

The five kinds of fear are: first, the fear of not being able to subsist; second, the fear of ill repute; third, the fear of death; fourth, the fear of the evil realms; and fifth, the fear of lacking majestic power.
The four kinds of fearlessness are: first, fearlessness regarding omniscience; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows; and third, fearlessness regarding the resolution of doubts.
Fourth is the fearlessness regarding the path to the exhaustion of suffering.
Regarding the meaning of "guiding" (*niyama*) and "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*): if the principles of the Dharma can guide and give rise to understanding in sentient beings, they sustain their own nature.

For example, when a practitioner attains awakening to their own nature in a single moment based on conditions, this very cause of awakening arises from the guiding principle of that nature; it is not obtained from without.
Therefore, teachings such as those concerning practice and so forth can serve as a standard to correctly align the body and mind, maintaining them so they are not lost.
The *Commentary* states: "The teachings of other vehicles are defiled; the Wheel-Turning King speaks of precepts and goodness; Śakra speaks of renouncing desire;

[it is taught that] there is truly goodness which should be practiced and evil which should be ceased; the Two Vehicles speak of the Four Noble Truths and the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination."
Furthermore, there is truly birth and death to be loathed and nirvana to be rejoiced in; yet both are defiled by ignorance and are not pure.
If the Buddha were to preach the Dharma of a single vehicle, then defilement and purity would both collectively belong to the category of empty flowers.
Birth and death and nirvana are nothing other than dreams and illusions. Only this one reality is true; the other two are not real. This is what is meant by "pure and singular."
It is a mixture, yet it possesses the characteristics of the pure and white Brahma-conduct.

Regarding "awakened rather than belonging to the class of the deluded": ordinary beings are deluded regarding all three truths; those of the Two Vehicles are not deluded regarding the Truth of Reality (the True) but are deluded regarding the Truth of Phenomena (the Conventional);

Bodhisattvas are not deluded regarding the Truths of Reality and Phenomena but are deluded regarding the Middle Truth. The Buddha, however, is fully awakened to all three truths simultaneously; thus, he transcends the sentient beings of the nine realms.

Regarding the statement "the Buddha is identical to sentient beings": if one speaks in terms of the contrast between sentient beings and the Buddha, then the nine realms constitute sentient beings, while the Buddha is the Great Awakened One.
Now, when it is said that the Buddha is identical to sentient beings, a sutra states: "The unsurpassed among sentient beings is the Buddha.
Thus, the Buddha is the unsurpassed sentient being.

Regarding "the Buddha being of a different category": this is said in contrast to the nine realms; the Buddha is of a different category [from them]. If he were born within all ten realms, then he would be of the same category.

The fivefold Dharma-body (pañca-dharmakāya) is common to both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna; the "fivefold" mentioned here refers specifically to the Mahāyāna transformation of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) of body and mind.
One attains the fivefold Dharma-body.
Regarding the "fragrance" of all humans, devas, asuras, non-Buddhists, and those of the two vehicles: humans and devas possess the fragrance of precepts and wholesome deeds;

asuras possess the fragrance of the lower grade of the ten wholesome paths; non-Buddhists likewise possess the fragrance of false concentration and false wisdom; and those of the two vehicles possess—
"The fragrance of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Commentary: Regarding the two virtues of abandonment and wisdom, the Tathāgata’s fruition possesses the three virtues of wisdom, abandonment, and grace;
here, the virtue of grace is omitted.

Commentary: To say that "the cessation [of afflictions] can only extinguish evil" and thus possesses substance but lacks function means that although the Śrāvakas sever their afflictions and realize Nirvāṇa, they cannot emerge from emptiness to manifest in the provisional realm to extensively deliver sentient beings.

They possess only the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body, yet lack the light of great function; this is what is meant by "having substance but lacking function. The Buddha, however, internally severs afflictions and is fully endowed with the fragrance of merit and virtue.
Externally, it delivers sentient beings and brings forth the light of great function; thus, essence and function are both manifest.

Regarding the inherent nature-virtues possessed by the Dharma-body: although it is said that the body is adorned with ten thousand virtues, these ten thousand virtues belong to the realm of cultivation.

Cultivation is not distinct from cultivation; all cultivation arises from the nature. Because there are sands-of-the-Ganges virtues within the nature, there are consequently sands-of-the-Ganges virtues of cultivation.
Otherwise, if cultivation did not arise from the nature, it would be a contrived cultivation that has no bearing upon the essence of the nature;
how then could it adorn the Dharma-body?

The four virtues of the Buddha overturn and destroy the four inversions of ordinary beings, such as regarding the impermanent as permanent, and the four inversions of the two vehicles, such as regarding the permanent as impermanent.
When the Buddha realizes the secret treasury of the three virtues, he is said to be "permanent" (*nitya*) because he is not transmuted by the four marks [of birth, abiding, change, and cessation].
He is like a precious flower that does not bloom in spring nor wither in autumn; he possesses the unsurpassed awakening and the joy of the Dharma. There is no... [end of fragment]
The supreme bliss of the tranquility of *nirvāṇa* is called "bliss. It is like a precious flower, rare, exquisite, and pure, which delights the human heart.
Possessing the eightfold mastery (*aṣṭa-vaśitā*), it does not depend on external conditions; thus it is called "self" (*ātman*).

It is like a precious flower that does not require the warmth of spring, nor does it rely on rain or dew, and is not defiled by the five abodes (*pañca-sthāna*); it is not burdened by the two types of death; thus it is called "pure" (*viśuddha*). It is like a precious flower, refined...
"Gold and fine jade are pure, being free from even the slightest speck of dust.
Regarding the commentary’s statement that "the dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds are immeasurable, and thus their meanings are immeasurable":

the mundane dharmas refer to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*); the mundane meanings refer to accumulation, engagement, and so forth. The supramundane dharmas refer to... [text continues].
The truths, conditions, the six perfections, and so forth, constitute the meaning of the supramundane. In contrast, [the mundane] consists of oppression, karmic retribution, and the like.
Because ordinary beings know the near but not the far, they only know worldly dharmas and do not know supramundane dharmas.
The followers of the Two Vehicles know the partial but do not know the perfect; they loathe existence and cling to emptiness because they do not know that emptiness and existence are unimpeded.

Bodhisattvas at the initial stage of resolve know the general but do not know the particular, for they have only awakened to the mind of nirvana and do not know the meaning of its differentiated aspects.
They know the reality but do not know the skillful means; they only know that which is within the realm of True Suchness (tathatā-dhātu), but do not know the gateway of the Buddha’s activities.
Therefore, the Buddha possesses the five eyes perfectly clear and the three wisdoms perfectly manifest, such that there is nothing he does not see.

Commentary: "The essence is utterly free from攀缘 (pān-yuan, objectification/clinging)" means that while Prajñā is like a great mass of fire, the minds of sentient beings are able to objectify everything everywhere, yet they alone do not objectify upon Prajñā itself.
Regarding Vimalakīrti taking fragrant food from the upper direction, the sutra states:

At that time, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi and, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested to the great assembly that in a region above, beyond lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there was a land named Sarvagandhasugandhā.
The Buddha there was named Gandhottamakūṭa and was currently residing there. The fragrance of that land, compared to the [fragrances] of all the worlds in the ten directions...
The fragrance of the humans and devas in the Buddha-world is the most supreme. In that land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas;
there are only assemblies of pure great bodhisattvas. The Buddha preaches the Dharma for them. Even the lay devotees dispatch transformed bodhisattvas to that land to request fragrant food, saying:
"We pray to receive the remains of what the World-Honored One has eaten, so that we may [bring it] to the Sahā world."
The realm. Regarding the performance of Buddha-works and so forth, the Commentary states:
"Avalokiteśvara’s faculty of hearing is the teaching-substance (*deha*) for this region. In Mañjuśrī’s verse on the selection of the perfect penetration, it says:
"The true teaching-substance of this region is purity found in sound and hearing. If one wishes to attain *samādhi*, one must truly enter through hearing. This brings one free from suffering.
They attain liberation. How excellent, Avalokiteśvara!

As for Śrī-Ākṣepa and the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) not being considered the most perfect method of penetration (*avivartika-saṃbodhi*), the verse says: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; the nature of mindfulness is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing.
Since cause and effect now yield different results, how can this be called the perfect penetration?"
Commentary: The faculty of hearing does not encompass the practice of nianfo (recitation of the Buddha’s name), yet nianfo is able to encompass the faculty of hearing.
If we discuss the dharma-gate, there are two modes of nianfo: phenomenal holding and principle-holding. Principle-holding involves returning to the Buddha so that one becomes the Buddha;

this is precisely "returning the hearing to hear itself. This is how nianfo can encompass the faculty of hearing. However, the faculty of hearing itself possesses no method of phenomenal holding; thus, the faculty of hearing does not [encompass it].

This refers to the inclusion of the practice of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*). If we discuss the inclusion of sentient beings, Buddha-remembrance universally encompasses those of both dull and sharp faculties.

From the lowest—those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, and ordinary worldlings—to the highest—those endowed with hearing, reflection, and cultivation who have entered *samādhi*—all are born in that land.

Thus, it is clear that Buddha-remembrance can include the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). However, regarding the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, those of inferior capacity are entirely excluded.
This means that the faculty of hearing does not encompass the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha.
Now, this faculty of hearing is like those who follow the *Shi* and *Li* (the Odes and Rites); it is uniquely suited to the capacities of beings in this region and does not extend to other regions.
Just as the study of the *Shi* and *Li* is based on a single district and does not encompass the entire nation, so too this practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo*) is like the *Zhou Yi*:
it universally accommodates the capacities of beings throughout the ten directions and is not restricted to a single region.
As it is said in the *Zhou Yi*: "The Way penetrates and unifies the words of the entire nation; it does not belong to a single district alone.

Regarding the section on "Substituting Principle for Phenomena": within the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*), not even a single speck of dust is established. How, then, could there be purity or defilement?

Why must there be vows and aspirations? It is because one wishes to manifest the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) that the matters of vows and aspirations regarding purity and defilement are set aside;
it is not that the matter of being born in the Pure Land through purity and defilement truly does not exist.

As for "Direct Pointing and Single Transmission": the Chan school directly points to the human mind, so that one may see one's nature and become a Buddha. It is the single transmission of the Mind-Seal, which does not rely on words or letters.
This Way has neither Buddhas nor sentient beings; this Way would kill even if a Buddha were to come, and it would kill even if a Mara were to come. Above, there is nothing...
The Buddha-way can be realized because there are no sentient beings below to be saved.
This Way is such that to raise the mind is immediately an error, and to stir a thought is immediately to deviate. As the ancients said: "Do not move it;
if you move it, horns will grow. They also said: "The moment one attempts to deliberate, white clouds stretch ten thousand miles," and so forth.

Regarding this path where both mind and objects are quiescent, the ancients said: "Externally, cease all conditions; internally, let the mind be without agitation. Let the mind be like a wall or a screen, and you may enter the Way.
They also said: "The outgoing breath does not engage with manifold conditions; the incoming breath does not dwell within the realms of the aggregates," and so forth.

"Even if the places were exchanged, it would be the same for all. This means that when the Sixth Patriarch lived during the time of the masters of the Pure Land school, the Sixth Patriarch likewise praised the Western Paradise.
And when the masters of the Pure Land school lived during the time of the Sixth Patriarch, those masters of the Pure Land school likewise propagated solely the "Direct Pointing."

Commentary: Regarding the two lines, "The numinous light shines alone," "numinous light" is spoken in contrast to deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*). Deluded consciousness is precisely the light of the eight consciousnesses (*aṣṭavijñāna*);
since each of the eight consciousnesses perceives its own respective object, they do not transcend the center or the periphery. Numinous light, however, is the light of true nature (*dharmatā*).
The true nature transcends all dualistic opposition; therefore, it is utterly devoid of center and periphery.

Regarding the two phrases "true illumination is impartial": "true illumination" is spoken in contrast to "deluded illumination. Deluded illumination refers to the illumination of the six consciousnesses—the illumination of the six consciousnesses as they confront objects—and thus does not transcend the duality of self and other.
True illumination, however, is the illumination of the self-substance itself; this self-substance is fundamentally...
There is neither subject nor object; therefore, it is said that self and other are not divided.
Because the center and the periphery are utterly transcended, one Buddha is many Buddhas, and many Buddhas are one Buddha.

There is no obstruction between the one and the many, for the one and the many are exhausted within the discrimination of deluded consciousness, whereas the numinous light is not deluded consciousness.
Because there is no distinction between self and other, Amitābha as the principal is the companions of all Buddhas, and the Buddhas as companions are Amitābha as the principal.

The principal and the companions mutually accomplish one another, for both principal and companions are established through deluded illumination; since true illumination is devoid of deluded illumination.
Being unimpeded means that although a thousand differences are separated, they are not distinct, for it is like the thousand jewels of Indra’s net, where each layer interpenetrates the others.
Being mutually formed means that the myriad dharmas naturally converge without being sought, for it is like the dense array of all phenomena, which does not depart from the great void.
As for where this sutra should now reside: the six directions act as the eulogizer, and this sutra is that which is eulogized.
The Buddha who eulogizes is not separated by even a foot or a hair’s breadth from it. As for the sutra being eulogized—where does it reside? Aha!
It is not separate from its own place, eternally serene and still; yet when you seek it, you will find it cannot be seen.
The Commentary states: In response to the phrase "the merits of Amitābha," there are two meanings. The former meaning involves condensing the many into one;

the latter meaning involves expanding the one into the many. Although there are these two meanings, in reality, the one and the many are mutually identical, such that expansion and contraction are unimpeded.
This is because all Buddhas share the same Dharma-body.

Commentary: Regarding the statement, "Bodhisattvas who wish to hear [the Dharma] but do not obtain it," someone may ask: "Now, there are many ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who hear [the teachings];

will they then transcend [to become] Bodhisattvas? Answer: There are great differences in the levels of hearing the sutras. Although the ears of ordinary worldlings may hear the names [of the teachings], their minds do not savor them.
Or, although their minds may reflect upon them, they do not practice with joyful diligence. This is merely listening with the ears.

When one explains [the teachings] but does not grasp their ultimate meaning, it is as if one has not heard them at all. What is called "hearing" now is to attain the ultimate meaning through explanation;
when sorrow and joy mingle within, and one practices with sincere faith, this is "hearing with the mind. Is this not indeed transcending the ordinary and the small?
Commentary: Regarding "the self-nature as its own standard" and so forth: the Sūtra possesses the meaning of "standard" (*nīti*) and "support" (*dhāraṇa*).
Since the self-nature is inherently the standard and support, it is itself the true Sūtra; where else could one seek the Sūtra?
The Buddha possesses the meaning of awakening and illumination. His self-nature is inherently lucid and radiant; this is the true Buddha. Where else could one seek the Buddha?
If one seeks the Buddha-dharma apart from one's own nature, it is much like riding a cow while searching for another cow—it is abandoning one's home to wander aimlessly.
The Commentary states: "That which is true *prajñā* never ceases to revolve the sutra throughout the day, yet it does not know that the sutra revolves, for it is not a literal sutra.
Now, where there is neither speaking nor hearing, this is precisely true *prajñā*. This is what is meant by 'constantly revolving such a sutra'—one hundred thousand million billion volumes."
Regarding the phrase "this is called the Tathāgata": seeking an external Buddha with marks has no connection to me, for such is not the true Buddha.
Now, that which is nameless and markless is precisely the true Tathāgata; what is called the "True Buddha" sits within the house, yet people of this age do not recognize it themselves.
Once one knows true Prajñā, then Amitābha preaches the Dharma everywhere; thus it is vividly clear.
Once one recognizes the True Tathāgata, then all Buddhas appear before one at every moment; thus they resound in the ears, vividly clear.
Then, regarding the sutras that Ānanda has not yet heard, there is nothing he does not hear; yet his discourse on faith already forms two separate poles—how much more so when doubt is involved?
When [the teachings] resound in one's ears, then as for the various Buddhas served by the Night Goddess, she serves each and every one of them;
yet her discourse on non-emptiness already contradicts this, let alone the fault of asserting actual emptiness.
Commentary: Regarding the "ultimate and supreme fruit": the path reaches its consummation in wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), and the stage culminates at the *tathāgata*.

One realizes all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) and perfectly contemplates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is termed "unsurpassed" in contrast to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksa-bodhi*), because Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment still have subtle ignorance (*avidyā*) that has not been severed and are thus designated as "surpassable beings."
Regarding those who correctly contemplate the True Reality (*tattva*): the followers of the Two Vehicles cultivate all-knowledge and correctly contemplate the True Reality.
