This is termed "correct" in contrast to the false views of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), for the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist schools each cling to divergent doctrines, all of which are false views.
Regarding "equally contemplating conventional truth": when a Bodhisattva cultivates the path and realizes the knowledge of the modes (*mārgajñatā*), they equally contemplate conventional truth.
This is termed "equal" in contrast to the partial contemplation of the Two Vehicles, for the latter abandon existence and contemplate only emptiness, thereby falling into one-sided views.
The term "Perfectly Awakened" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) carries two meanings: it is called "perfect" (*samyak*) when compared to the followers of the Two Vehicles, as they are superior to non-Buddhists;

yet even for the Bodhisattvas, it is called "erroneous" (*mithyā*) when they abandon existence to contemplate emptiness. This is because what follows [in the lower stages] serves as the reason for what precedes [the higher stages].

That Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally non-dual refers to the essence of original enlightenment (*prakṛtisthagotra*); as the cause-mind and the fruition-realization, they are neither two nor distinct.
That they become deluded and confused, being shrouded by ignorance, means that they do not know that the *dharmatā* of True Suchness is one; thus, they are unaware of the mind.
When thoughts arise, they subsequently form the three subtleties and six coarsenesses. This is therefore perverse awareness and is not called correct.
This means that although ordinary beings possess spiritual awareness, it is entirely delusory and not correct.

As for the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who merely cease and destroy the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*): the Śrāvakas contemplate the Four Noble Truths, while the Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Although their methods of practice differ, that which they sever is the same—the views and afflictions of the Three Realms.

The Pratyekabuddhas merely penetrate the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), and thus rank above the Śrāvakas; yet, although they attain *bodhi*, their path is not central, and thus they are not called "Equal."

"Bodhi" refers to all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*). Because they can only enter from the conventional into emptiness, but cannot enter from emptiness into the conventional, their path is not the Middle Way.
Because they only realize the truth of partiality, this is a "partial awakening. Because they have not yet cultivated the contemplation of equality, it is not called "equal."
"All Bodhisattvas who have exhausted the dust-like sands [of afflictions] but have not yet exhausted ignorance" refers to all such Bodhisattvas:

in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), from the tenth stage of Dedication (huixiang) through the ten stages (bhūmi) up to Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) and Wondrous Enlightenment (miaoqiao); and in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), from the tenth stage of Faith (xin) up to Equal Enlightenment. These are all such Bodhisattvas.

In the Separate Teaching (*bie*), after the Ten Dedications (*shixiang*), the dust-and-sand-like afflictions are exhausted, yet ignorance (*avidyā*) has not been severed. It is only at the First Ground (*prathamabhūmi*) that one first severs one grade of ignorance, continuing until the Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*), where twelve grades of ignorance are severed;
thus, it is not yet exhaustive. In the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), after the Ten Faiths (*shixin*), the dust-and-sand-like afflictions are exhausted, yet ignorance has not been severed.

It is only at the First Abiding (*dizhu*) that one first severs one grade of ignorance, continuing until the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*dengjue*), where forty-one grades [of ignorance] are severed.

Because ignorance has not yet been exhausted, even though one has attained right and equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), the stage of a Buddha remains far off; thus, one is not called "unsurpassed.

Enlightenment (*bodhi*) refers to the partial realization of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is able to simultaneously negate and simultaneously illuminate.
With every thought they enter the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), and thus they attain perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that although Bodhisattvas of the ten stages fill lands as numerous as motes of dust and cultivate the practices of a Bodhisattva for *nayuta* eons, the wisdom they produce cannot compare to the wisdom of a single Tathāgata;
it does not equal even one hundredth part, nor even a fraction of an *upaniṣad*.

It does not equal even one part [of it]. Therefore, it is said that the stage of Buddhahood is still far off. This applies not only to bodhisattvas of various stages, but even when reaching the level of Samyaksambodhi (Equal Enlightenment), there is still something further to surpass;
thus, it is called a "surpassable" state and is not termed "unsurpassed."

Only the Buddha alone has exhausted all delusion and perfected awakening. This is like the stage of the Bodhisattva’s culmination, where skillful means are fully realized and the mind of awakening is attained through a single moment of correspondence.
When the mind first arises, it is without the characteristic of a beginning; because one is far removed from even subtle thoughts, this is called the exhaustion of delusion.

Having thoroughly exhausted the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, with the wisdom of the ultimate limit fulfilled and the various types of awakening suddenly perfected, this is called "fulfillment of awakening.
It is like the moon on a night of the full moon; there is no awakening beyond this. The *Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* states:

"The Unsurpassed One" means there is nothing further to be severed. "The Unsurpassed One" means there is no one who surpasses him. He is like the moon on the fifteenth day, perfectly complete and fully endowed.
This is the king among all stars, the most supreme and most excellent, whose majestic virtue is uniquely honored. [From the] *Chao*:
"The numinous shines alone below. Because deluded illumination involves having something to illuminate, there are things it does not illuminate; true illumination is without illumination.

Therefore, there is nothing that is not illuminated. Deluded cognition perceives knowing, and thus there is something it does not know; true cognition is non-knowing, and thus there is nothing it does not know.
This knowing and this illuminating do not diminish the ground of ignorance, nor do they increase the ground of *prajñā*. At the time of awakening, there is nothing attained;
at the time of delusion, there is nothing lost.
"Bodhi is myself" follows below. "Bodhi" refers to true awakening (*bhūta-avabodha*); "myself" refers to the deluded sovereign.

If, in the state of delusion, there were decrease or loss, and in the state of awakening, there were increase or gain, then true awakening would not be the deluded sovereign, and the deluded sovereign would not be true awakening.
Now, since there is neither decrease nor loss during delusion, the false ruler is entirely the true awakening.

Since there is neither increase nor gain upon awakening, the true awakening is entirely the false ruler. If the true awakening and the false ruler were two, one might use one's own false ruler to displace the other's true awakening;
but now that they are one, it is utterly impossible to find any sign of advancement. How can this be?
Is there regression? The *Chao* (Excerpts) states repeatedly and without ceasing: "Faith is unstained and turbid; the mind is pure. Faith enables one to give all things without stinginess.
Faith enables one to enter the Buddha-dharma with joy. Faith enables the increase of wisdom and merit. Faith enables one to surely reach [the goal]."

Regarding "the stage of the Tathāgata and so forth," "deeply enduring, delighting in, and desiring" the reality, qualities, and capacities means: one deeply endures the reality, deeply delights in the qualities, and deeply desires the capacities.
As stated in the *Eight Consciousnesses’ Rules* (*Ba shi gui ju*): "Deep endurance refers to [endurance] regarding the real nature of all phenomena."
"Deep conviction" means that one's mind accepts the principle through a profound, mystical resonance, such that it cannot be diverted by false phenomena or principles.

"Deep delight" means that within the pure Dharma-body, prajñā, and liberation—the true and pure virtues of the Triple Gem—one possesses deep faith and joy, such that one is not deluded by false defilements or perverse virtues.
"Deep aspiration" refers to [the desire for] all mundane and supramundane...
Excellent. Deep faith possesses power; it can bring about a favorable retribution and can accomplish the fruit of the Path.

Because one gives rise to a heart of aspiration and seeks with the certainty that one will attain it, therein, patient acceptance is the cause of faith, while joyful desire is the fruit of faith. To know [the truth] is necessarily to love it.
Regarding "having purity of mind as its nature": because the mind is predominant, the term "mind" alone implies both the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

This means that this cause-and-effect faith is not only pure in its own essence, but can also purify all minds and mental factors—just as an extremely fragrant object is not only fragrant in itself but can also perfume all other things, or like a water-purifying jewel which does not merely [purify itself].
It purifies itself and is further able to clarify all turbid waters; its power is most supreme. Therefore it is said: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;
from this flow issues forth, and from this goodness is born. Faith enables one to surely reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
Other [objections] may be difficult, yet faith can resolve them.
Why is it said that "the purity of mind" constitutes the following four lines? These are the direct explanation that the nature [of the mind] is purity.
Furthermore, the nine lines beginning with "all defiled phenomena" are the indirect clarification that the nature [of the mind] is purity. "All defiled phenomena" refers to...
Regarding the six afflictions such as greed and the twenty secondary afflictions such as lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), each has its own specific characteristic.

For instance, the mental factor of greed has the nature of being stained by attachment toward existence and the requisites for existence; its function is to obstruct non-greed and to give rise to suffering.
Lack of shame has the nature of disregarding oneself and the Dharma, and of slighting and rejecting the virtuous and the good; it functions to obstruct shame and to cause unwholesome conduct to grow.
This refers to [the category of] karma and so forth. There is only non-faith (*āśraddhya*). Non-faith is a mental factor (*caitasika*);

it is defined as the inability to endure, find pleasure in, or desire [the truth]. Its essence is the defilement of the mind. Its function is to obstruct pure faith and to serve as a basis for indolence (*kausīdya*).

Regarding its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of being turbid, it further causes other minds and mental factors to become turbid; this is because non-faith does not merely consist of its own substance...
It is defiled and can further corrupt all mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), just as an extremely foul-smelling object can permeate everything else.
Therefore, the power of lack of faith (*aśraddhā*) surpasses all defiled minds; faith (*śraddhā*) is its direct opposite.
Now, the mental factor of faith is the direct opposite of the mental factor of lack of faith (*āśraddhya*).
Since lack of faith defiles oneself and defiles others, faith purifies oneself and purifies others; therefore, purification is its characteristic.
Regarding the mastery of mental purity, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra states: "If a bodhisattva wishes to obtain a pure land, they should purify their own mind;
according to the purity of their mind, so shall the buddha-field be pure."
Commentary: To take the awakened fruit-enlightenment as the object of one's own confidence means to regard that Buddha of the fruit as the causal mind within oneself.
If one speaks of "confidence" apart from the essence of awakening, it is called false confidence; it is not the correct confidence of the Great Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden teaching.
Regarding the fact that within the minds of sentient beings there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment at every moment of thought, a sutra states:

"One should know that within one's own mind there is always a Buddha attaining perfect enlightenment at every moment of thought. Why is this? Because perfect enlightenment is attained without departing from this very mind."
Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the self-nature is neither past, future, nor present; it is the meaning of having been born, being born, and about to be born":

if one says that the past has already been born, the present is currently being born, and the future is yet to be born, this constitutes the flux of the three periods of time and the circulation of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
This is not birth in the Pure Land, but rather birth in *Sahā* [World]. Only when the self-nature does not fall within the three periods of time is it "already born."
"Present life" (*jinsheng*) has the meaning of "life as it arises.

According to the *Chao* (Excerpts): "Ten thousand years in a single thought-moment" means that throughout the ten ages of past and present, the beginning and end do not depart from the present thought-moment.

Ten thousand years constitute the "ancient," and a single thought-moment constitutes the "present. Since ten thousand years and a single thought-moment are one, what is ancient and not present? A single thought-moment is ten thousand years.

This means to universally contemplate immeasurable kalpas in a single thought-moment. A single thought-moment is the present; ten thousand years are the past. When a single thought-moment is ten thousand years, how can the present not be the past?
How can the past not be the present? By means of the present, one subsumes the past. Thus, how could the present not be the past?

By using the ancient to subvert the present, and by mutually subverting both until they are lost, then both the ancient and the present become empty. Severs the three periods of time while remaining right where one is;
this is the West. Who is not one who attains rebirth? This is the emergence from the three periods of time.
Looking downward into the past, one seeks the mind across the three periods of time, yet the mind is not found. Where the mind is not found, delusion is fundamentally non-existent.
Where delusion is fundamentally non-existent, that is itself Bodhi. Birth-and-death and Nirvana are fundamentally equal; then who is it that transmigrates?
This is the emptiness of the mind across the three periods. Furthermore, who is it that transmigrates? It is birth that is without birth. Who is it that does not transmigrate? There is none.
Born, yet born; born, yet without birth; without birth, yet born. This is called that which has already been born, that which is being born now, and that which is to be born hereafter.
Regarding the appearance of the signs of the fire chariot: the *Amitābha Sūtra* (Kuan-ching), in its section on the lowest grade, states:
"There may be sentient beings who steal the property of the Saṃgha, preach the Dharma with impurity, and lack shame or remorse. Adorned by such evil karmas, such evil..."

When a person’s life is about to end, the various fires of hell arrive all at once; yet, meeting a virtuous friend who instructs them to recite the Buddha’s name, they immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land, and so forth.
Regarding "a kalpa-stone that can be worn away": there is a stone, square and circular, one yojana in size.
If one were to wipe it once every five hundred years with a garment of six *zhu* made of heavenly cloth, the time required to wear this stone away completely is defined as one *kalpa*.
The Commentary states: "Taking that which is true and not false as faith" means that faith possesses the meaning of reality, for if there were no faith, all things would be empty and deceptive.

"Taking the production of inexhaustible wisdom as aspiration" means that aspiration possesses the meaning of giving birth, for all myriad virtues and myriad practices arise from one's desire and resolve.
Commentary: One body is the Dharma-body; one wisdom is Prajñā; powers and fearlessnesses are Liberation. Commentary:
Regarding the two lines on the kindness surpassing that of a compassionate mother—while a mother’s kindness extends through this single lifetime, she may not necessarily extend it to future lives.

While the benevolence of Heaven (the Great Void) reaches only this single realm, it may not necessarily extend its benevolence to other realms. The compassion and benevolence of the Buddha, however, [pervades all].

There is no place or time where he is not compassionate and benevolent; thus, it is said that he "surpasses" [all others]. Regarding the two lines beginning with "To grind one's bones and shatter one's body," the ancients said:

"Even if one were to carry [the scriptures] upon one's head for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, or offer one's body as a seat throughout the trichiliocosm, if one does not transmit the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, there would ultimately be no way to repay his kindness."

The Commentary states: "Expedient means" refers to skillfully adapting to the capacities and circumstances of beings; this is the talent for delivering sentient beings. "Supreme virtue and vast grace" refer to the universal benefit bestowed upon all categories of existence;
this is the virtue for delivering sentient beings. To have talent without virtue is to lose the foundation for delivering beings, and thus one cannot deliver them.

To have virtue without talent is to lose the function for delivering beings, and likewise one cannot deliver them. Only when talent and virtue are fully integrated can one realize the essence [of the practice].
By employing identical giving, one is then able to deliver sentient beings.

Being limpid and unmoving, all myriad conditions are suddenly stilled; this is the cessation of the sphere where the mind operates. Being desolate and forgetting words, one is forever free from frivolous proliferation;
this is the severance of the path of language. If there remains even a single thing not forgotten, then the wild mind has not yet ceased, and the life-root has not yet been severed.
To realize the principle, both thought and deliberation must be extinguished; only then can one realize the principle.

From "Because compassion is itself wisdom" onwards: because of great compassion, one comes and goes within the triple world and appears and disappears among the four modes of birth, spending all day delivering sentient beings.
Because of great wisdom, all sentient beings are the very mark of quiescent extinction, such that there is no birth to be delivered.

Regarding "wisdom is itself compassion" and below: because of great wisdom, one realizes that all phenomena are empty; thus, not a single thought arises, and one does not abide within birth and death.
Because of great compassion, one does not dwell in empty stillness, but constantly delivers sentient beings without realizing nirvana.
The reason for citing only two characters is that compassion (*karuṇā*) is itself wisdom (*prajñā*), and thus "the Capable One" (*Nengren*, *Śakya-muni*) inherently includes "quiescence";

and wisdom is itself compassion, and thus "quiescence" inherently includes "the Capable One. This extends even to a single word: "Capable" inherently includes "benevolent," because function is the essence;

"benevolent" inherently includes "capable," because the essence is the function; and "quiescent" inherently includes "silent," because where the mind's activity ceases, the path of language naturally comes to an end.
"Severed. "Silence" implies both stillness and quiescence; because the path of speech is severed, it is said that "the sphere of mental activity has ceased.

Regarding the phrase "solely realizing the Samādhi of Self-Vow": "realization" means patience (*kṣānti*). The "Samādhi of Self-Vow" refers to the Four Great Vows made by the Tathāgata during his stage as a Bodhisattva:
the vow to attain the Buddha-way, the vow to deliver all sentient beings, the vow to sever all afflictions, and the vow to cultivate [all wholesome dharmas].
This Dharma-gate has now already attained Buddhahood; having severed ignorance, it has realized the Buddha-way and turned the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
Therefore, it is uniquely realized. This is named after the Tathāgata; it is named in reliance upon the Lord who has transcended the world.
At the beginning of the eon, the Brahmā King was named Kṣānti (The Patient One). Before the empty eon, this realm had no inhabitants;

it was only after the Brahmā King descended to be born that human beings first appeared. Because the Brahmā King at the beginning of the eon was named Kṣānti, the realm was consequently named the Kṣānti World (Sahā-lokadhātu).
This name was derived from the Brahmā King; it was named after the sovereign of the world.
Regarding the analogy of clear water in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the scripture states: "Ānanda, it is like clear water, which is inherently pure and pristine.
As for such things as dust, soil, ash, and sand, their essential nature is obstructive; these two substances are thus by their very nature, and their characteristics do not conform to one another."
There are people in the world who take soil from that earth and cast it into pure water;
the soil loses its solidity and the water its clarity, becoming turbid in appearance—this is what is called "turbidity. Your fivefold turbidity is likewise thus.
When there is a virtuous age free from the five turbidities, it is prior to the time when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years.
At that time, false views did not arise, afflictions were slight, the four realms of existence were empty and desolate, and lifespans were long; such a period is called a pure and virtuous age.
Commentary: Those who cling to "self" and "what belongs to self" internally grasp at [the aggregates] as the self, and externally grasp at them as what belongs to the self.
Alternatively, among the five aggregates, they grasp one aggregate as the self and the remaining aggregates as what belongs to the self.

Those who cling to annihilationism or eternalism either grasp at all phenomena as non-existent, thereby giving rise to the view of nihilism, or they grasp at all phenomena as existent, thereby giving rise to the view of eternalism.
The Middle Way is precisely the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);

because the eight consciousnesses perpetually evolve like a torrential stream, their constancy means they are not annihilated, and their evolution means they are not eternal. To now cling to annihilationism or eternalism is to lose the Middle Way.
Regarding those who perceive what is not a cause as a cause: they regard that which is not a cause for nirvana as being a cause.

This includes such practices as plucking out one's hair, fumigating the nose, lying on thorns, casting oneself into ashes, or observing the precepts of cattle, dogs, and so forth—various ascetic practices that are devoid of benefit.
Those who grasp at the coarse as supreme cling only to their own views as correct, regarding all others as false. Even if they were to encounter a Buddha, they would not believe or accept him.
This is like those who carry hemp as if it were treasure while casting aside gold without a second thought. Regarding "carrying hemp and discarding gold":
long ago, two men entered a mountain, each carrying a load of hemp. By chance, they encountered countless bolts of fine cloth along the way. One of them was wise...
The wise man said, "I shall discard my load of hemp and take the cloth. One foolish man said, "The road I have traveled carrying this is long;

it is indeed a load of hemp. We have not gone far yet. Then they saw countless pieces of white silver. The wise man discarded the cloth and took up the silver, while the foolish man continued as before to carry the hemp.
As they went forward, they again saw countless pieces of gold. The wise man discarded the silver and took up the gold, while the foolish man continued as before.
Those who merely carry hemp, who rely solely on their own views and refuse to follow others, are for the most part like this.
Denying cause and effect and falling into a nihilistic emptiness, they do not believe that performing good leads to happiness or that performing evil leads to suffering;

instead, they claim that all things—good and evil, suffering and happiness—are entirely empty. They fail to understand that there is no self, no agent, and no experiencer, yet they speak of good and evil.

The karma of these [views] does not perish. Because one falls into a vacuous emptiness and gives rise to the view of annihilationism, each of the five aggregates—form and so forth—possesses four propositions.
When these are applied across the three periods of time, sixty positions are formed. For example, regarding the aggregate of form:
(1) the self is large and form is small; (2) the self is within form; (3) the self is large and form is small; (4) form is within the self. Or else, [the self and form are identical].
"Form is the self; apart from form is the self. Since form is thus, the other four aggregates are likewise so. These five and four together constitute twenty propositions.
When these are applied across the three time periods, they become sixty propositions.
The Commentary states: "That which is slightly more heavy and sluggish than the former arises only when these five fetters (pañca-kaṣāya) encounter their respective objects;
this is unlike the five sharp faculties (pañca-tīkṣṇa), which arise as soon as they touch [an object] because they are so subtle and rapid."

As for the division into ninety-eight [afflictions]: there are eighty-eight afflictions of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). These are formed by taking the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and calculating their increase or decrease across the four truths of the three realms, resulting in eighty-eight.
Specifically, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the ten underlying tendencies are fully present under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*);

there are seven underlying tendencies each under the truths of origin (*samudaya*) and cessation (*nirodha*), excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and there are eight underlying tendencies under the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), excluding the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes.
Under the Four Truths of the [Desire Realm], these combine to form thirty-two. Under the Four Truths of the two upper realms, all other factors are the same as in the Desire Realm;
however, because the latent tendency of hatred (*pratigha-anuśaya*) is excluded from each truth, each realm has twenty-eight, totaling fifty-six for the two upper realms.

Combined with the previous thirty-two, this totals eighty-eight. To these are further added the ten latent tendencies of the afflictions of deliberation (*vicikitsā-kleśa*), namely: desire... [text truncated].
The afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride in the [desire] realm, together with greed, delusion, and pride in the two upper realms, constitute ninety-eight [afflictions].
To elaborate further on how these become eighty-four thousand: the ten *anusayas* (latent proclivities), when mutually combined, form one hundred;

multiplied across the ten dharma-realms, they become one thousand; with the seven branches of body and speech, they become seven thousand; spanning the three periods of time, they total twenty-one thousand; and when each of the four mental states [of the four modes of birth] is applied...
When these twenty-one thousand [afflictions] are combined, they total eighty-four thousand;
by applying the eighty-four thousand codes of discipline (*vinaya*) as their antidotes, eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates are established.

Regarding the manifestation of the three calamities: first is the minor triad of calamities. Initially, there is famine; when the human lifespan has decreased to thirty years, the heavens do not send down rain.
Due to this great drought, grasses and vegetables do not grow, such that even the desire to see water cannot be fulfilled.
How much more so regarding food and drink? For this reason, the number of people in the world who die of famine is immeasurable.
Second is pestilence: when the human lifespan decreases to twenty years, there will be a great pestilence with all manner of diseases.
All these arise. For this reason, the number of people in the world who die from pestilence is immeasurable.
Third, when the human lifespan diminishes to ten years due to the calamity of weapons, people engage in mutual strife;
grasping at grass and wood, these immediately become swords and spears, and they slaughter one another. For this reason, the number of people in the world who die by the sword is immeasurable.
Their number is immeasurable. Regarding the two great and three minor calamities: first is the calamity of fire. This refers to the time when the kalpa is destroyed;
seven suns appear, whereby the great earth and Mount Sumeru gradually crumble and disintegrate, and the four great oceans of water gradually evaporate until they are exhausted.
The great trichiliocosm, as well as the heavens of the first dhyāna, are all completely incinerated without exception;
this is called the calamity of fire. Second is the calamity of water, which occurs below the first dhyāna heaven.

After the world has been destroyed by seven successive cycles of the calamity of fire and has subsequently re-formed, during the period of the kalpa of destruction, heavy rains gradually descend, with drops as large as chariot axles, further augmented by the earth...
The water wheel descends, surging and boiling upward until it fills the entire trichiliocosm, reaching as far as the Second Dhyāna Heaven.
Everything is destroyed, like salt dissolving in water; this is called the calamity of water. Third is the calamity of wind:
below the Second Dhyāna Heaven, after seven successive cycles of the calamity of water, the world is reconstituted. Furthermore, at the time of the kalpa of destruction, from the winds below—
Upon the wheel [of the world], fierce winds arise; furthermore, because the karmic force of sentient beings is exhausted, winds are generated everywhere.
These blow and strike everything from the great trichiliocosm up to the third dhyāna heaven, sweeping it all away until nothing remains. This is called the calamity of wind.
Furthermore, one should know that fire burns the first dhyāna fifty-six times, water submerges the second dhyāna seven times, and [wind...]
There is one cycle for each of the three dhyānas; taken together, there are sixty-four cycles. These are all categorized according to their kind:
hatred brings about calamities of fire, greed brings about calamities of water, and delusion brings about calamities of wind.
The Commentary states: "To falsely reckon a sovereign as the self constitutes the view of self. "Falsely reckoning" means to give rise to false conceptualization.
"Sovereign" refers to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). This is the conceptually constructed grasping at a self (*vikalpa-ātmagrāha*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says:

"The conceptually constructed grasping at a self arises due to the power of external conditions in the present; it does not coexist with the body. It must depend upon false teachings and false conceptualizations before it can arise."
Therefore, it is called "discrimination. It exists only within the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

To perceive the self as one calculates—namely, that the self is identical with form, that the self is separate from form, that the self is large while form is small, that form is within the self, that the self is large while form is small, or that the self and form are equal—all such views constitute the discrimination of the self arising from the instructions of false teachers.
"That which takes the innate sovereign as its object is the innate pride of 'I'. "Innate" (*sahaja*) is said in contrast to the conceptual (*vikalpita*);

it arises simultaneously with birth, rather than being produced through forceful reflection or deliberation. "Sovereign" refers to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). This is precisely the innate grasping at a self. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The innate grasping at a self, from time beginningless, due to the internal causal power of false habitual tendencies, is constantly associated with the body..."
Both [types of pride] operate spontaneously without depending on false teachings or false discrimination; therefore, they are called "innate" (*sahaja*). These are further divided into two types:

first, that which is constantly continuous, residing in the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*); second, that which is intermittent, residing in the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). This is it. There are seven types of pride regarding the self:
first, the pride of self (*asmimāna*); second, pride (*māna*); third, excessive pride (*adhimāna*); fourth, pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*); fifth, overweening pride (*abhimāna*); sixth...
The pride of inferiority and the seven types of false pride—these seven all arise based on the mark of self (*ātman*). They all consist of conceiving oneself;
thus, one does not accept instruction. They exist from birth and constitute the innate self (*sahaja-ātman*).
Commentary: The eighth consciousness is precisely the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). "Seeds" refers to the seeds themselves;

that is to say, within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), there are specific functional capacities that directly produce their own respective fruits. Regarding the phrase "specific functional capacities," the commentary explains: "Directly producing their own fruits" means that from their own seeds, they directly produce manifesting fruits.
"Specific functional capacities" indicates that these seeds are not of a single kind. However, this...

The seeds, the eighth consciousness, and the fruits produced by them are neither identical nor different. Their essence is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), while their fruit is the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).
From the perspective of the consciousness-essence, the seeds function as its activity; from the perspective of the manifest fruit, the seeds function as its cause.

Therefore, these three dharmas, according to principle, ought to be neither identical nor different. The *Zongjing* states: "The fundamental consciousness is the essence; the seeds are its function. The seeds are the cause."
That which is produced is the fruit. These three principles should be understood as neither identical nor different.

Regarding "that which is drawn forth by karma," this refers to the arising of wholesome, unwholesome, and other states according to the power of past causes; it is when their functional capacity is determined that they constitute seeds.

External form refers to the breath and warmth; it belongs to the eighth consciousness’s *sākāra-bhāga* (objective aspect). Internal mind refers to the eighth consciousness in its active state (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*);

it belongs to the eighth consciousness’s *darśana-bhāga* (subjective aspect). By the power of seeds and karma, these three maintain one another without dispersing; this is called the non-interruption of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

First, they do not support one another. Whether the warmth leaves the body, or the inhalation and exhalation cease, or the separation of the physical form is seen—this is called the severance of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Commentary: These five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) are stated here according to their results; that is to say, the five turbidities explained in the preceding text are, for the time being, [treated as such].
This is explained from the perspective of the result (*phala*), and is not like what is taught in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which applies it to both cause and result.

As for those who correlate this with the "three subtleties" (*san-xi*), these are various masters who explain the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) by means of the three subtleties and six grossnesses (*liu-cu*).
As for those who correlate it with the "five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*), this is Guishan’s approach, which defines the five turbidities based on the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates.
"Meaning is also not different" means that although the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) differ, their underlying principle (*arthanaya*) is without distinction.

Regarding the "three subtleties" and so forth, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because one does not know that the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is one, the mind arises through non-awakening (*abodhi*), and thus there is thought.
Based on this non-awakening, three kinds of marks arise: first, the mark of the karma of ignorance (*avidyākarma*)."

First is the characteristic of appearance (*nimitta-lakṣaṇa*): because it relies on non-awakening (*a-vibodha*), the mind moves; this is called karma. When there is awakening, there is no movement. Where there is movement, there is suffering, for the fruit does not depart from its cause.
Second is the characteristic of the capacity to see (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*): because it relies on movement, there is the capacity to see. Without movement, there is no seeing.
Third is the characteristic of the objective realm (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*): because it relies on the capacity to see, the objective realm falsely manifests. Apart from seeing, [it does not exist].

There is no objective realm (*viṣaya*). Because there is the condition of an objective realm, six kinds of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) further arise: First is the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Based on the objective realm, the mind gives rise to discrimination between what is pleasant and what is unpleasant. Second is the characteristic of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*). Based on cognition, feelings of pleasure and pain arise;
the mind gives rise to thoughts that correspond [to these feelings] without interruption. Third is the characteristic of grasping (*upādāna-lakṣaṇa*)...
1. The characteristic of appearance (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*). Based on the continuity of conditioned objects, it sustains suffering and pleasure because the mind gives rise to attachment.

2. The characteristic of false imagination (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*). Based on deluded grasping, it discriminates the characteristics of provisional names and words. 3. The characteristic of the arising of karma (*karma-samutthāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Based on names, one seeks out names and grasps at them, thereby creating various kinds of karma. 4. The suffering bound by karma (*karma-bandhana-duḥkha*). [The text continues: ...the suffering of being fettered by karma.

The characteristic of retribution (*vipāka-lakṣaṇa*): Because one receives retribution based on karma and lacks self-mastery, the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) is assigned to the characteristic of karma.
"Eon" (*kalpa*) refers to time. The nature of the mind is fundamentally pure, yet from the moment it is first stirred by ignorance (*avidyā*), it becomes turbid;
hence it is called the turbidity of the eon. Now, the characteristic of karma is likewise: when ignorance first arises, it constitutes the characteristic of karma.

Therefore, next, the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) is assigned to the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*). "View" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the subject that sees and the object that is seen. Previously, in the stage of the causal phase (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), the subject and object were not yet differentiated;

subsequently, the evolving and manifesting consciousnesses are established. Although they lack conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), the subject and object are perfectly distinct, such that the mind and its objects are fully present. For this reason, [the defilement of views is assigned].

The turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) corresponds to the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the manifesting consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Next, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are correlated with the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*), as well as grasping (*upādāna*) and conceptualizing names (*nāma-saṃketa*).

Afflictions do not transcend the two types of grasping: the grasping at self (*ātma-grāha*) and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Furthermore, these are divided into the innate (*sahaja*) and the discriminative (*vikalpita*).

Here, cognition corresponds to the innate aspect of phenomena; continuity corresponds to the discriminative aspect of phenomena; grasping corresponds to the innate aspect of self; and names correspond to the discriminative aspect of self.
I. Since all four characteristics belong to the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).

Next, regarding the assignment of sentient beings (*sattva*) to the characteristic of the arising of karma: "sentient beings" refers to those for whom many dharmas arise and who undergo birth in various places;
hence they are called "sentient beings. It is because they perform wholesome, unwholesome, and immovable karma that they subsequently evoke these manifold dharmas in various locations.
Regarding "because of birth":

next, as for the correlation of the defilement of lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) with the suffering of karmic bondage, the defilement of lifespan is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of the eight consciousnesses.
It serves as the presiding lord of the collective retribution for a single lifetime of sentient beings; being bound by karma, its duration is fixed, and thus liberation cannot be attained.

Regarding the correlation of the *kalpa-kāṣāya* (the turbidity of the eon) with the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "When you perceive empty space pervading the worlds of the ten directions, space and seeing are not distinguished.
There is space but no substance; there is seeing but no awareness. These interweave to falsely constitute [this state]. This is the first layer, called the turbidity of the eon.
This is precisely the correlation of the *kalpa-kāṣāya* with the aggregate of form. Because they "interweave to falsely constitute" [reality], this is space and...

The interaction of the perceived object and the perceiving subject falsely constitutes the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha). This is precisely what is called the turbidity of the kalpa (kalpa-kaṣāya). Is this not, indeed, the correlation of the turbidity of the kalpa with the aggregate of form?

For the four great elements, the sense organs, and their objects are all collectively termed the aggregate of form; it is at the time when emptiness and the seeing-faculty are not yet distinguished that this occurs.

When the faculties and their objects are in total confusion, how can this not be the turbidity of the eon? To differentiate between space and seeing is fundamentally without boundary; thus it is said that "space and seeing are not distinguished.

Using space, which has no substance, to weave together seeing, which has no awareness, and using seeing, which has no awareness, to weave together space, which has no substance—this is to falsely perceive space while both are devoid of reality. This profoundly still, perfect, and luminous mind becomes dull...
The emptiness becomes turbid, thereby forming the kalpa-turbidity; this nature constitutes the turbidity.

Next, regarding the assignment of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) to the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states: "Your body currently takes the four great elements as its substance.

Seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are congested and rendered obstructive; water, fire, wind, and earth revolve and cause sensation and cognition. Interwoven together, they falsely constitute [this state]. This is it.
The second layer is called the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*). This is precisely the correlation of the turbidity of views with the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
It is formed through mutual entanglement and delusion; that is, the six sense organs and the four great elements entangle one another and delusively form the aggregate of sensation.

Because it perceives objects and undergoes reception, it muddies the true nature; thus it is named the turbidity of views. Is this not indeed the correlation of the turbidity of views with the aggregate of sensation?
Next, regarding the correlation of the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) with the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):

the Sūtra states, "Furthermore, within your mind, that which recollects, cognizes, and rehearses—its nature gives rise to cognition and vision, and its capacity manifests toward the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). Apart from the objects, it has no form; apart from awareness, it has no substance.

These forms interweave to falsely constitute [existence]. This third layer is called the turbidity of afflictions. This is precisely the correlation of the turbidity of afflictions with the aggregate of perception. By means of these forms...

They are woven together through delusion. One should know that when the faculty of perception and the six sense objects interweave, they falsely constitute the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Once one becomes attached to what is perceived, the agitation becomes even greater than before. Since this clouds the true nature, it is called the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).
Is this not, then, the assignment of afflictions to the aggregate of perception?

Next, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) is correlated with the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, your births and deaths ceaselessly proceed day and night;
your cognitions and perceptions constantly desire to remain in this world, while the movement of karma perpetually shifts the lands.

These weave together to form delusion—this is the fourth layer called the turbidity of sentient beings. This is precisely the correlation of the turbidity of sentient beings with the aggregate of formations. By means of these characteristics...

Weaving delusion into completion: this refers to the interweaving of cognition and perception with the movement of karma, whereby the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is falsely established.
Through the provisional conjunction of departure and remaining, the true nature is turbidized; this is precisely what is called the "turbidity of sentient beings" (*sattva-kaṣāya*).

Is it not the case that the turbidity of sentient beings is thus assigned to the aggregate of formations, and the turbidity of life (*āyuṣ-kaṣāya*) is subsequently assigned to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)? As the Sūtra says: "Your seeing and hearing originally possess no distinct natures; [they are merely] the various dusts..."

Separated by an unaccountable difference from ordinary beings, they recognize one another within their natures yet oppose one another in their functions; the standards for identity and difference are lost, and they interweave to form delusion.
This fifth stage is called the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*). This is the correlation of the turbidity of life with the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
It is through mutual entanglement and delusion that these are formed as one and yet as distinct, like warp and woof woven together to constitute the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Consciousness abides when life exists, and when consciousness departs, life ceases. That which turbidly obscures the true nature is called the turbidity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).
Is this not, indeed, the assignment of the turbidity of life to the aggregate of consciousness?

The explanations provided differ slightly, yet their meaning is largely the same: apart from the nine aspects there are no five aggregates, and apart from the five aggregates there are no nine aspects;
thus, while the names differ, the substance is one.
Commentary: "Turbid, evil, and unwholesome" means that "turbid" refers to the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), and "unwholesome" refers to the ten unwholesome actions.
"The five sufferings" refers to the five realms of existence (*pañca-gati*), as they are not states of bliss.

Sub-commentary: Regarding the sufferings of the five realms: the suffering of hell is being burned and boiled; the suffering of hungry ghosts is hunger and thirst; the suffering of animals is slaughter...

The suffering of severance; the eight kinds of suffering in the human realm; and the suffering of the five signs of decline in the heavenly realms. This first section explains the five sufferings by showing that the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) are not sources of happiness.
Alternatively, regarding the "five pains," "five burnings," and "five evils": the five evils refer to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and [malicious intent].
Drinking alcohol. The five pains are the immediate retributions in this life for the five evils; the five burnings are the karmic retributions in the three miserable realms for the five evils.
This sequence explains the five sufferings as being summoned by the retributions for the five transgressions.

Regarding those whose bodies belong to the four modes of birth: the egg-born arise from thought; the womb-born arise from emotion; the moisture-born are produced by contact; and the transformation-born respond to separation.
Through these emotions, thoughts, contacts, and separations, they undergo mutual transformations; all the karma they receive follows them as they soar or sink.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "initial enlightenment is darkly identical to original enlightenment" and so forth: that the Buddhas have long since attained realization is the meaning of original enlightenment;

that Śākyamuni has now attained realization is the meaning of initial enlightenment. When initial enlightenment is within the bonds of affliction (*saṃsāra*), it is called "original"; when original enlightenment emerges from those bonds, it is called "initial.
That initial and original are non-dual is the meaning of the mutual praise among all Buddhas.
Śākya signifies great compassion that benefits sentient beings; this is the meaning of illumination. Muni signifies great wisdom that penetrates the principle; this is the meaning of stillness.
The simultaneity of stillness and illumination is the meaning of the Benevolent One’s silent composure.

The five turbidities have the meaning of defilement; bodhi has the meaning of non-defilement. To be undefiled while following conditions, and to follow conditions while remaining undefiled—this is the meaning of the five turbidities as bodhi.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit," etc.: "The cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit" means that the beginning is itself the fundamental source. "The fruit penetrates to the source of the cause" means that the fundamental source is itself the beginning.
Function does not depart from essence; thus, the Capable Sage (Śākyamuni) is itself quiescent silence. Essence does not depart from function; thus, quiescent silence is itself the Capable Sage.

Therefore, know that what follows is explained below. Since it speaks of the two types of awakening—initial and fundamental—as being "this Buddha" and "that Buddha," and as the tranquil illumination of one's own mind, it is not only this Buddha who is the tranquil illumination of one's own mind;
rather, this Buddha and that Buddha both ultimately return to the tranquil illumination of one's own mind.
This is because initial awakening and fundamental awakening are the very essence of tranquil illumination. Furthermore, since it says "stained while unstained," this refers to Bodhi.
To explain the meaning of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*): being defiled yet undefiled is the meaning of the five turbidities as bodhi.
Thus, afflictions (*kleśa*) and bodhi do not transcend the single thought-moment of awakening or delusion.

Since this Buddha and that Buddha both return to one’s own mind, and afflictions and bodhi are not separate from a single thought-moment, then the Original Teacher is myself, and I am bodhi. Since I am bodhi, I have attained bodhi.
Who is it that can attain? What is it that is attained? The *Chao* [Commentary] states:
"The ten kinds of things difficult to believe generally do not exceed the two maladies of madness and folly.
The first eight concern the fool who, by exalting the sacred realm beyond reach, does not believe. The ninth concerns the madman who, by despising the West, does not believe. The tenth..."

Both types are combined here: because the ignorant hear that principle is non-existent, they doubt and do not believe; because the deluded hear that phenomena are existent, they doubt and do not believe.
The Commentary states: "Desiring to cause all sentient beings to hear and know the Dharma that is difficult for all the world to believe" refers to Mañjuśrī’s words addressed to Maitreya.
This means that what was taught forty years prior—namely, that there are three vehicles (*yāna*) and five natures (*gotra*)—was easily believed by all people.
However, if one were to say that the three vehicles are in fact a single vehicle and the five natures are in fact a single nature, people would [not believe it].

It is difficult to believe. Ordinarily, it is taught that only the Buddha alone attains perfect enlightenment; now you say that even Arhats of the Hīnayāna shall all become Buddhas, which people find hard to believe.
Furthermore, it is ordinarily taught that one only becomes a Buddha after practicing through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
Now it is said that "the mind itself is Buddha," which is difficult for people to believe.

Since I now wish to expound this difficult-to-believe Dharma, desiring to cause sentient beings to realize the principle that the mind is Buddha—without duality and without triad—I have manifested this auspicious omen.
This sutra is difficult to hear; it is likewise difficult to believe and accept. This is the "Chapter on the Dharma Master," spoken by the Buddha to Bhaiṣajyarāja.
It is because those who practice the bodhisattva path must see, hear, read, and recite this sutra before they can truly and skillfully practice the way of a bodhisattva.
Those who seek the Buddha-way, whether they see or hear this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, and having heard it, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it,
shall draw near to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Those who, upon hearing this sutra spoken, have their minds immediately become deranged and harbor doubts and disbelief, do not possess the faculties required for the Mahāyāna and are unable to uphold or recite it.
The merit they would otherwise inspire cannot be heard by ordinary people; were they to hear it, they would inevitably doubt and disbelieve.
This is because the meaning and intent of this sutra, as well as its karmic fruition, are inconceivable. Because they are not startled...
Regarding "to hear it without fear is rare": the Dharma of the Mahāyāna is inherently difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Those who lack the faculties of a Mahāyāna vessel will inevitably be struck with alarm, doubt, and dread upon suddenly hearing this Dharma.
That one can hear this Dharma and yet remain without fear is truly rare.

Commentary: Regarding the phrase "one cannot seek it with a mind," its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not existent; to have a mind [seeking it] is to fall into the attachment of superimposition (*samāropa*).
Its intrinsic nature is not non-existent; to be without a mind is to fall into the attachment of denial (*apavāda*). Its intrinsic nature is beyond the characteristics of verbal expression;

to employ language is to fall into conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*). Its intrinsic nature is beyond the characteristics of mental objects; to remain in silent silence is to fall into the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Regarding those of superior virtue on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa who ultimately suffered defeat: this refers to the five thousand who withdrew from their seats at the assembly on Vulture Peak, as well as those such as Śākyamuni who were not present at the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
"Defeat" (paibuk) means that when an army is defeated in battle, it is called "north" (buk).
Regarding the "Vajra of the Han Land" who first sought to extinguish the Southern School: De Shan was known as Zhou Vajra.

Disbelieving the doctrine of the Southern School’s direct transmission of the pointing-out instruction, he composed the *Qinglong Chao* (Blue Dragon Commentary) and set out directly for the South, intending to destroy the Southern School.

On the road, he encountered an old woman selling *dianxin* (refreshing snacks). The woman asked, "What is that you are carrying? He replied, "The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Qinglong [Commentary].*"
The Commentary states: The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāpāramitā Sūtra* says, "The three minds cannot be apprehended.

Which mind did the Venerable One wish to point out? Mazu had no reply, so he went to Longtan to continue their inquiry and debate. Upon this, he attained sudden enlightenment and said: "To exhaust all my verbal eloquence is like placing a single hair in the vast void;
to exhaust all the world's pivotal mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a great abyss. Thereupon, he burned the *Qinglong Commentary*.
The *Yun Chao* states:

"As for the accounts of exhausting the preaching of all other sutras, tossing Mount Sumeru with one's hand, or shaking the great trichiliocosm with one's foot, these belong to the 'Many Treasures' chapter (*Prabhūtaratna-parivarta*), where the Tathāgata universally addresses the great assembly.
To exhaustively preach all other sutras, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, is indeed difficult."
These matters are all discourses adapted to the capacities of beings; people can easily believe them, so they are not difficult to accomplish.

If one were to take Mount Sumeru in the palm of the hand and hurl it beyond the world, or move the great trichiliocosm with a toe and cast it into another land—though these are indeed difficult feats—they could still be performed by those possessing supernatural powers and spiritual strength, and thus would not yet be considered difficult. Only in this degenerate age...
To proclaim this sutra is the most difficult of tasks, because people will not believe it, because they will give rise to resentment and jealousy, because they will subject one to insults and abuse,
because they will inflict blows with sticks and staves, and because, if one lacks a great vow, one will succumb to despondency and retreat.
That this sutra is now difficult to expound is likewise so: sentient beings have minds of self-conceit that are loftily elevated; their ignorance is firm and thick;
they are unwilling to believe or accept it; and they frequently give rise to resentment and jealousy—it is just like this.
Regarding those who are stubborn and difficult to subdue: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that in this Sahā world, people are for the most part corrupt and evil;
they harbor overweening pride (*adhimāna*), their merit is meager, and their minds are turbid with anger, deceitful, and insincere.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that the sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform; therefore, the Buddha speaks harsh words to subdue them, saying, "This is hell."

"These are hungry ghosts; these are animals," and so on, until it says: "For example, just as elephants and horses that are obstinate and untamable must be subjected to various forms of pain and torment before they can be tamed, so too, for sentient beings who are stubborn and difficult to transform, one can only bring them into the discipline through words of all kinds of harsh admonition."
Commentary: "The simultaneous fusion of mind and object" refers to the meaning of practicing these two difficult tasks. Attaining the Way is the thorough realization of the internal mind;
preaching the Dharma is the transformation of external objects for others. Thus, "mind" signifies the meaning of attaining the Way, and "object" signifies the meaning of preaching the Dharma.
Now, within the nature, mind and object are simultaneously fused; this is the meaning of the two difficult tasks being carried out in tandem.
Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the mind follows [objects]," when the mind arises in pursuit of objects, the mind has no self-nature;

the essence of the mind is fundamentally quiescent. To attain the Way is to thoroughly awaken to this inner mind. Now, since the essence of the mind is fundamentally quiescent, that which is "attained" is non-attainment—this is called attaining Bodhi.
Since objects manifest in accordance with the mind, objects have no self-nature; the essence of objects is inherently empty. To preach the Dharma is to transform others.
Regarding external objects: if the essence of the object is itself empty, such that there is no dharma that can be spoken of, this is called "preaching the Dharma.
When the internal mind and external objects mutually cancel each other out and both vanish, the two modes of awakening—awakening oneself and awakening others—are both extinguished.

Commentary: The Bodhisattva’s true and conventional realities are fused as one, responding to sentient beings according to their capacities. Ordinary beings are attached to the conventional and do not penetrate the true;
those of the Two Vehicles are immersed in the true and do not engage with the conventional. They are like the six blind men carrying a single plank, each grasping only one side.

The Bodhisattva, however, fuses the true and the conventional, neither lingering in birth-and-death nor dwelling in nirvana. Thus, they may manifest as those of the Two Vehicles in accord with the true, or they may manifest...

The six classes of ordinary beings share commonality with the mundane world; they respond to capacities according to their respective types and are not comprised solely within the category of bhikṣus.

As for asuras, there are four types in detail: first, those born from eggs, which are subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati); second, those born from a womb, which are subsumed under the realm of humans (manuṣya-gati);

third, those who exist through transformation, which are subsumed under the realm of devas (deva-gati); and fourth, those who exist due to moisture, which belong to the realm of animals (tiryagyoni-gati).
[This is] the summary.
Commentary: "Ultimate perfection" refers to the statement "having finished preaching the sutra.

If one says that the Tathāgata is about to leave the Dharma seat because he has finished preaching the sutra, this refers to the sutra of written teachings; it is not the sutra of self-nature. The sutra of self-nature, however, begins with...

The tail is perfectly round; there is nothing lacking and nothing superfluous. Before the teaching for those of appropriate capacity has been concluded, the meaning of "pervasively containing all worlds" is as follows:
if one were to take the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas, to be "all worlds," this refers only to the world of sentient beings and not to the world of perfect enlightenment.
The world of perfect enlightenment encompasses both the ordinary and the holy.
"Thoroughly satisfied, utterly fulfilled. Before the *ghanṭā* (wooden gong) had even been struck, humans and devas had all assembled.
Regarding the "Excerpt on the Wondrous Head Who Strikes the Gong": One day, when the World-Honored One ascended the seat, Mañjuśrī struck the gong and said:
"Observe clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King. Thereupon, the World-Honored One descended from the seat. Tian Tong’s verse says: "A single piece of truth..."
Do you see the wind? The subtle mother of transformation employs the shuttle of principle; she weaves ancient brocade containing the image of spring.
What can be done about the Lord of the East leaking it all away?

As for the one who struck the sounding block at the Twin Trees—it was Emperor Wu of Liang. He invited the Great Being Fu to lecture on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The Great Being ascended the seat.
With a single strike of the ritual tablet, he immediately descended from his seat. The Emperor was struck with astonishment. Master Zhigong asked, "Your Majesty, do you understand?
The Emperor replied, "I do not understand. Master Zhigong said, "The Great Being has finished preaching the sutra."

Commentary: Regarding "mindfulness of all Buddhas and mindfulness of all dharmas": "all Buddhas" refers to ultimate principle (*tattva*), which is what is called the equal *dharmakāya* pervading all places.
"All dharmas" refers to ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), which is what is called the perfect secret treasury and the immeasurable, wondrous gates of Dharma.
Upon the first stage (*bhūmi*), one realizes the pervasive *dharmakāya*, which flows like the stream of the Dharma of Wondrous Enlightenment.
Because they connect [with the Dharma], they are able to recollect the teachings of all Buddhas and give rise to great joy.

Regarding the arising of joy through the turning away from all objective spheres (*viṣaya*): the Bodhisattva of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) realizes the threefold naturelessness (*trividhā niḥsvabhāvatā*).

They are forever free from the grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-grāha*) and do not cling to external objects. Furthermore, the conceptualization of grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) no longer manifests; therefore, it is said that they "turn away from" them.
Regarding "transcending all worldly realms and generating joy through intimacy with all Buddhas":
on the first stage (*bhūmi*), one attains non-conceptual mind (*nirvikalpa-citta*) and becomes congruent with the wisdom and activity of all Buddhas.
Relying solely on the power of the Dharma, one practices spontaneously; by perfuming *tathatā* (suchness) and extinguishing ignorance (*avidyā*), one proceeds.

Therefore, it is said that they draw near to all Buddhas. Furthermore, in a single moment of thought, the Bodhisattvas of this stage are able to reach all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception, making offerings to all Buddhas and requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma; hence, it is said that they draw close to all Buddhas.
The initial stage is also called "Joyful. In this stage, the bodhisattva primarily practices the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).

He bestows everything, both internal and external, as gifts. Upon seeing a beggar approach, his heart is filled with great joy, thinking, "I have gained a sublime benefit," for the recipient of the gift likewise rejoices.

The first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is also called "attaining boundless joy. This is because a Bodhisattva at this first stage, through faith, knows that all phenomena have been in *nirvāṇa* from the very beginning.
Furthermore, in this stage, one can accomplish the path through the eight aspects (*aṣṭākāra*), awakening oneself and awakening others.
Therefore, one attains boundless joy.

As for those who attain the joy of the Dharma according to their respective capacities: even those of the initial stage, ordinary beings at the lowest level, though unable yet to penetrate the principle to subdue afflictions or give rise to wholesome qualities, still derive the benefit of joy upon hearing the *loka-samvṛti-satya* (the worldly standpoint).

The Commentary states: "To give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is the first stage of the Perfect [Teaching] (the First Faith). To attain the purity of the Dharma-eye is the first dwelling of the Perfect [Teaching].
When one perceives the external world from afar and internally departs from defilement, then the Dharma-eye becomes perfectly luminous, free from all blemishes and obscurations.

'Anāgāmin' refers to the third fruit of the Tripitaka [Teaching]; in terms of the Perfect [Teaching], it corresponds to the sixth faith. 'The exhaustion of outflows and liberation of the mind' refers to the [third fruit of the] Tripitaka..."
Regarding the four fruits: according to the perfect teaching (*yuan*), this corresponds to the seventh stage of faith (*xin*).
As for "attaining non-retrogression," there are three types of non-retrogression: destroying the afflictions of views and thoughts (*jian-si*) is called non-retrogression in position;

destroying the afflictions of the sands of dust (*chen-sha*) is called non-retrogression in practice; and destroying ignorance (*wu-ming*) is called non-retrogression in mindfulness. What these forty billion bodhisattvas have attained also accords with this.
This corresponds to their respective magnitudes.
As for the six kinds of shaking, they are: trembling, rising, surging, quaking, roaring, and crashing. Three of these are forms; three are sounds.
Within the categories of form and sound, one example is cited from each; thus it is said, "trembling. To sway and oscillate without stability is called "moving.
To rise from below upward is called "arising. To suddenly leap up is called "surging. To produce a deep, rumbling sound is called "thundering.
To emit a fierce and powerful roar is called "roaring. To emit a crashing and resonant sound is called "striking. Together, there are eighteen marks.

Movement in one direction is called "movement. Movement in all four directions simultaneously is called "universal movement. Movement in all eight directions simultaneously is called "thorough universal movement.
The same applies to the remaining five [types of trembling]. Furthermore, direct movement is called "movement. Movement throughout the four continents is called "universal movement.
Movement throughout the great trichiliocosm is called "equal universal movement. The same applies to the lower five [types of shaking].

Non-retrogressive patience (*avivartika-kṣānti*) is precisely the patience of compliance (*anuloma-kṣānti*). Its stage is located within the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
This is explained in terms of the three patiences of the Pure Land. If explained in terms of the Path of Doctrine (*jiaodao*), it refers to the three patiences of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

This non-retrogressive patience is also identical to the patience of compliance, because this patience belongs to the Ground of Nature (*xingdi*), and one attains non-retrogression only upon reaching that ground. As for the five patiences of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), these are... [text truncated]

Non-retrogressive patience (*avaivartika-kṣānti*) is identical to patient acceptance through faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), because patient acceptance through faith belongs to the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), and those in the ten abodes have already attained non-retrogression.

Within the four patiences of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), this non-retrogressive patience is also identical to conforming patience (*anuloma-kṣānti*), for it is precisely during the seventh stage of faith (*saptama-śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching that one truly belongs to the state of non-retrogression.

He had never previously resolved [to attain enlightenment], but now he has for the first time begun to do so; this is precisely the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), or perhaps the initial dwelling (*vihāra*).
This is because the subsequent text mentions his gradual attainment of Buddhahood and his sharing the same name, "Wonderful Sound" (*Ghoṣadatta*).

Attaining the dharma-patience of receiving the prediction of enlightenment is the first stage of the Perfect [Teaching], because one obtains the light of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);
alternatively, it may be the eighth stage, because this is truly called the attainment of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
Commentary: "Entrusting" (zhūlèi) means taking this Dharma-gate and entrusting it to you, charging you with its propagation.
An ancient worthy said: "If you were not such a person, they would naturally not come to look up to you. Furthermore, regarding "entrusting":

This was the entrustment made by the Tathāgata’s golden mouth, intended for its widespread circulation. As for this repeated charge, the Bodhisattva now holds it suspended in his heart, never to forget or lose it.
The Commentary states: "To cause others to be instructed and to have them write down and uphold [the teaching]" refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*’s opening of five types of Dharma-preachers:
first, receiving and upholding (*udgrahaṇa-dhāraṇa*). "Receiving" refers to the power of faith; "upholding" refers to the power of mindfulness—this is precisely what is meant here by "to uphold.
Second, reading; third, reciting. "Reading" refers to facing the text; "reciting" refers to not forgetting it. These two are also subsumed within the present "to uphold. Fourth, explaining.
"Expounding" means to proclaim and explain; this refers to the present act of revealing [the teaching] for others. "Writing" refers to the present act of copying.
Regarding "transcribing" (*chao*):
to maintain other honored teachings through *dhāraṇī* (total retention) serves as the cause for the circulation of the doctrine and its principles. This is equivalent to "easy" (*yi*).
This is the meaning of the *Qian-yuan* (the Source of Qian) in the hexagrams. Indeed, there is fundamentally no duality between worldly and world-transcending principles.

As for worldly dharmas, they begin with the *Qian-yuan* providing the initial commencement; through the virtue of *zheng* (permanence), they gather and store [all things], serving as the mechanism for future development.
As for world-transcending dharmas, they begin from the first discourse of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and culminate in the final nirvana of Amitābha, serving as the transmission for subsequent kalpas.

If it were not for the fundamental principle of "the firm and constant" (gan-jin), the life-force of the world would be utterly extinguished; if it were not for Amitābha, the wisdom-life of those who transcend the world would all be severed.
Thus, this sutra and its underlying principle constitute the wisdom-life transmitted from Buddha to Buddha and the very source of the emergence of all sentient beings.
How could their significance be considered a minor cause or condition?
Commentary: "The self-nature is free from affliction; this is true joy and faithful acceptance.

If one says that they rejoice upon hearing the Dharma and accept it upon receiving the Dharma, this is merely being externally shifted by objective conditions; it is not true joy and faithful acceptance.
The meaning of the self-nature possessing afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is what constitutes true joy and faithful acceptance.
The self-nature is non-abiding; this is the meaning of "prostrating and departing.

If one speaks of rising with diligence to prostrate and then withdrawing from one's seat to depart, this is to be moved by the power of delusive conditions and winds; it is not true prostration and departure.
The self-nature is non-abiding and utterly devoid of root; this is true prostration and departure.
Commentary: Regarding "the afflictions are fundamentally quiescent," the previous statement that "the absence of affliction is the meaning of joy" implies that joy still remains;
yet joy is not itself the Land of Bliss. Now, however, since the afflictions are fundamentally quiescent and even joy is empty, who would not regard this land of suffering as the Land of Bliss?

The previous statement that "non-abiding" is the meaning of "going" still implies the existence of going; yet, this going is not a birth in another realm. Now, since coming is truly no-coming, what is there to go when one goes?
Thus, birth in another realm is ultimately no-birth. This is because those who are born in that land are themselves born through [the realization of] non-arising.
This is "being born in that land," which is not being born from one's own mind. Because there is no "birth" in being born in that land, it is not being born in that land;

rather, it is truly being born from one's own mind. Thereafter, without being asked, he speaks of himself: "The World-Honored One does not exempt me from this empty talk. Above this, he does not fail the Master who propagates the Dharma;
alone he takes responsibility for the occasion, and Śāriputra does not render the heavy entrustment solitary. Below this, he does not fail those who receive [the teaching].

I entrust this to you. Although principle is not outside of phenomena, and nature is at the very limit of form, if one were to seek the land of the nine lotuses of Ultimate Bliss as something external, or speak of "Mind-Only" while setting aside the name of Amitābha’s myriad virtues, or seek one's own nature apart from him, that would be like crossing a ford without knowing its location, or seeking fire by looking at a lamp.
Thus it is said: "Not knowing the pass or the ferry, one asks how to cross the river even while standing on this side. This was long ago...
One knows that the lamp is fire. It has been a long time since the rice was cooked.
[Note: *Saindhava* is a Sanskrit term; it has four meanings: salt, water, horse, and vessel. Only a wise minister is able to discern them.
For example, when the king is about to eat and calls for *saindhava*, one knows he requires salt. When the king is washing his hands or rinsing his mouth...
When he calls for *sindhava*, it is known that he requires water; when the king is engaged in various affairs and calls for *sindhava*, it is known that he requires a vessel;
and when the king goes out on an excursion and seeks *sindhava*, it is known that he requires a horse.
Other points may be understood by analogy: "Single-mindedness without distraction" is the Great Illuminating Mantra that severs ignorance and reveals one's own nature;

"rebirth in that land to ultimately attain Buddhahood" is the Unsurpassed Mantra; and "realizing the patience of non-arising, returning to the Sahā world to universally deliver sentient beings" is the Peerless Mantra.
