Commentary: "Self-nature emptiness" refers to the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. This is what is meant by "when one is empty, all are empty": there is no provisional, no middle, and nothing that is not empty.
"Self-nature existence" refers to the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. This is what is meant by "when one is provisional, all are provisional":
there is no empty, no middle, and nothing that is not provisional. "Self-nature neither existent nor empty" refers to the empty-and-non-empty [tathāgatagarbha].
The *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). This means that within one, all are contained; there is neither emptiness, nor the provisional, nor anything that is not the Middle Way.

The *Commentary* states: "When seeking the mind, it is utterly unobtainable. This refers to when the Second Patriarch visited the First Patriarch during the height of winter, when the accumulated snow reached his knees.
He stood firm and motionless. The First Patriarch asked, "What do you seek? The Second Patriarch replied, "I beg the Master to act for me..."
"Rest the mind. The First Patriarch said, "Bring forth your mind, and I shall rest it for you. The Second Patriarch replied, "I have searched for my mind, but it is utterly unobtainable.
This indicates that he had already attained the emptiness of the mind and reached the stage where the awakening-mind first arises—a state in which the mind has no initial characteristic.
That which the mind itself possesses without exception refers to the meaning that its own essence contains the great light of wisdom;
the meaning that it universally illumines the Dharma-realm; the meaning of true and authentic cognition; the meaning of intrinsic purity; the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
and the meaning of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty. It is thus endowed with qualities exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges.
To contemplate the Buddha-dharma until it is fully perfected without deficiency is what is called the Tathāgata-garbha of the Dharma-body.

That which should be maintained through total retention (*dhāraṇī*) yet remains free from even a speck of dust is that wondrous existence is itself true emptiness. Therefore, existence is precisely...
The existence of emptiness: that which arises from the absence of fundamental basis as the source of all phenomena is that true emptiness is itself wondrous existence.
Therefore, emptiness is the emptiness that is identical to existence; being identical to existence, it is not empty—this is non-emptiness as it truly is.
Being identical to emptiness, it is not existent—this is emptiness as it truly is. Thus, non-emptiness as it truly is and emptiness as it truly is do not depart from the one True Reality.
As with the mind, the single True Suchness-mind is precisely the Land of Tranquil Light and Purity; therefore it is said that "there is only this one mind," which is called the Pure Land.
*The Commentary on the Annotated Sub-commentary to the Amitābha Sūtra*, Fascicle Four (End).

Preface to the Re-engraved Commentary and Sub-commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra* I have often heard that the Ultimate Way is wordless and originally does not depend upon written characters; yet, as its wondrous meaning is profound and deep, it must await commentaries and sub-commentaries.
For this reason, Great Spiritual Friends, out of their earnest compassion, frequently employ their sublime skill and wisdom toward the scriptures.
Regarding the "Eye" (the title), this commentary on the phrases and characters is intended to enable those who study it for verification to directly realize the supreme point beyond.
Now, the *Sūtra of Amitābha* has already been annotated by the Great Being (Venerable Master) Lianchi, and subsequently expounded upon by the Great Master Gudé;
their elucidation of the wondrous meaning is even more intimate and direct. However, the old woodblocks no longer exist, and it is difficult to obtain a newly carved edition. [In] the Capital...

This master presides over a land of preeminent virtue, where great monasteries gather like clouds. Among those who have ascended the path, there are often sighs of lamentation regarding the loss of guidance.

(I, Cheng,) having personally witnessed these circumstances, could not bear that the meaning of the scriptures would be further obscured; thus, I sought out the original texts and once again entrusted them to the carver’s blade.
May this spread throughout the land so that those of like mind may investigate it with diligence and attain understanding. The Great Way is most subtle and wondrous;

once the true source is realized, there is no longer any dependence on language or written characters. In this way, one may not fail the great compassionate heart behind the sub-commentaries and expositions, thereby repaying [that kindness].

The Buddha’s grace is but one in ten thousand; yet we who share this same aspiration especially hope that wherever there are lost scriptures or missing commentaries, they shall be restored and preserved.
This alone constitutes the merit of ten million eight hundred thousand Ganges-sands. This is the preface.
In the seventeenth year of the Qianlong era, the year of Ren-shen, on an auspicious day in the second month,
this was re-carved by the junior disciple, the śramaṇa Weicheng.
